docs.title: fix(next/image): require valid ftyp box size when sniffing AVIF/HEIC
docs.body:
### What

`detectContentType` treated the first 4 bytes of the AVIF/HEIC signature as wildcards (`[0,0,0,0,'f','t','y','p',...].every((b,i) => !b || buffer[i] === b)`). Any file with `ftypavif` / `ftypheic` at bytes 4..11 was typed as `image/avif` / `image/heic`, e.g. an SVG starting with ` `. Since AVIF isn't subject to the `dangerouslyAllowSVG` check (which only applies to `image/svg*`), such a file ends up being passed to sharp as if it were AVIF.

### Fix

Match the ISO BMFF `ftyp` box properly: the size field (bytes 0-3, big-endian) must be a plausible value (>= 16, 4-byte aligned, <= 4096), a leading `<` (0x3c) is never accepted, and bytes 4..11 must equal `ftyp` + brand. Regular AVIF/HEIC files are unaffected.

With this change ` <svg ...>` is detected as `image/svg+xml` (via the existing fallback detector), so it's handled by the normal SVG policy.

### Tests

Added unit tests to `test/unit/image-optimizer/detect-content-type.test.ts` for the ` ` SVG and for non-ISO-BMFF data with an `ftypavif`/`ftypheic` brand at offset 4. Existing avif/heic tests still pass.

Fixes #100299 (also reported as #100298; both auto-closed by the issue template bot). Follow-up to GHSA-2464-fhr4-w9xw.

## For Contributors

### Fixing a bug
 
 
 

### Signed commits
 
 
 

## For Maintainers

### What?
Preserves written headers directly in `metadata.headers` during `prerenderToStream` when `res.sent` is `true`.

### Why?
Fixes #100255.

During background revalidation (`cacheComponents`, ISR, PPR), `res.sent` is already `true` because the initial request has been served. `patchSetHeaderWithCookieSupport` intentionally drops live writes to `res` to avoid write-after-send errors.

However, `setMetadataHeader` was reading values back via `res.getHeader(name)`, which returned `undefined`. As a result, when a redirect occurred during a background revalidation, `metadata.statusCode` was saved as `308`, but the `Location` header was omitted from `metadata.headers`. All subsequent cached responses returned a `308 Permanent Redirect` with no `Location` header.

### How?
Updated `setMetadataHeader` in `packages/next/src/server/app-render/app-render.tsx` to record the written header value directly into `metadata.headers` when `res.sent` is `true` instead of reading back from `res.getHeader()`.

Fixes #100255

docs.title: fix: discard stale cross-request 'use cache' fills joined after updateTag
docs.body:
Fixes #100345

A request that finds another request's in-flight `'use cache'` fill joins it and forks the result after checking only the root params. It never runs the staleness checks the leader path applies, so a fill that started before `updateTag()` expired one of its tags gets served after the expiration. That breaks read-your-own-writes: the issue's repro fails 10/10 with a concurrent reader.

This applies the same checks to the joined invocation's metadata before forking: `shouldDiscardCacheEntry`, plus the cache handler's per-tag expirations against the entry timestamp. If the joined fill is outdated, the request retries and becomes the leader instead of forking stale data. The implicit-tags expiration logic is factored into a `getImplicitTagsExpiration` helper shared by the leader path, so both paths compute it the same way.

The patch matches the reporter's tested fix from the issue (their repro passes 10/10 in all four modes with it). I traced the join path and the leader path in `use-cache-wrapper.ts` and verified the file still parses; I did not run the full repro suite here since it needs a built Next.js.

Note: my commit is unsigned. If the signed-commit check blocks this, let me know and I'll sort out signing.

docs.title: Fix stale route cache entries after an in-place deploy
docs.body:
Runtime route cache entries now live under a directory for the build that wrote them, so a build synced over an existing `.next` no longer serves the previous build's responses.

## Why

Since #99482, an entry in `.next/server/route-cache` is keyed only by route and pathname, and the first request for a prerendered page copies the prerender there. Deploys that sync a new build into the server's `.next` (rsync, DeployHQ) leave those runtime files in place, so the restarted server keeps serving the old HTML, whose chunks and Server Action IDs no longer exist.

## How

`FileSystemCache` now stores runtime entries under `route-cache/<hash of BUILD_ID and deployment ID>/`. The deployment ID is part of it because a configured `deploymentId` makes the build ID a constant. Cache keys don't change, so custom cache handlers aren't affected. When the build's directory has no entry, the prerender is read as before, including the scoped files an adapter build writes to `route-cache`. Directories of other builds are removed on the first lookup.

## Test

Added a production test that serves a page, keeps `route-cache`, rebuilds with a change, restores the folder and restarts, once with a generated build ID and once with a changing deployment ID. It fails on canary and passes with this change. Unit tests cover the build directory, the cleanup and adapter seeds. The reporter's repro now serves

docs.title: fix(jest): emit `with` for import attributes on Node.js 20.10 and later
docs.body:
### What?

With `next/jest` in ESM mode, a test that imports a module with attributes, such as `import data from './data.json' with { type: 'json' }`, fails to load on Node.js 22 and later with `SyntaxError: Unexpected identifier 'assert'`.

### Why?

`getBaseSWCOptions` sets `emitAssertForImportAttributes: true`, so the Jest transform prints the import with the old assert keyword, which Node.js 22 removed. Switching it to `with` everywhere isn't enough, because Node.js 20.9, the oldest version Next.js supports, only accepts assert.

### How?

`getJestSWCOptions` now picks the keyword from the running Node.js, assert before 20.10 and with from 20.10 on. The webpack loader options are unchanged.

I added a unit test that runs the transformed import in a child `node` process, and a case in `test/production/jest` that runs jest in ESM mode with a JSON import. Both fail on canary with Node.js 22 and pass with this change.

Fixes #87143

docs.title: Stamp FileSystemCache revalidations and entries with the monotonic clock
docs.body:
### What?
`FileSystemCache` dates tag revalidations and cache entries with the wall clock, but since #94457 `areTagsExpired` compares them against the monotonic clock (`performance.timeOrigin + performance.now()`).
When the wall clock runs ahead, a revalidation is dated in the future, so it's ignored and the old page keeps being served.

### Why?
I ran into this with `next start`, when our E2E tests kept getting stale pages after `revalidateTag`. In a fresh 16.4.2 app with the wall clock 5ms ahead, 30 out of 30 reads right after a revalidation returned the old page. With this change, it's 0 of 30.

The two clocks drift apart in ordinary setups, for example when NTP, a VM or WSL2 corrects the wall clock while the server runs.

### How?
Use the monotonic clock everywhere that `FileSystemCache` dates something, as `incremental-cache/index.ts` already does:

- `revalidateTag` and `set()` stamp with `performance.timeOrigin + performance.now()` instead of `Date.now()`.
- `set()` also stores that timestamp on disk, as `routeCacheLastModified` in the `.meta` file and as `lastModified` in the fetch cache entry. Reads used to take the file's mtime(wall-clock time).
  Files without a stored time, from `next build` or an older Next.js version, still fall back to the mtime. They were written before the server started, so their mtime is earlier than any revalidation it records.

docs.title: fix(next-routing): match dynamic API routes with locale group when i18n is enabled
docs.body:
## What?

When i18n is configured, dynamic API routes like `pages/api/blog/[slug].js` return a 404 when requested without a locale, for example `/api/blog/first`. Static API routes like `/api/hello` still work. This happens in adapters that use `@next/routing`, not when running the app with `next start`.

## Why?

Since #97327, the dynamic API route regex includes the `nextLocale` group, which expects a locale in the path. At the same time, `resolve-routes.ts` skips locale handling for `_next` and `api` routes. Because of this, `/api/blog/first` reaches the regex without a locale and the match fails.

The existing test didn't catch this because the regex used in that test didn't include `nextLocale`.

## How?

I added a small helper that first tries the normal route match. If that fails for an `/api/` route, it retries the match with the default locale added to the path. For example, `/api/blog/first` is retried as `/en/api/blog/first` when `en` is the configured default locale.

I kept the build output unchanged because #97327 added the locale group back for the Vercel adapter and reverting that change would bring back the issue fixed by #96935. Instead, the fix is applied in `@next/routing` so its routing behavior matches the generated regex. The helper is used at all three relevant call sites, and `basePath` is also handled.

## Tests

Added two unit tests for the dynamic AP

docs.body:
### What?

Fix `next dev` route discovery when Watchpack encounters `EPERM` during its initial directory scan.

When the initial scan fails for a route directory, Watchpack can omit valid page files from its known files and fail to emit a subsequent aggregation. This can cause the development server to hang during startup and leave affected routes returning `404` until another filesystem event or restart.

Fixes #100268

The existing initial-scan protection correctly prevents Next.js from publishing an incomplete route graph while Watchpack is still performing its normal initial scan.

- Recover snapshot page files that still exist but are missing from Watchpack's known files.

## Motivation

We want to use faster TypeScript alternatives such as tscrs (`tsc-rs`) without keeping the official `typescript` package installed solely for Next.js.

docs.title: [turbopack] Fix GC/eviction race by dropping task resurrection
docs.body:
## Summary

Fix a panic in development: `connect_child` → `increase_active_count` hit a task that GC had collected and eviction had already removed (`task is missing in memory or persistent storage`).

**The race.** GC marks tasks deleted under the snapshot exclusion. The exclusion is released before the snapshot commits the tombstones, and eviction then removes the deleted tasks with no exclusion. A concurrent `get_or_create_task` could read a deleted task's id from the in memory `task_cache`, eviction could remove the task, and the connect would then panic. Resurrection only worked if the connect finished before eviction.

**The fix.** A deleted task's id is never handed out again from the disk cache:
- GC removes collected tasks from `task_cache` while operations are still excluded.
- `task_by_type` skips candidates that are deleted or already gone. 
    - This is only possible for calls that race with snapshotting.  We treat deleted tasks as absent (in other words like the commit already happened).
- Eviction no longer touches `task_cache` for deleted tasks. (it doesn't need to, there are no entries)

**Resurrection is removed.**  The only thing resurrection is really saving is allocating a new `TaskId` (cells and edges are already gone), so it is simpler to remove this path.

Since nothing outside GC can legitimately reach a deleted task now, `ExecuteContext:

docs.title: fix(turbopack): emit client references for Route Handlers
docs.body:
### What?

A Route Handler that renders a Flight payload containing client components fails under Turbopack with "Could not find the module ... in the React Client Manifest": its client reference manifest has empty clientModules. The same route works with `webpack`.

### Why?

Two causes:

- Client references are chunked per enclosing server component entry. Route Handlers have none, so their references ended up in the list meant for the first layout segment and were dropped when there was no segment. 
- clientModules entries are only written when an SSR chunking context exists, and Route endpoints had SSR chunking disabled.

### How?

Client references now get one client chunk group, parented to the chunk group the module graph assigned to them, preferring the one created for the endpoint's entry over one created under a page.

Route endpoints now get an SSR chunking context (`crates/next-api/src/app.rs`), so clientModules gets written.

The fix does not have an impact on routes without client components: tested 200 Route Handlers without client components, 3 alternating builds each, all 1,400 route handler output files byte-identical. No impact either in build time.

turbo-tasks-backend: remove racy ungated collectibles_outdated_dependency test
docs.body:
### What?

Removes the`collector_is_not_re_executed_for_collectibles_it_has_not_read_yet` test from `turbo-tasks-backend`'s `collectibles_outdated_dependency.rs`. The other variant (`gated_collector_is_not_re_executed_for_collectibles_it_has_not_read_yet`) stays, and its behaviour is unchanged.

### Why?

The ungated test failed intermittently on canary with `take=…: executions after the input change` (left 2, right 1).

The cause is the race that the module's doc comment already described, not a backend bug. `State::set` invalidates its readers one by one. When the collector is invalidated before the emitter, it re-executes right away, its strongly consistent read of the still-clean source returns at once, and it reads the **old** collectibles. When the new collectibles arrive, it re-executes again, as it should. Instrumentation confirmed this in every failure: the extra execution read `count=200` but saw 5 collectibles. It reproduced in about 2 of 120 serial release runs under CPU load.

So "exactly one execution" can't be asserted without controlling that order.

I was not very confident about this test when it was added, so dropping it seems reasonable.

docs.title: Turbopack: dependent of an async module without top-level await can read its exports before they are registered (`x is not a function`, cached for the process lifetime)
docs.body:
https://github.com/yunsii/turbopack-async-race-repro
 

```bash
npm install
npx next build
node repro.cjs race        # n FAILED: (0 , d.D) is not a function   (a later import of n fails the same way)
node repro.cjs sequential  # n evaluated OK
```

`repro.cjs` loads the Turbopack server runtime and chunks produced by `next build` and drives two loaders deterministically. Module graph:

```
lib/root.mjs   top-level await                         -> async, hasAwait=true  (has its own queue)
lib/m.js       imports root, no top-level await         -> async, hasAwait=false (no queue of its own)
lib/n.js       imports m and calls m's export at module scope
```

**Current:** `n` throws `TypeError: (0 , d.D) is not a function` during module evaluation. The error is cached in the module cache, so every later import of `n` (and of everything that depends on it) fails for the lifetime of the process.

**Expected:** `n` waits until `m` has finished evaluating (as it does when the loads are sequential), or more generally: a module must never observe the exports of a dependency that has not finished evaluating unless they are part of an actual

remove Static render stage
docs.body:
Since the introduction of `NavigationStatic`, the `Static` stage hasn't really been very useful, but we kept it as a "marker" stage that delineates where a static prerender ends (after `NavigationStatic`, containing all the finished accumulators).

However, things get weird in the presence of caches with hanging inputs, because `createHangingInputAbortSignal` waits until `finalStage` (currently `Static`), which means that the keys for caches with hanging inputs would only finish in the `Static` stage. We were still running the `Static` stage in a separate task, before resolving the accumulators, so in practice this didn't cause any problems, but semantically we expect all userspace code to be done after the `NavigationStatic` task, and this behavior of caches breaks that expectation.

I don't want to risk any weird staging bugs because of this, so removing `Static` seems like the easy choice.

docs.title: Nest middleware-triggered instrumentation spans in the middleware span
docs.body:
## Summary

Top of a stack: #100349 → #100294 → #100324 → #100350 → this PR.

When a Node.js middleware entrypoint triggers registering `instrumentation.ts`, #100350 emits the lifecycle spans as siblings of `middleware GET`. This PR nests them inside the middleware span instead, since the middleware triggered registration:

```
route / page entrypoint (unchanged):
 [P →] GET /page (BaseServer.handleRequest, backdated to cover registration)
        ├─ load instrumentation module
        ├─ register instrumentation
        └─ prepare route module → render …

Node.js middleware entrypoint, no parent:
 GET (Next.request, backdated)
  ├─ middleware GET
  │   ├─ load instrumentation module
  │   └─ register instrumentation
  └─ GET /page

Node.js middleware entrypoint with host span / incoming traceparent P:
 P
  ├─ middleware GET
  │   ├─ load instrumentation module
  │   └─ register instrumentation
  └─ GET /page
```

### How

- The middleware adapter calls the deferred emitter first thing inside the `Middleware.execute` span, rather than right before starting it.
- When this request triggered registration, the middleware span is backdated to the request start so it covers registration; otherwise its timing is unchanged.
- The shared parent is still captured before entering the middleware span, so the middleware and the render stay siblings, and `traceparent` handling / forwarding

docs.body:
Closes #100398

### What?
Ensures that an empty `_rsc` search parameter (e.g. `/target?_rsc`) is forwarded to the rewritten destination URL for RSC requests.

### Why?
In `packages/next/src/server/web/adapter.ts`, the check:
```typescript
if (response && rewrite && isRSCRequest && rscHash) {
```
evaluates to `false` when `rscHash` is an empty string (`""`).

During Server Action `redirect()`, `createRedirectRenderResult` deletes `Next-Router-State-Tree` and fetches `/target?_rsc` with an empty hash, which is valid and expected per `base-server.ts` ("When no headers are present, expectedHash is empty string and client must send `_rsc` param").

When `rscHash` is dropped by middleware on external rewrites or proxy destinations that only see the rewritten URL:
1. The destination server sees no `_rsc` query param (`actualHash` is `null`).
2. `expectedHash === actualHash` (`"" === null`) fails.
3. The server responds with `307 -> /target?_rsc`.
4. The client/undici fetch follows the redirect back through the same rewrite, the hash is dropped again, causing an infinite redirect loop until undici aborts with `TypeError: fetch failed (redirect count exceeded)`.

### How?
Updated the condition to check `rscHash !== null`:
```typescript
if (response && rewrite && isRSCRequest && rscHash !== null) {
```

- When `_rsc` is present (even if empty `""`), it is preserved and set o

docs.title: Fix Pages Router `next/dynamic` rendering the loading state for concurrent SSR requests
docs.body:
### What?

`Loadable.preloadAll()` now waits for loads that are already in flight before rendering.

### Why?

On SSR pages that use `next/dynamic`, concurrent requests can race: a request's `preloadAll()` resolves immediately instead of waiting for the loading that another request already started, so that request renders the loading state.

### How?

In-flight preloads are tracked in a Set. A preload is added when it starts and removed when it settles, and each `preloadAll()` call also waits for whatever is in the Set.

Fixes #100410

docs.title: fix(next/dynamic): share in-flight preload promise across concurrent SSR requests
docs.body:
### What?

Prevents a race condition in `next/dynamic` (`Loadable.preloadAll`) where concurrent server-side render (SSR) requests render the dynamic component's loading fallback state instead of the loaded component subtree.

### Why?

Fixes #100410

When multiple SSR requests hit the server concurrently, the first request executes `Loadable.preloadAll()`. In `flushInitializers`, `ALL_INITIALIZERS` is drained via `.pop()` to invoke the loaders.

Any concurrent requests arriving while those loaders are still in-flight call `Loadable.preloadAll()`, see that `ALL_INITIALIZERS` is already empty (`ALL_INITIALIZERS.length === 0`), and resolve their `preloadAll` promise immediately without awaiting the in-flight loaders.

As a result, those concurrent requests proceed immediately to render the page while the components are still in `state.loading === true`, sending the `loading` fallback HTML to the client instead of the loaded component subtree.

### How?

- In `packages/next/src/shared/lib/loadable.shared-runtime.tsx`, introduce a shared in-flight `preloadAllPromise` across calls to `Loadable.preloadAll()`.
- Run a loop `while (ALL_INITIALIZERS.length > 0 || preloadAllPromise)` ensuring that concurrent calls await the in-flight preload and that any newly registered initializers (e.g. from dynamic imports evaluated during preloading) are fully flushed before resolving.
- Reset `prelo

docs.title: Reuse chunk loads within a render
docs.body:
- **Cause:**
  - React loads every chunk listed for a client reference during SSR, and Turbopack lists the whole chunk group for each reference.
  - On a large projects `/login`, that's 13,391 `__next_chunk_load__` calls for 242 unique chunks per render in production, and 3,306 calls for 50 chunks in dev.
  - In dev with `cacheComponents`, every call creates a promise, and React's dev async debug tracking captures a stack trace for each one: ~54 ms per render in the profile.
- **Fix:** the chunk-load handler remembers each chunk's first load and returns the same promise for repeat calls. The memo is scoped to the handlers each render installs, so it can't keep chunks reloaded in dev.
- **Numbers (warm `/login`, Node 24):**
  - `next dev`: 200 → 148 ms (−26%)
  - `next start` with client component load tracking on (`NEXT_OTEL_PERFORMANCE_PREFIX`): 18.4 → 16.9 ms CPU (−8%)
  - `next start` without tracing: no measurable change
- **Metrics:** `next.clientComponentLoadCount` only counts requires, so it's unchanged.
- **Tests:**
  - `client-reference-chunking`, `dynamic-chunk-dedupe` and `opentelemetry/instrumentation` pass in production and dev.
  - `cache-components-dynamic-imports` passes in production.
  - Its dev case "does not instrument import() in external packages" fails, and fails the same way with the change reverted.

docs.title: Turbopack: preserve chunk load promise identity
docs.body:
## Summary

#98836 added an on-demand `__turbopack_ensure_chunk__` hook to the Turbopack Node dev runtime by overriding `__turbopack_context__.l`. The override returned `ensured.then(() => loadChunkAsync(...))`, so every call that hit a not-yet-cached chunk produced a **new promise**, and the first caller's promise never matched the one later callers got from `chunkCache`. That broke referential identity for `__next_chunk_load__` (which wraps `.l`), which React relies on. It also created extra promises for React's dev async tracking to process.

This change makes `loadChunkAsync` itself aware of `__turbopack_ensure_chunk__`:

- The hook is called synchronously on a cache miss. If it returns `undefined` (nothing to compile), the chunk is required synchronously and the shared pre-resolved promise is cached, exactly as without the hook.
- If it returns a promise (the chunk is being compiled on demand), a single `ensure → require/install` promise is cached in `chunkCache` immediately. Concurrent and later callers all get the same promise until `clearChunkCache()`.
- If ensuring the chunk fails (a synchronous throw or an async rejection), the failure is not cached, so the next load retries. `require` failures stay cached as `ChunkLoadError`, as before.
- The separate `.l` override and `chunksBeingEnsured` map in `dev-base.ts` are removed. The Node runtime snapshots are regenerated.

docs.title: turbo-persistence: don't shrink the shard count before the first bottom merge
docs.body:
## What

Defer shrinking shard counts of turbo-persistence families until there has been a bottom merge.  This reduces the maximum sizes of initial compaction jobs at the cost of slightly more SST files until that happens.  The benefit is more parallelism and smaller job sizes for initial bottom runs.

## Why

A 'bottom' merge is when we have performed a 'full compaction' of a single shard of a family (aka table).   Families are divided into shards to accelerate lookups and reduce the size of compaction jobs.  Part of the compaction strategy is to occasionally compress the full shard into a 'bottom' a set of hot and cold files that do not overlap (well hot and cold can overlap, but hots cannot overlap with hots and colds cannot with colds).

Before a family has a 'bottom', its shard count can shrink. Commits compute the count too, so after a small first commit (e.g. the first snapshot in dev) the next commits already wrote files spanning all of the family's initial shards. Such files tie every shard into one component, so the first bottom merge of the family was a single job over all its files.  e.g. for next-site TaskData went from 8 to 4 shards and TaskMeta from 4 to 1, doubling and quadrupling the job sizes.

Now the count only grows until the family has bottom runs. Shrinking afterwards is free: the bottom runs of the former shards are disjoint, so together they a

docs.title: Turbopack: keep env and preview props invalidations key-granular on warm start
docs.body:
### What?

Narrows the invalidations a warm `next dev` start triggers when project options are republished:

- `Project` keeps the draft-mode (preview) props in their own cell instead of inlining them.
- `EnvMap` uses keyed cells, and `EnvMap::read(name)` depends only on the requested variable.

### Why?

Every dev start republishes the project options, and two of them always differ from the previous run: the preview props are randomly regenerated, and the env contains per-process values like `NEXT_PRIVATE_START_TIME`. Re-running `ProjectContainer::project()` is cheap by itself. The cost comes from cells whose content actually changes:

- With the preview props inlined, the `Project` cell changed on every start and invalidated every task reading `Project`, across all routes.
- `EnvMap::read(name)` depended on the whole env map. Any key changing, even one nobody reads, re-ran every per-key env read. Its intermediate uppercase map also wasn't persisted, so after a warm restore it had no previous content to compare against and invalidated all of its readers whenever it recomputed.

### How?

- **Preview props:** `Project` stores a reference to a private cell holding the preview props. The `Project` cell stays equal when only the preview props change, and only `edge_env`, which genuinely embeds them in the edge manifests, is invalidated.

docs.title: turbopack: use reverse postorder priority in compute_chunk_group_info
docs.body:
## Summary

`compute_chunk_group_info` runs a fixed-point traversal over the module graph, ordered by BFS (minimum) depth. A module can gain new chunk groups after it was already visited, for example through a longer path from another entry or from a chunk group that is created later. When that happens, it is queued again and its whole subgraph is propagated again. On app-shaped graphs this means many visits per module.

This PR adds `ModuleGraphSnapshot::reverse_postorder_ranks`. It ranks every module by the reverse postorder of a DFS from the entries, using an iterative DFS that resolves `VisitedModule` aliases to the canonical node. Using `Reverse(rank)` as the priority visits a module only after all of its importers, except across cycles. On a DAG, each module is therefore visited exactly once.

`compute_chunk_group_info` now uses this rank instead of its own BFS depth pass.

`traverse_edges_fixed_point_with_priority` also now tracks initial entries in `queue_set`:
- an entry reachable from another entry is no longer queued twice;
- duplicate entries are ignored.

This is the first PR of a stack. `collect_graph` (#100429) and `compute_merged_modules` (#100430) follow in separate PRs.

### Benchmarks

**Setup:**
- `next build --experimental-build-mode compile` with Turbopack.
- `next-swc` release builds (LTO disabled and 16 codegen units, to keep the native builds feasible).

docs.body:
### What?

Resolves the `TODO merge AggregatedDataUpdate` in `inner_of_upper_has_new_followers` (turbo-tasks-backend aggregation update queue). The diffs produced while connecting several new followers to an upper are now merged into a single `AggregatedDataUpdate`, and at most one `AggregatedDataUpdateJob` is enqueued for the upper's uppers.

### Why?

When an upper gains N new inner followers, applying their data produced up to N diffs, and each one was enqueued as its own job with a clone of the same `upper_ids`. Every one of those jobs then locks and updates each grand-upper separately, even though a single combined update has the same net effect.

### How?

- New `AggregatedDataUpdate::merge`:
  - Dirty container updates are summed per field. All diffs returned by `apply` on the same task carry that task's id, which is a documented precondition and checked with a debug assertion. If the sums cancel to zero, the dirty container update is dropped.
  - Collectible entries are concatenated. The existing `optimize` then sums them per collectible and drops zero entries, so `+1`/`-1` pairs from successive diffs cancel.
- At the call site, the diffs are merged and optimized after the upper's lock is released. The optimize pass is skipped when there is only a single diff. Nothing is enqueued if the merged update is empty or the upper has no uppers.

docs.title: turbo-tasks: unemit taken collectibles in a single backend operation
docs.body:
### What?

`take_collectibles` / `drop_collectibles` now unemit all taken collectibles in a single backend operation instead of one operation per collectible.

### Why?

`TurboTasks::unemit_collectibles` looped over every collectible and called `Backend::unemit_collectible` for each. In `TurboTasksBackend` every one of those calls locked the task, built its own aggregation update queue and propagated a single-entry collectibles update through the aggregation graph. With many collectibles that means one task lock and one aggregation graph update per collectible.

### How?

- New required `Backend::unemit_collectibles` trait method. `TurboTasks::unemit_collectibles` calls it once, and does nothing when no count is positive.
- `TurboTasksBackend` implements it with a batched `UpdateCollectibleOperation::run_batch`:
  - locks the task once and checks the root-task restriction up front;
  - reconciles each collectible against its outdated count, with the same per-collectible semantics as before;
  - invalidates collectible dependents at most once per collectible type;
  - propagates all remaining changes as one aggregated data update, so the aggregation queue runs once.
- `AggregatedDataUpdate`'s collectibles update is now a `SmallVec<[_; 1]>`, so single-collectible updates don't heap-allocate and the batch is handed over without conversion.

docs.body:
Stacked on #100430 (#100428 → #100429 → #100430 → this).

### What?

Two changes in `compute_binding_usage_info`:

1. **Reverse postorder priority.** The fixed-point traversal now uses `Reverse(rank)` from `ModuleGraphSnapshot::reverse_postorder_ranks` (added in #100428) as its priority, instead of the constant `0`. Modules are visited roots first, so in an acyclic graph each module is processed exactly once, after all of its importers and with its final usage. Cycles still rely on the fixed point.
2. **No clone of the parent's usage on passthrough edges.** The `ExportUsage::Passthrough` branch cloned the parent's `ModuleExportUsageInfo` to work around borrowing two entries of `used_exports` at once. It now inserts the target's entry, borrows both entries with `HashMap::get_disjoint_mut`, and merges directly. A self-edge (`parent == target`) is handled explicitly, because merging a usage into itself never changes it and `get_disjoint_mut` would panic on the duplicate key.

### Why?

With the constant priority, the traversal pops the most recently queued node first, which makes the order DFS-like. That gives no ordering guarantee: a shared module can be processed before all of its importers, and is then revisited whenever a later importer adds new export names.

On the apps measured below this happens rarely, so there is no speedup here. The extra rank traversal makes the analys

docs.title: turbopack: store unused reference edges in a keyed Vc
docs.body:
### What?

Moves the unused reference edges of `BindingUsageInfo` into their own keyed Turbo Tasks value, `UnusedReferenceEdges`. `ModuleGraphSnapshot` now holds only those edges, not the full binding usage info.

### Why?

`ModuleGraphSnapshot` needs binding usage info for one thing: deciding which graph edges to skip during traversal. Because the edge set was stored inline in `BindingUsageInfo`, graph snapshots depended on all of the binding usage info. Any change to the edges also changed `BindingUsageInfo` itself, which invalidated readers that only needed the other data (export usage, circuit breakers, partial-namespace modules).

### How?

- `BindingUsageInfo` stores the unused edges as a `ResolvedVc` to the new `cell = "keyed"` transparent set and exposes it via `unused_references_edges()`.
- `ModuleGraph` and `ModuleGraphLayer` read only that value into their snapshots. The removed `is_reference_unused_edge` helper is replaced by keyed `contains_key` checks on the edge set at the traversal sites.
- Traversals are synchronous, so the snapshot holds a `ReadRef` of the edge set. Traversal behavior is unchanged: the same edges are skipped and the double-analysis guard still fires.

### Verification

- `cargo check -p next-core -p next-api`

docs.title: Turbopack: compute client reference manifest parts once per reference, not per page
docs.body:
## Summary

When Turbopack builds an app's client reference manifests, it builds one per app entry (page). For each client reference a page uses, `build_manifest` recomputed:

- the reference's server path;
- its client, SSR and RSC module ids (each read goes through the chunking context's id strategy, the module's ident and a keyed module-id map read);
- for every JS chunk, its component chunks (the merged chunk's runtime info plus each component chunk's path and file size).

None of these depend on the page, and pages usually share most of their client references. So the number of reads grew as pages × references, and with `experimental.turbopackChunking.generateComponentChunks` as pages × references × chunks × component chunks. Every read was also another dependency edge on each page's `build_manifest` task.

This PR moves that work into two turbo-tasks functions that are keyed only on page-independent inputs:

- `client_reference_ids`: keyed on the client reference module, the client chunking context and the optional SSR chunking context. It returns the server path and the client, SSR and RSC module ids.
- `client_chunk_components`: keyed on the chunk and the client-relative path. It returns the chunk's component chunk paths and sizes.

Each page's manifest now does one cached read per reference and one per chunk. Values and insertion order are unchanged, so the generated m

docs.title: Turbopack: propagate late partial namespace provenance to passthrough targets
docs.body:
### What?

Namespace provenance from a late partial-namespace read now reaches the module's passthrough targets, even when that module was already processed with `All` usage or with the same names.

### Why?

`compute_binding_usage_info` tracks modules read through a namespace value (`namespace_object_may_escape`). Export-name mangling uses this to keep original names. Passthrough edges such as `export * from './y'` forward that provenance to their target.

Take a module that was reached first through a plain named or `All` edge, so its passthrough edge has already run. If a partial-namespace edge for it arrives later and adds no new export names, the module joins the provenance set but the visitor reports no change. It is never revisited, so its passthrough target stays out of the set.

### How?

Direct partial-namespace edges now count adding the target to the provenance set as a change, the same way the passthrough branch already does. The export-usage merge still always runs. Each module can only be added to the set once, so this triggers at most one extra revisit per module and the fixed point still terminates.

New `turbopack-core` graph tests build a small module graph with explicit edge usages and check the result directly. In the graph, `x` re-exports `y` through a passthrough edge, and `x` is reached by both a short path and a longer path. The tests cover:

docs.title: turbo-tasks: batch schedule invalidated tasks and cell dependents
docs.body:
### What?

Tasks that become dirty together are handed to the turbo-tasks scheduler (`PriorityRunner`) as one batch instead of one by one, at two sites:

- `invalidate()` (explicit invalidation of a set of tasks)
- `invalidate_cell_dependents()` in `update_cell` (all dependents of a changed cell — the main fan-out path)

Also adds a `cell_fan_out` criterion benchmark to `turbo-tasks-backend`.

### Why?

`PriorityRunner` keeps all non-lowest-priority work in a `Mutex<BinaryHeap>`. Scheduling N tasks one by one locks that heap up to N times and grows it incrementally, contending with the workers that pop from it. This is a first step towards reducing that contention.

Note: in-tree, `invalidate()` is currently only reached with a single task (`TurboTasks::invalidate` → `Backend::invalidate_task`); `invalidate_tasks` / `invalidate_tasks_set` have no in-tree callers. The real fan-out is a cell change invalidating its dependents, which is why `update_cell` is batched too.

### How?

- **`PriorityRunner::schedule_many`**: behaves like calling `schedule` for each item. While there is free worker capacity, items are handed directly to new workers using the same slot reservation as `schedule`. The remaining items are queued in bulk: each item is still inserted into the claimable map before its key is published, lowest-priority keys still go to the lock-free queue, and all other keys are

docs.title: Preserve cached values for the final runtime prerender
docs.body:
A final runtime prerender could omit cached content or use a different value from the prospective prerender. This also affected embedded cached navigation streams, which reuse the Resume Data Cache (RDC) from the document or navigation render (#98005). Background revalidation replaced the recorded stale entry with a promise for a new value. The final prerender could then encounter pending data or consume the new value. The same overwrite caused development validation to incorrectly report uncached data.

Static prerenders do not start background revalidation; they revalidate usable stale entries in the foreground. Requests and prospective runtime prerenders can serve a stale handler entry immediately and revalidate it in the background. `cacheReady()` does not wait for that revalidation.

Background revalidation now writes only to the cache handler. The RDC keeps the entry recorded by the prospective prerender so the final prerender can reuse it. For embedded cached navigation streams, it keeps the entry recorded by the document or navigation render. Those entries must remain available independently of background revalidation. Later reads that reach the cache handler can still observe the revalidated entry.

Fixes #99884

docs.title: Fix cache revalidation queued during streaming
docs.body:
Next.js previously flushed revalidations after preparing the HTML stream or running a Route Handler, before the response body finished streaming. That flush dispatched queued tags and collected existing background cache promises. Work added during streaming was omitted, so later cache regeneration lacked `waitUntil` coverage and later tag invalidations were never dispatched.

This extends the response-close approach proposed in #99772 beyond dynamic HTML to Flight responses, Route Handlers, and streamed Server Actions. `AfterContext` registers a `waitUntil` promise before the handler returns and flushes newly queued work at close. Its snapshot excludes earlier flushes and runs before `after()` callbacks start, so their invalidations wait for callback completion. The change also handles already-closed Node responses and Edge error paths that must release close waiters. Server Action barriers retain their existing ordering.

Fixes #99339
Fixes #99566
Closes #99772

docs.title: AGENTS.md: prefer e2e/execution tests over implementation-mapped unit tests
docs.body:
### What?

Adds two bullets to the "Writing Tests" section of `AGENTS.md`:

- For Next.js features, prefer e2e tests (`test/e2e/`, `test/development/`, `test/production/`). For Turbopack features, prefer execution tests (`turbopack/crates/turbopack-tests/tests/execution/`).
- Avoid unit tests that map directly to the implementation; complicated algorithms are the exception. Agents may write unit tests temporarily to check their work, but should not commit them or add them to the PR unless they are necessary.

### Why?

Agents often add unit tests that mirror the implementation. These tests add maintenance cost and catch few real regressions. Integration-level tests cover behavior through the real entry points.

### How?

docs.title: turbopack: speed up and share reverse postorder ranks
docs.body:
Stacked on #100440. The lower PRs of the stack (#100428, #100429, #100430) are merged.

### What?

Two changes to the reverse postorder ranks that the RPO stack computes before each fixed-point traversal:

1. **A faster `ModuleGraphSnapshot::reverse_postorder_ranks`, with identical ranks.**
   - Visited nodes are tracked in one `FixedBitSet` per graph instead of an `FxHashSet<GraphNodeIndex>`. `DiGraph` node indices are dense, and `VisitedModule` aliases are resolved first.
   - `postorder` is preallocated, and the result map is created with capacity. Collecting a `Result` iterator into a map gives it no capacity hint, so it rehashes as it grows.
   - One DFS stack is reused across roots.
   - DFS order and rank numbering are unchanged.
   - The method now asserts it's called on the whole graph, not on an individual graph layer, where `VisitedModule` nodes can't be resolved. This matches the existing check in `traverse_edges_fixed_point_with_priority`.
2. **One shared rank computation for chunk group info and merged modules.**
   - The new `ModuleGraphSnapshot::entry_ranks` computes the ranks from the entries of the graph (derived from its chunk groups) on first use and caches them in a `OnceLock` on the snapshot.
   - `compute_chunk_group_info` and `compute_merged_modules` already computed exactly these ranks (same entries, same order) on the same graph, so they now share one

docs.title: turbo-tasks-backend: parallelize decoding of large batch lookups
docs.body:
### What?

`TurboBackingStorage::batch_lookup_data` now decodes the `TaskStorage` entries of a batch in parallel when the batch has at least `PARALLEL_DECODE_THRESHOLD` (2048) items. Smaller batches still decode sequentially. This PR also adds an opt-in Criterion benchmark that measures where parallel decoding starts to pay off.

### Why?

Batched task restores read all entries with a single `batch_get` and then decoded every entry one after another on the calling thread. With large restore batches, that single-threaded decode is a bottleneck.

### How?

- `batch_lookup_data` is now split into two steps:
  - a raw fetch (`batch_lookup_raw`), unchanged I/O;
  - `decode_task_storage_batch`, which takes the parallel cutoff as a parameter.
- Both paths share the same decode closure, so ordering, `None` for missing keys, and failing the batch on a decode error behave exactly as before.
- The parallel path uses `turbo_tasks::parallel::map_collect`. It borrows the raw bytes, keeps result order and the turbo-tasks context, and doesn't add another thread pool.
- `turbo_tasks::scope_bounded` (behind `parallel::*`) now enters the turbo-tasks context once per helper instead of once per job:
  - #100485 fixed re-entering the context while the caller holds a borrow (restores can run inside `with_turbo_tasks`). Its fix is `ensure_turbo_tasks_scope`, which compares the current task-local on ev

docs.title: turbo-tasks-backend: skip dirtying removed cell dependents
docs.body:
### What?

`invalidate_cell_dependents` in turbo-tasks-backend no longer dirties a dependent task when none of the invalidated dependency keys are still current or outdated dependencies of that task.

### Why?

A cell's dependents are collected while the cell task is locked, and each dependent is locked separately afterwards. In between, the dependent can finish an execution that no longer reads the cell, and `cleanup_old_edges` removes the dependency. For hashed cells, the dependent may also track only other keys of the same cell.

The code was meant to skip such removed dependencies, but its `continue` only continued the inner per-key loop. So the task was always marked dirty and rescheduled after the loop, even when every key had been removed.

Follow-up to https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/100446#discussion_r4327450882.

### How?

Every key is a separate dependency. Keys are only grouped per dependent to reduce task locking, so the decision is made per task after all keys have been checked:

- An **outdated** dependency hasn't been read in the current execution yet. It marks the task dirty, but not stale, so the task is no longer treated as a recomputation (unchanged behavior).
- A **current** dependency has already been read. It marks the task stale, which also makes it dirty (unchanged behavior).
- A **removed** dependency contributes nothing.

docs.body:
### What?

Adds an opt-in (`#[ignore]`) benchmark, `bench_compute_chunk_group_info`, to the `turbopack-core` module graph tests. It times `compute_chunk_group_info` on a deterministic, synthetic, app-shaped module graph.

### Why?

`compute_chunk_group_info` runs a fixed-point traversal over the whole module graph that unions RoaringBitmaps per module, so its cost depends heavily on graph shape and traversal order (see e.g. #100428). There was no easy way to measure it in isolation or to check that a change keeps the same output. This benchmark is meant to support future work on this function, such as sharing or interning the chunk group bitmaps.

### How?

- **Graph generator:** a seeded generator builds a graph with npm-like packages (including intra-package cycles and skewed popularity), shared components, a layout tree, many route entries, and async imports into a pool of lazily loaded modules. All sizes are configurable via `BENCH_*` environment variables (`BENCH_ROUTES`, `BENCH_ITERATIONS`, `BENCH_SEED`, `BENCH_LIBS`, `BENCH_COMPS`, `BENCH_ROUTE_SIZE`, `BENCH_ASYNC_PER_ROUTE`, `BENCH_DYN_POOL`).
- **Real code path:** it reuses the existing `TestRepo`/`MockModule` test helpers to build a real `ModuleGraph` through turbo-tasks, so it exercises the actual code.
- **What is timed:** only the `compute_chunk_group_info` call. Graph construction and result hashing are excluded.

docs.title: fix(segment-cache): prevent infinite prefetch loop on redirected routes
docs.body:
Closes #100431

### Why?
When optimistic routing is active, the client learns route patterns from previously discovered routes (e.g. `/[...slug]`). If an unvisited link (`/old/b`) matches an already-known route pattern, `matchKnownRoute` creates a synthetic fulfilled route cache entry for it, bypassing the initial `/_tree` fetch and immediately scheduling per-segment prefetching.

On Vercel (or when redirected with HTTP 307), segment prefetch requests to legacy or redirecting URLs answer with a `307 Location: /docs/two`. The browser follows or Next.js replays the redirect, receiving a response that carries the destination pathname (`/docs/two`) and destination parameters rather than the requested route's.

Previously:
1. `fetchAndWritePerSegmentPrefetchResponse` did not check `response.redirected` or verify that `renderedPathname === expectedPathname`.
2. When the destination's segment data arrived, `writeResponsePayloadsIntoCache` fulfilled `spawnedEntries` (which was spawned for `/old/b`), but keyed and inserted the entry in the cache map under the redirected target's path (`/docs/two`).
3. This left the original route (`/old/b`) empty in the segment cache map.
4. Fulfilling `spawnedEntries` immediately pinged the prefetch task. In the very next microtask, the scheduler revisited the task for `/old/b`, matched the optimistic route pattern again, saw `/old/b` had empty segment

docs.body:
### What?

`invalidate()` now opens its tasks with a bulk optional read (`ExecuteContext::for_each_try_task_all`) instead of one `try_task` per id. Non-resident persisted tasks are restored with one batched disk lookup per category instead of one lookup per task.

### Why?

Follow-up to #100446 (https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/100446#discussion_r4326845752). The existing bulk read APIs (`prepare_tasks` / `for_each_task*`) are `MustExist`: a task missing in memory and on disk panics. Invalidation needs `try_task` semantics instead, because a task being invalidated may legitimately be gone.

### How?

- `prepare_tasks_with_callback` takes a `TaskAccess` mode.
  - `MustExist` is the existing behavior and keeps the same panics and messages.
  - `AllowMissing` skips any task that `try_task` would not return, and the callback isn't called for it:
    - a soft-deleted task, which is left in place
    - a task that isn't restorable (transient, or no backing storage) and isn't resident, which is discarded
    - a task whose requested category has no disk key, including when only one category is missing; it is discarded and its restoring claims are cleared
- The existing restore phases are reused for both modes:
  - ready tasks are handed off first
  - claimed reads are done as batched I/O
  - claims are applied and waiters notified before callbacks run for the tasks this call res

## Summary

### What?

Simplifies how Turbopack expresses strict mode for chunk module factories:

- **Mixed chunks** (strict and non-strict factories) are no longer wrapped in a strict IIFE. Each strict factory keeps its own `"use strict"` directive, and factories stay in their original order.

docs.body:
### What?

In production builds, Turbopack removed side-effecting IIFEs whose callee is a PURE-annotated call, for example `(/* @__PURE__ */ __name(function () { … }, "x"))()`. esbuild emits this shape for `keepNames` output, so Radix UI dists are one affected example.

This PR fixes that, along with the member-expression form `(/* @__PURE__ */ f()).g()`, both with and without scope hoisting.

### Why?

Turbopack runs SWC's `fixer` on every module after codegen, but it passed no comments. SWC's fixer intentionally keeps the parentheses around a PURE / NO_SIDE_EFFECTS-annotated callee or member object, but it can only do that when it can see the comments. Without them it drops the parens.

The printed code then reads `/* @__PURE__ */ f()()`. When the minifier re-parses it, the annotation applies to the outer call, and the whole call is removed as an unused pure expression. webpack is unaffected.

### How?

  - `has_flag` is overridden to only read. It shares its matcher with `ImmutableComments`, because SWC's default implementation takes the comments and re-adds them.

docs.body:
### What?

Adds `max_chunk_size` to Turbopack's production chunking config as a best-effort upper bound on JavaScript chunk size. Merging respects the limit; chunks already oversized on their own are split deterministically.

Next.js enables separate defaults:

- **Client:** 1,000,000 bytes, overridable with `experimental.turbopackChunking.maxChunkSize`.
- **Server (Node.js and edge):** 10,000,000 bytes, overridable with `experimental.turbopackChunking.maxServerChunkSize`.

Each option affects only its own side. `0` disables it.

### Why?

Production chunking can produce arbitrarily large chunks from shared dependencies or merging. These take longer to load and parse, and changing one module invalidates the whole chunk. A merge-aware limit and deterministic splits keep chunks manageable while reducing cache churn.

### How?

**Deterministic grouping**, based on webpack's `deterministicGrouping`, simplified to a scalar size:

- When splitting is needed, extract items sized at least the maximum into standalone groups, then sort the rest by module identifier.
- Recursively cut where adjacent identifiers share the shortest prefix (usually a package/directory boundary). Break ties by balanced size, then the leftmost cut.
- Keep both sides at least `min_chunk_size` where possible. If that conflicts with the maximum, prefer smaller chunks over oversized ones.

docs.title: Default 'use cache' handler keeps a 64 KB buffer-pool slab alive per small entry, so cacheMaxMemorySize undercounts memory
Default 'use cache' handler keeps a 64 KB buffer-pool slab alive per small entry, so cacheMaxMemorySize undercounts memory
docs.body:
https://github.com/thevuong/next-use-cache-pool-repro
 

1. `pnpm install`
2. `pnpm build && pnpm start` (the start script adds `--expose-gc`)
3. In another terminal: `pnpm load`. It requests 5,000 distinct `/[id]` URLs. Each renders at request time and calls a `'use cache'` function keyed by the segment (about 1.5 KB per entry). Then it reads `process.memoryUsage().arrayBuffers` after a full GC.
4. Repeat with the workaround handler: `EXACT_COPY=1 pnpm build && EXACT_COPY=1 pnpm start`, then `pnpm load`.

`pnpm handler` reproduces the same thing against `createDefaultCacheHandler` directly, without a server.
 

Results on Node 24.21.0, next 16.4.1:

| Handler | Values stored | `arrayBuffers` retained after GC |
| --- | --- | --- |
| default | ~7.2 MB (5,000 × 1.5 KB) | +116 to +127 MB |
| exact-size copy (`exact-copy-handler.mjs`) | ~7.2 MB | +7.5 MB |

`createDefaultCacheHandler` buffers each value with `streamToBuffer`, which is `Buffer.concat`. A result smaller than `Buffer.poolSize >>> 1` is a slice of Node's shared 64 KB pool slab, so a long-lived cache entry of a few KB keeps a whole slab alive. The LRU sizes the entry by `value.byteLength`, so the `cacheMaxMemorySize` budget (50 MB) counts a fraction of the memory the cache holds.

A heap snapshot of the default run shows ~1,780 retained 64 KB `ArrayBuffer`s, each retained through `Buffer.buffer ← Object.value ← LRUNode

docs.title: fix: persist cacheControl for Pages Router ISR entries in FileSystemC…
docs.body:
### What?

Fixed ISR cache lifetime persistence for Pages Router pages using the default `FileSystemCache` implementation.

### Why?

Pages Router ISR cache entries did not persist their revalidation interval to disk. After restarting the server, the cache lifetime defaulted to 1 second instead of the configured `revalidate` value.

As a result, previously generated pages could be treated as stale immediately after a restart, and the expected `Cache-Control` header was not preserved.

This complements #99289, which addressed the same issue for the App Router, and covers the missing Pages Router case. See also #99288.

### How?

- Persisted the cache lifetime when writing Pages Router cache entries to disk.
- Restored the persisted cache lifetime when reading cache entries from disk.
- Added a Pages Router test case to `test/production/app-dir/isr-cache-control-restart/` to verify cache behavior after a server restart.

Before the fix, the test failed because the first request after restarting the server returned a `STALE` cache status instead of `HIT`.

Verified that all 5 tests pass with both Turbopack and webpack using:

- `pnpm test-start-turbo`
- `pnpm test-start-webpack`

Experiment for benchmarking react/react#37930. Not meant to merge as is.

## Today

A dynamic App Router request renders the RSC payload to a Flight stream, splits it in two, sends one copy to the browser as the inline hydration data, and parses the other copy back so that Fizz can render the HTML from it.

Production dynamic renders on the Node runtime do this instead:

const result = renderToResult(RSCPayload, {onError, signal});
// Fizz reads the Result directly, in process

// once the shell is ready, the same Result is serialized for the hydration data

docs.title: fix(app-router): fulfill pending segment data when reused during pushState or traversal
docs.body:
Closes #100489

### What?
When a navigation or `history.pushState` traversal occurs while an earlier action's refresh or navigation is still streaming in (or was superseded), the shared route segments may reuse the existing cache node.

Previously, `updateRenderTreeOnNavigation` and segment cache reuse paths hardcoded `needsDynamicRequest = false` without checking if the reused cache node's `rsc` was still a pending `DeferredRsc`. As a result, `spawnDynamicRequests` skipped requesting dynamic data for the unfulfilled segments, leaving React's transition lanes suspended (`pendingLanes = suspendedLanes = entangledLanes = 0b111000000000`) and `useTransition.isPending` stuck on `true` forever until a full page reload.

### Why?
`finishNavigationTask` case `NavigationTaskExitStatus.Canceled` intentionally leaves pending cache nodes untouched under the contract:
> *"Its cache nodes may already be reused by the newer navigation, so leave them untouched for the newer request to fulfill."*

However, because reusing the existing segment unconditionally set `needsDynamicRequest = false`, the newer request was never spawned, and nothing fulfilled the pending deferred RSC promises.

### How?
1. In `updateRenderTreeOnNavigation`, check `oldRscDidResolve = !isDeferredRsc(oldRsc) || oldRsc.status !== 'pending'` when reusing `oldRenderTree.data`. If `oldRsc` has not resolved, set `needsDynamicR

docs.title: Store exact-size buffers in the default use cache handler
docs.body:
Fixes #99848
Closes #100492

### What?

The default `"use cache"` handler now stores an exact-size copy of each entry's buffer instead of a slice of Node's shared Buffer pool.

### Why?

`set()` stores the result of `streamToBuffer`, which is `Buffer.concat(chunks)`. For results smaller than `Buffer.poolSize >>> 1`, `Buffer.concat` returns a slice of the shared pool slab. A long-lived small entry therefore keeps the whole slab (8 KiB, or 64 KiB on newer Node versions) alive, while the LRU sizes the entry by `byteLength` alone. `cacheMaxMemorySize` then undercounts the memory the cache actually holds. The reports in #99848 and #100492 measured a large gap between counted and retained memory.

This storage was introduced by #97941, which fixed request-context retention (#97934). That fix is kept: the entry is still a plain buffer.

### How?

- Added `toExactSizeBuffer` in the default handler. It copies the buffer into a `Buffer.allocUnsafeSlow` allocation when the buffer is a slice of a larger backing store, and returns it unchanged when it already owns an exact-size backing store (results larger than half the pool), so large entries don't pay for a second copy.
- Applied it in `set()` only. `streamToBuffer` is shared and pooled buffers are fine for its short-lived callers, so it is left untouched.

docs.body:
`durableUseCache` + a use-cache function loading a Node.js worker previously crashed because of the `bail!("shouldnt be called")` in `entry_chunk_group`

For this implementation-hash computation, we don't actually perform any chunking. We just codegen the individual modules and hash those together. docs.title: [test] Reproduce two cache-sharing bugs
docs.body:
A cache handler lookup for a `'use cache'` function started for one route can be shared with another route that has different implicit tags. The reproductions show that the route passed to `revalidatePath()` can still receive the old value instead of regenerating it. Another case shows that a route can bypass its cache handler while a fill is pending.

Shared invocation results also preserve the first caller's rendering decision. A direct prerender caller can leave a nested cache waiting on a hanging promise, and one prerender can pass its hanging promise to another. Direct and nested callers can also inherit the wrong revalidation decision for a stale entry.

These tests deliberately assert the current incorrect behavior. #100511 corrects the assertions alongside the wrapper rewrite.

docs.title: Clarify `'use cache'` coordination and fix cache sharing
docs.body:
The wrapper separates invocation preparation, Resume Data Cache reads, cache handler lookups, generation, and cache entry consumption. The foreground and background paths express reuse and lookup retries directly. Pending and completed invocations have separate types, and their state updates show which cache handler lookup and result they replace.

Intra-request deduplication shares cache handler lookups and generated entries within a `WorkStore`. Cross-request generation deduplication shares only pending generation and its cache handler writes. Each `WorkStore` validates handler entries with its own implicit tags, so a concurrent request cannot bypass path revalidation by joining another handler lookup.

Each invocation applies cache-life rules and propagates metadata to its own outer scope. A direct prerender invocation can omit a short-lived entry while a nested cache consumes it. Separate prerenders create their own hanging promises when they omit handler entries. The Resume Data Cache records the omission for later render phases.

The downstack tests extend PR #100652 and characterize the sharing bugs. This change updates their expectations for independent handler lookups and per-invocation rendering decisions. Background revalidation preserves the Resume Data Cache consistency behavior from PR #100447, and the stream error and cancellation handling from PR #100673 remains

docs.title: turbo-tasks: make scope_unbounded worker churn test deterministic
docs.body:
### What?

Makes the turbo-tasks test `scope_unbounded::tests::test_unbounded_busy_queue_does_not_churn_workers` deterministic, and tightens its worker-lifetime bound from 16 to 4.

### Why?

The test failed intermittently with errors like `a saturated queue should not churn drainers, got 20 lifetimes for 20000 items`. The calling thread enqueued trivial items one at a time while the scope workers drained them immediately. If the producer was preempted for longer than `WORKER_IDLE_TIMEOUT` (100µs), the workers idled out and the next enqueue respawned them. Under CPU load this exceeded the loose bound in about 1 of 5 runs.

The old shape also didn't prove much: with the idle timeout set to 0 it still usually passed.

### How?

The test still processes 20,000 items, but the queue is now kept saturated by construction rather than by out-racing the scheduler:

- **Parents.** Half the items are seeded as parents. Each parent waits until the seed iterator is exhausted, so no worker can sit on an empty queue while the producer is still seeding.
- **Children.** Each parent spawns one child, so a worker that exits too early will be re-armed by a later `spawn`.
- **Child gate.** Children wait until every parent's `spawn` call has returned. The queue is FIFO, so all parents are already in flight by then and the wait cannot deadlock. While any `spawn` is still pending, no drainer can find

docs.title: Fix prerender manifest update race in dev
docs.body:
in dev, we update the prerender manifest based on the `generateStaticParams` result. we were using `fs.promises.{readFile,writeFile}` for this, which made it possible for parallel requests to interfere with each other -- when a file is opened for writing by `fs.promises.writeFile`, it gets truncated, and if another request tries to read the manifest in the meantime, it can observe an empty file. this [has caused intermittent crashes](https://app.datadoghq.com/ci/ci-cd/explorer/executions?query=test_level%3Atest%20%40git.repository.id%3A%22github.com%2Fvercel%2Fnext.js%22%20%40test.name%3A%22use-cache-fallback-root-params%20resolves%20cached%20and%20uncached%20roots%20on%20ordinary%20requests%22%20%40test.status%3A%22fail%22&agg_m=count&agg_m_source=base&agg_t=count&ci_cd_explorer_tab=tests&currentTab=overview&eventStack=&fromUser=true&start=1789839150900&end=1792431150900&paused=false) in `use-cache-fallback-root-params > resolves cached and uncached roots on ordinary requests` which has a couple requests hitting the same route in parallel with different params and attempting to update the manifest.

switching the reads/writes to be synchronous avoids this problem. i was unable to reproduce this race in 100 runs of `use-cache-fallback-root-params`, which previously would get a failure in around 20 runs

## Summary

Non-eager `import.meta.glob` matches were referenced with a parallel chunking type, so every matched module was compiled and shipped in the importing module's chunk group. Only evaluation was deferred to the thunk, so the "lazy" mode did not actually code-split.

Lazy matches now use an async edge and load through their async loader, the same as a dynamic `import()`. Each match gets its own chunk, loaded when its thunk is called. Eager matches are unchanged.

- New snapshot test `turbopack-tests/tests/snapshot/imports/import-meta-glob` shows lazy matches in separate async chunks and the eager match in the entry chunk.

docs.body:
## Summary

`require.context()` used a hand-written virtual module with its own references and codegen. It is now a synthetic CommonJS source next to the calling module (`<file>.require-context.cjs`) that lists the matched files and `require`s each one. That module goes through normal module handling, so resolution, transforms and chunking all come from the standard paths, and about 270 lines of special-case code go away.

The synthetic source has a source map that maps all of its code to the `require.context()` call, so issues located in it (e.g. a match that fails to resolve) are reported at the call.

Behaviour changes:
- The filter regex is now part of the module ident. Before, two contexts over the same directory with different filters in one file collided.

The filter applies to these keys, and they are sorted. This enables the previously disabled "no regex" case of `test/e2e/app-dir/require-context`, which now gives the same keys with both bundlers.

docs.title: Settle pipeToNodeResponse when the socket closes before finish
docs.body:
## What

`createWriterFromResponse` waited on `res` `'finish'` inside `WritableStream.close()`. If the client resets the socket after `res.end()` but before that last write flushes, Node emits `'close'` and never `'finish'`, so `pipeToNodeResponse` never settles and the request listener (and everything it closed over) stays alive for the rest of the process.

`pipeNodeReadableToNodeResponse` in the same file already resolves its finished promise on `'close'`. This does the same for the web-stream writer.

Fixes #100528

## How

Resolve the `finished` promise on `'close'` as well as `'finish'`. Happy-path `finish` still settles immediately; the reset path no longer hangs.

## Test

Added a unit test that calls `end()` and then emits `'close'` without `'finish'`, and asserts `pipeToNodeResponse` settles.

docs.title: Turbopack: report unknown module types at the import
docs.body:
## Summary

A file that no module type applies to (e.g. a `.txt` without a loader) never becomes a module, so it has no place in the module graph. Its "Unknown module type" error had no location and no import trace, and did not say which import pulled the file in. This was worst for requests the user did not write by hand, like dynamic `require(`./dir/${x}`)` requests, globs and contexts.

`handle_resolve_error` now records the location of the import on such files in the resolve result. When a file turns out to be needed as a module, it is reported at that import, naming the file. Files that are only resolved and never needed as modules (e.g. traced externals like `sharp`'s `require.resolve` of a `.dylib`) are still not reported, as before. Files resolved without a known import location are reported without one, as before.

This also replaces the custom "import.meta.glob() matched a file that has no module type" issue, since the general one now points at the call.

Stacked on #100681.

## Verification

- New execution tests `unknown-module-type` and `require-context-unknown-type`; updated issue snapshots for `dynamic-unrelated` and `import-meta-glob-unknown-type`.
- `test/production/app-dir/import-meta-glob-unknown-type` (the code frame is syntax highlighted, so the test now strips ANSI codes).
- `test/e2e/app-dir/next-image` (start, Turbopack): no new errors for traced files.

## Summary

`import.meta.glob()` used a hand-written virtual module with its own references, chunking and codegen. It is now a synthetic ES module next to the importing module (`<file>.import-meta-glob.mjs`) that imports every matched file and default-exports the object of them:

- lazy matches are dynamic `import()`s, so async chunks and lazy compilation come from normal `import()` handling,
- eager matches are static imports, and the `import` option becomes a named import (eager) or a `turbopackExports` comment (lazy) so tree shaking narrows exports and scope hoisting can trigger

The call site reads the default export through a hoisted import, the same mechanism a free variable provided by a module uses. As a result:

- an eager match with top-level await now makes the importing module async, instead of yielding an unresolved value,
- scope hoisting can merge the synthetic module and its matches into the importing module.

The synthetic source maps all of its code to the `import.meta.glob()` call, so issues located in it are reported at the call. Matched files are no longer resolved up front. About 420 lines of special-case code go away, including the code from #100522 and #100523, which this subsumes.

docs.title: fix(shared): keep IPv6 brackets when reading the Host header
docs.body:
## What

`getHostname` reads the `Host` header with `headers.host.toString().split(':', 1)[0]`, which cuts at the *first* colon. IPv6 literals contain colons inside their brackets, so they are truncated:

```ts
getHostname({}, { host: '[::1]:3000' })          // '['     — expected '[::1]'
getHostname({}, { host: '[2001:db8::1]:8080' })  // '[2001' — expected '[2001:db8::1]'
```

The `parsed.hostname` branch uses `URL.hostname`, which already keeps the brackets, so the two paths disagree for the same request.

## Fix

When the host starts with `[`, cut after the closing `]` instead of at the first `:`.

## Tests

`packages/next/src/shared/lib/get-hostname.test.ts` gains a header-host table:

```ts
{ host: '[::1]', expected: '[::1]' },
{ host: '[::1]:3000', expected: '[::1]' },
{ host: '[2001:db8::1]:8080', expected: '[2001:db8::1]' },
{ host: '[::1', expected: '[' },          // unterminated bracket falls back to the old split
{ host: 'example.com:3000', expected: 'example.com' },
{ host: 'example.com', expected: 'example.com' },
```

The IPv6 cases return `'['` / `'[2001'` before the change.

**Verification note:** this checkout has no `node_modules`, so the jest suite was not run. The TypeScript source was imported directly with Node 24's type stripping and all table cases pass, including the malformed host.

docs.title: Preserve deferred middleware instrumentation spans when the adapter throws
docs.body:
### What?

Direct Node.js middleware/proxy entrypoints now emit the deferred `instrumentation.ts` lifecycle spans (`load instrumentation module`, `register instrumentation`) even when the adapter rejects the request before it runs the middleware.

### Why?

Follow-up to #100350. When a request to the Node.js middleware entrypoint triggers `instrumentation.ts` registration, the lifecycle spans are deferred and emitted inside the `Middleware.execute` span. If adapter setup throws first (e.g. the configured cache handler throws while the adapter builds the request's incremental cache), the emitter is never called. Registration has already completed, so no later request receives it either, and those spans are lost for the lifetime of the instance.

This only affects direct entrypoints (adapters, deployments). `next start` / `next dev` register instrumentation at startup.

### How?

- The middleware entrypoint template, which owns the deferred emitter, now awaits the adapter in a `try/catch`. On error it calls the emitter, then rethrows the original error unchanged. The adapter and its options are unchanged.
- The emitter already emits at most once, so the fallback does nothing when the spans were already emitted inside `Middleware.execute` (e.g. the user's middleware threw). Successful requests keep their existing span parentage. In the fallback case there is no middleware span, so

docs.body:
https://github.com/infiniteregrets/next-cancel-repro
 

1. Install and start:
   ```bash
   pnpm install

   curl localhost:3000/api/cancel-node
   curl localhost:3000/api/cancel-edge
   ```

3. **Results:**

```ts
const res = await fetch(upstream);
const reader = res.body!.getReader();
await reader.read();

docs.title: turbo-tasks: use per-priority lock-free queues in PriorityRunner
docs.body:
### What?

Changes the internal queue of `PriorityRunner` (`turbo-tasks`) to reduce lock contention on machines with many cores. Adds a benchmark that reproduces the problem.

> [!WARNING]
> **Draft: not ready to merge.** In a cold full `next build` with 16 workers, this PR increases the peak memory of the largest process by about 100 MiB (+2.0%, ranges disjoint), which fails the memory gate. With 32 workers the difference is within noise. There is **no real-app wall-time gain**, and the cause of the memory increase is unknown. See [Results](#results).

### Why?

Every queued job with a priority other than the lowest one went through a single `Mutex<BinaryHeap>`. Each push and each pop took that lock and did an O(log n) heap operation over all queued jobs. The lock-free special case for the lowest priority (`TaskPriority::Initial`) helps initial builds. In warm builds with many changes, almost every job has an `Invalidation`/`Recomputation` priority, so they all go through the mutex.

The new `turbo_tasks_backend_priority_contention` bench reproduces this. On an earlier base, warm recomputation on 32 cores got *slower* with more threads: 32 threads were ~40% slower than 4–8 threads. Temporary instrumentation (not committed) showed ~4–7 s of cumulative mutex wait per ~300 ms iteration, i.e. a large share of all worker time.

docs.title: turbo-bitset: add Bitset, a fast bitset over a bounded bit range
docs.body:
Stacked on #100452. This PR only adds the crate; the PRs above use it: #100643 (`compute_chunk_group_info`) → #100567 (`collect_graph`) → #100568 (`compute_merged_modules`) → #100630 (persisted chunk group sets) → #100724 (removes the FixedBitSet/Roaring comparisons from the benchmarks).

## Summary

The module graph fixed-point traversals track set membership with `RoaringBitmap`, which is built for compact storage, not speed. They check "would `current |= parent` change `current`?" on every edge and then do the union; on array containers both cost time proportional to the number of bits.

This PR adds a new `turbo-bitset` crate with `Bitset`: a `Vec<usize>` of blocks plus an offset counted in whole blocks.

- Bit `i` is stored at `i - offset * usize::BITS`, so a set only stores the word range between its lowest and highest bit. Sets whose bits are clustered at high indices stay small.
- Unions, intersections, differences, subset checks, `is_disjoint` and `intersection_len` are word loops over the overlapping range, so their cost is proportional to the range, not the number of bits. The subset check reduces chunks of 4 words before branching, so it vectorizes.
- `union_with` returns whether it added a bit. It ORs the words and collects the added bits in the same loop, so a traversal checks for a change and applies the union in one pass instead of a subset check plus `|=`. If t

docs.title: bench: add warm cached build benchmark to nested-deps-app-router-many-pages
docs.body:
### What?

Adds `bench-warm-build.mjs` (plus a `bench-warm-build` script entry) to `bench/nested-deps-app-router-many-pages`. It benchmarks warm Turbopack compiles of `next build` with the persistent filesystem cache, after changing N source files.

```bash
cd bench/nested-deps-app-router-many-pages
pnpm prepare-bench
node bench-warm-build.mjs --files=1000
```

### Why?

To measure the incremental rebuild work of a cached build after many changes on a large app, e.g. for turbo-tasks scheduler changes like #100561. Until now there was no easy way to do that.

### How?

- **Cold compile:** an optional cold compile (deletes `.next`) fills the cache. It is reported but not counted.
- **Warm compiles:** by default, 20 warm compiles run (`--iterations=20`). The first 5 are warm-up (`--warmup=5`): they are printed but excluded from the statistics.
  - Each warm iteration changes N component files from `components/`, picked deterministically with a seeded shuffle.
  - The change is a rendered JSX attribute with a per-run/per-iteration value (digits only), so it changes the emitted code (not just a comment) and always differs from what is cached. A file that is still changed from an earlier, killed run is changed again rather than failing.
- **Statistics:** wall time and the "Compiled successfully in" time are printed per iteration. Over the non-warm-up builds, the script prints count,

docs.title: [cd] Move release un-draft to a follow-up job
docs.body:
Follow-up to #100121. `publishRelease` no longer mints an App token at all.

Un-drafting the GitHub release must stay authenticated as the release App: events caused by `GITHUB_TOKEN` do not trigger workflow runs, and release-published automations depend on the event. Previously that meant the bot key had to be available to the `publishRelease` job. With this change a small `undraftRelease` job runs in `bot-autonomous` instead, after the gated publish succeeded (the tag is already trusted at that point), so the key never leaves the two `bot-*` environments.

Backports: #100572 (`releases/lts/active`), #100573 (`releases/lts/maintenance`) — their publish scripts read `lerna.json`, so the script is adapted there.
