fix: pass crossOrigin config to hoistable chunk script tags
docs.body:
Fixes #100533

With `crossOrigin` set, the segment's hoistable `<script async src=...>` (rendered in `get-layer-assets.tsx` and `create-component-styles-and-scripts.tsx`) did not carry the configured `crossOrigin`, unlike the CSS `<link>`s and bootstrap scripts. With Turbopack, the chunk loader inserts the same chunk as `<script crossorigin="anonymous">`, so the page chunk was fetched twice on client navigation (a CORS and a no-CORS request have different cache keys).

This passes `ctx.renderOpts.crossOrigin` to both hoistable `<script>` elements.

Test: added `test/e2e/app-dir/crossorigin-chunk-scripts`, which checks that after a client navigation every chunk `<script>` tag of the same `src` uses the same CORS mode. It fails without the change and passes with it on Turbopack and webpack.

docs.title: fix(turbopack): preserve unknown callback side effects
docs.body:
## Summary

Treat opaque values in known built-in callback slots as potentially effectful. For example, `new Promise(executor)`, `[1].map(callback)`, and `Array.from(items, mapper)` can invoke user code even though reading the callback value itself is pure.

Use a callback-slot index and a conservative opaque-value check. Keep the existing inline-function analysis, ordinary argument evaluation, and PURE handling. Do not resolve callback bindings: a referenced pure callback may conservatively retain its module.

Spread-bearing calls and their argument subtrees keep their existing analysis; this PR does not change spread/iterator assumptions. A baseline-preservation matrix covers nested and PURE cases. Deeply nested inline callbacks are analyzed once, not twice per level.

Bottom layer of the callback stack; #100587 improves invocation precision for non-spread calls. Rebased onto `canary` after #100588 merged, retaining its constructor-callee fix.

## Verification

- Full `turbopack-ecmascript` library: 642 tests passed.
- Four focused execution fixtures passed, including unknown Promise/map callbacks and constructor-callee effects surviving tree-shaking.
- 21 spread examples retain the pre-PR canary classifications.
- Rustfmt and diff checks passed. Full monorepo suite not run locally.

docs.title: fix(turbopack): distinguish callback invocation from function data
docs.body:
## Summary

Depends on #100586; this diff improves invocation precision for non-spread calls.

Do not invoke function-valued data merely because it is passed to a recognized pure operation. `Array.of(() => effect())`, constructor arguments, nested properties, and `thisArg` can be deferred data. Evaluate arguments normally, then explicitly analyze known callback positions and defaults. Preserve opaque callback effects and PURE handling.

Spread-bearing calls and their argument subtrees retain the old analysis through a scoped legacy fallback; this PR does not change spread/iterator assumptions. Adds analyzer regressions and an execution assertion that a module containing only deferred function data is absent from emitted modules. Inherits the merged constructor-callee fix from #100588 through its updated base.

## Verification

- Full `turbopack-ecmascript` library: 674 tests passed after rebasing onto updated #100586.
- Five focused execution fixtures passed, including both callback regressions and upstream constructor-callee coverage.
- 21 spread examples retain the pre-PR canary classifications.
- Rustfmt and diff checks passed. Full monorepo suite not run locally.

Preserve effects from evaluating a constructor callee even when construction is PURE-annotated. For example, `/*#__PURE__*/ new (getConstructor())()` must account for calling `getConstructor()`.

Visit the callee before arguments, matching pure call handling. Add analyzer and execution regressions while preserving upstream PURE callback handling from #100577.

Independent of the callback stack (#100586 / #100587); rebase whichever lands later if their `Expr::New` edits overlap.

docs.body:
Links from `global-not-found` to app routes can leave users stuck on the 404 page because the router does not recognize that leaving the global 404 changes the root layout.

Treat navigation away from `global-not-found` as a root layout change and perform a full-page navigation. Add an e2e regression test covering a link back to the home page.

docs.title: fix(cache): mark short-lived cache handler hits as session data
docs.body:
fixes #100364

Short-lived cache entries that hit the cache handler during static prerendering are omitted from the static shell as dynamic holes However, the reason for this omission is not recorded in the Resume Data Cache, causing the final prerendering pass to emit an `Unexpected cache miss` warning when the key cannot be found

The fix is to write a `SESSION_DATA` marker into the mutable Resume Data Cache before returning the hanging promise in this branch This allows the final prerendering pass to recognize the omission as intentional rather than an unexpected cache miss The implementation requires only 5 lines of code

A regression test has also been added to the existing custom cache handler test suite It covers two routes sharing the same short-lived cache entry, asserting that both reuse the same cached value and that no `Unexpected cache miss` warning is emitted The fixture also sets `experimental.staticGenerationMaxConcurrency: 1` in `next.config.js` so the two prerenders run sequentially, which makes the second route read the completed cache handler entry instead of joining the first route's in-flight generation The existing `use-cache-non-deterministic-args` suite still passes, so genuinely non-deterministic cache arguments keep emitting the warning

docs.title: docs: note that non-function exports of a use cache file are not available to Client Components
docs.body:

docs.title: Fix webpack build dependency cell creation order
docs.body:
## Summary

Fix the `no-map-async-cell` violation in webpack loader build-dependency tracking so `ast-grep scan --format github` passes again. Prepare resolver options concurrently, then create their cells synchronously in request order before resolving modules concurrently. This prevents async completion order from determining Turbo Tasks cell order.

CI context: bc37b30d5ad7be20a0f7e665a0bf99d0203a0574 (#100569) aligned the CI ast-grep version with the repository (0.31.0 → 0.42.0), restoring enforcement of lint failures. #100562 fixed the analyzer occurrence, but #99549 subsequently introduced this occurrence in `build_module_requests_changed`.

Tradeoff: the two phases add an intermediate vector allocation and a synchronization barrier: all options must be prepared before any module resolution starts. This may reduce overlap; the performance impact has not been measured. There may be a better approach, such as reading the shared resolver options once and synchronously cloning/customizing them before creating cells, avoiding the extra preparation join.

## Verification

- `pnpm exec ast-grep scan --format github`
- `ast-grep test` (7 passed)

docs.title: [otel] Don't set http.route on a parent span that has already ended
docs.body:
### What?

When an HTTP instrumentation owns the server span (for example `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http`), every route handler request logs `Cannot execute the operation on ended Span`, and the `http.route` attribute is dropped. This PR propagates `http.route` to the parent span only while that span is still recording.

### Why?

`handleRequest` captures `parentSpan = tracer.getActiveScopeSpan()`. After `handleRequestImpl()` settles, its `.finally()` sets `http.route` on that parent span. For a route handler, the instrumentation has already ended its server span when the response finished, so the SDK rejects the write and warns once per request.

#91655 reported the same warning and was closed as fixed in 16.3.2, but those fixes cover other paths; this base-server path still warns on 16.5.0-canary.22. #96752 described the same cause.

### How?

The propagation is guarded with `parentSpan.isRecording()`.

Test: `test/e2e/opentelemetry/instrumentation/opentelemetry.test.ts` gets a case with a custom server whose server span ends on the response's `close`, the way instrumentation-http does, hit with a route handler request. It fails without the guard ("attribute set on an ended span: http.route") and passes with it. The whole suite passes with `pnpm test-start-turbo` (118 passed, 15 skipped, 0 failed).

docs.title: Stop requiring build-all when bootstrapping a fresh clone or worktree
docs.body:
The agent instructions required a full `pnpm build-all` (JS and Rust) after every worktree creation or branch switch. That is unnecessary when bootstrapping a new clone or worktree: `pnpm install` already pulls in recent published native bindings, so there is nothing to build until source changes.

The new guidance:

- Bootstrapping a new clone or worktree does not start with `pnpm build-all`. Build only what your work changes: `pnpm --filter=next build` for core-only JS edits, `pnpm build` when JS changes span packages.
- Switching branches or pulling can still require a build when it moves JS or Rust source relative to your build outputs; rebuild the affected parts before running tests.
- `pnpm build-all` is reserved for Rust/Turbopack changes, or for when Next.js fails to start because native binding changes landed on canary after the last npm publish (cross-referenced from the Stale Native Binary section).

The `backport-pr` skill repeated the old branch-switch rule and is updated to the same policy.

docs.title: Turbopack: a missing module factory is not cached on the requiring module
docs.body:
### What?

In the build runtimes (browser and Node.js), a module whose instantiation fails because a module it requires has no factory yet no longer keeps that error. A later `require` instantiates it again once the chunk with the missing factory has registered. An error thrown by a module's own code is still kept and rethrown, as `evaluation-errors/basic` expects.

### Why?

In an App Router production build, a dynamic `import()` can throw `Module <X> was instantiated because it was required from module <Y>, but the module factory is not available.` The runtime then keeps that error on `<Y>`, so every later import of `<Y>` rethrows it until a reload, even after `<X>`'s chunk has registered. We see this in production in a large App Router app.

The loader of an `import()` is emitted under one module id with a different chunk list in each chunk group that embeds the importer, and the runtime installs the first copy that registers (#98099). "Any variant can be used" doesn't hold under the App Router: a copy counts on everything its own chunk group brings, but it registers as soon as its own chunk lands, while the rest of that group may still be loading. An importer instantiated from a group that has already completed then uses that copy and instantiates the target before its dependencies have registered.

docs.title: Simplify webpack loader build dependency caching
docs.body:
## Summary

Remove the private `Module._resolveFilename` hook and cached-child request reconstruction introduced in #99549, including the resolver-option cell machinery fixed in #100597.

Instead, mark loader evaluations with cached CommonJS children as session-dependent. This deliberately trades persistent reuse across restarts for a smaller implementation that does not depend on Node's private resolution API. Evaluations remain memoized within a session; unrelated compilation caching and persistent reuse for loaders without cached CommonJS children remain intact. Implicit CommonJS resolution changes require a restart; selected-file tracking, explicit build dependencies, and uncached-module tracing remain.

Add restart regressions for changed package exports and a nearer package replacing a symlinked dependency, plus coverage that leaf loaders retain persistent caching.

## Verification

- Loader dependency suite: 24 Turbopack tests passed; 15 webpack tests passed with 9 existing Turbopack-only gates.
- Standalone adversarial checks: shared-worker cache isolation and two successive production builds preserved leaf-loader caching while recomputing dependency-bearing loader results after restart.
- `pnpm typescript` and the Turbopack Node runtime TypeScript check.

docs.title: Cap bot user-agent matching at 1KB
docs.body:
No known real UA string we're aware of exceeds ~500 bytes (uap-core: longest 492 B across 30,873 distinct strings; Matomo DeviceDetector: longest 482 B across 40,348), so oversized UAs are never bots we need to identify. This bounds regex work on attacker-controlled input as DoS defense-in-depth, mainly for user-configured `htmlLimitedBots` patterns which may be more expensive than the built-in one.

A >1KB UA containing a bot token (e.g. `WhatsApp`) is now treated as a non-bot (streaming metadata served, `isBot()` false).

Hosting providers likely already cap the `User-Agent` header (or any header value) e.g. [Vercel caps at 16kb](https://vercel.com/docs/errors/request_header_too_large)

### What?

Normalize `location` and `options` in `loadWasm`'s `codeFrameColumns` wrapper (`packages/next/src/build/swc/index.ts`) before passing them to `rawBindings.codeFrameColumns`.

### Why?

The N-API binding (`crates/next-napi-bindings/src/code_frame.rs`) accepts `color: boolean` and `maxWidth: undefined` via `NapiCodeFrameOptions` and fills in defaults before converting to `CodeFrameOptions`.

Client reference manifests (`*_client-reference-manifest.js`) are loaded by parsing their JSON instead of executing them as JavaScript. Executing them is now only the fallback.

docs.body:
### What?

`next build --experimental-cpu-prof` now writes a `build-static-worker-*.cpuprofile` for every static worker. Previously only the main process (and webpack compiler workers) produced profiles. Profile filenames now include the process id.

### Why?

The page-data/prerender phase runs in static workers and is often the slowest part of large App Router builds, but it could not be profiled:

- Workers are stopped with `SIGINT`, while the profiler only saved on `process.on('exit')`, which never fires when a process dies from an unhandled signal.
- Filenames had second resolution, so workers saving in the same second would overwrite each other.
- jest-worker's `end()` force-kills workers (`SIGTERM` after 500 ms, `SIGKILL` 500 ms later), which can cut off writing a large profile.

### How?

- **Worker signal flush:** when profiling is enabled in a Next.js worker (`IS_NEXT_WORKER`), `SIGINT`/`SIGTERM` handlers save the profile synchronously, remove themselves, and re-raise the same signal. The worker still terminates by that signal, so parent-side exit handling and jest-worker's restart logic behave as before. Non-worker processes get no new handlers.
- **Unique filenames:** `<name>-<timestamp>-<pid>.cpuprofile`, keeping the existing prefixes.

docs.title: perf(build): avoid O(pages²) original app path scan in static check
docs.body:
### What?

Removes a quadratic scan from the `static-check` phase of `next build`. The original app paths for each App Router page are now looked up from an index that is built once, instead of being rediscovered by scanning every route for every page.

### Why?

Inside the per-page `check-page` work, each app page walked all of `appPathRoutes` (allocating a fresh entries array each time) to find the original app paths that normalize to it. That is O(pages²), and it runs synchronously on the main thread before `isPageStatic` is dispatched, so build workers sit idle while it runs. On apps with thousands of routes this was a significant share of `static-check`.

### How?

Before the pages are fanned out, the build makes one pass over `appPathRoutes` and groups original app paths by their normalized pathname. It applies the same `mappedAppPages` filter the old per-page loop used, and preserves the same per-group order. Each page then does a single lookup and hands the result to the existing `selectAppPageEntry`, which picks the winning entry exactly as before. Pages with no matching entry keep the previous behavior. Pages Router handling is unchanged.

Cost goes from O(pages × routes) to O(routes) plus one map lookup per page.

### Verification

`bench/nested-deps-app-router-many-pages` (3,000 generated pages, Turbopack, 8 cores). Compiled once, then ran `next build --experimental

docs.body:
### What?

Parallelize large `TurboPersistence::batch_get` calls in `turbo-persistence`.

- Batches with **more than 2048 keys** (`PARALLEL_BATCH_GET_THRESHOLD`) are split into chunks and run on the database's existing `ParallelScheduler`. Smaller batches run serially, one chunk per shard.

docs.title: End the cache-signal read when `encryptActionBoundArgs` hits the RDC
docs.body:
### What?

End the `CacheSignal` read in `encryptActionBoundArgs` on the Resume Data Cache hit path, so a request's `cacheReady()` can resolve.

### Why?

`encryptActionBoundArgs` calls `startReadOnce()` before looking the serialized bound args up in the RDC. On a hit it returns the cached ciphertext immediately and never calls `endReadIfStarted()`, leaving the request's `CacheSignal` count at 1 forever.

With `partialPrefetching` the dynamic render embeds a runtime-prefetch stream in the initial RSC payload and only writes/closes it after `cacheSignal.cacheReady()` (`startRuntimePrefetchRender`). With the read never ended, that stream is never closed, the Flight stream never ends, the HTML `</body></html>` suffix is never flushed, and the HTTP response of every partially prerendered page that renders an inline Server Function with bound args never terminates in production (`next start`). curl waits for its timeout; browsers stay in `document.readyState === "loading"`.

The hit is the normal production case: the build-time prerender stores the encrypted bound args in the RDC, which is persisted in the postponed state whenever the page has at least one `"use cache"` entry.

### How?

Call `endReadIfStarted()` before returning `cachedEncrypted`, mirroring the miss path (which ends the read after `encodeActionBoundArg`) and the error path.

docs.title: fix(shared): keep .rsc in query parameters when normalizing
docs.body:
## What

`normalizeRscURL` runs `/\.rsc($|\?)/` over the whole URL, so a `.rsc` at the end of a **query value** is stripped:

```ts
normalizeRscURL('/test?file=foo.rsc')   // '/test?file=foo'
normalizeRscURL('/test?next=/a/b.rsc')  // '/test?next=/a/b'
```

`adapter()` applies this to `params.request.url` (full URL including the query) before constructing `NextURL`, so middleware and edge handlers observe a mutated query string.

## Fix

Strip `.rsc` only from the pathname, before the first `?`:

```ts
const queryIndex = url.indexOf('?')
if (queryIndex === -1) return url.replace(/\.rsc$/, '')
return url.slice(0, queryIndex).replace(/\.rsc$/, '') + url.slice(queryIndex)
```

The existing `'/test.rsc?abc=def' -> '/test?abc=def'` behaviour is preserved.

## Tests

Added to `app-paths.test.ts`:

```ts
expect(normalizeRscURL('/test?file=foo.rsc')).toBe('/test?file=foo.rsc')
expect(normalizeRscURL('/test?next=/a/b.rsc')).toBe('/test?next=/a/b.rsc')
expect(normalizeRscURL('/test.rsc?next=/a/b.rsc')).toBe('/test?next=/a/b.rsc')
```

Verified by importing the TypeScript source directly with Node 24 type stripping (plus the repo's TS resolution loader):
- before: `'/foo?file=/report.rsc' -> '/foo?file=/report'`
- after: unchanged, while `'/test.rsc?abc=def' -> '/test?abc=def'` still works.

**Note:** this checkout has no `node_modules`, so the jest suite was not run.

docs.title: Don't block the dev overlay on the npm registry version check
docs.body:
## Summary

A slow or unreachable package registry can delay the dev server's version-staleness lookup. Turbopack currently awaits that lookup before sending the HMR `sync` message. Webpack and Rspack await it during hot-reloader startup. A late `sync` can also replay an error snapshot captured before the wait and clear newer build errors.

On the original base, delaying `sync` kept the entire dev overlay invisible, including build-error redboxes. #100629 independently fixed that client-side rendering dependency and is now merged. This PR removes the server-side delay and stale-error replay.

The version check is now non-blocking:

- **Immediate sync.** Until the lookup resolves, `sync` includes the installed version with `unknown` staleness. Later connections get the resolved value.
- **Version-only update.** When metadata resolves, connected clients receive a `versionInfo` HMR message. It updates only version metadata, rather than replaying errors or hash state through a second `sync`.
- **Current errors.** Turbopack collects issues when `sync` is built, after the remaining asynchronous work, not before it.
- **Non-blocking Webpack/Rspack startup.** The middleware starts with pending metadata, then caches and publishes the result.
- **Explicit rejection handling.** Both background broadcast chains log rejections, including exceptions in their success callbacks. Webpack also a

docs.title: Show dev overlay errors before the indicator state is known
docs.body:
## Summary

In development, the dev overlay renders nothing until the HMR `sync` message arrives. That message tells the client whether the dev indicator is disabled, and the client waits for it so a disabled indicator doesn't briefly appear. The error overlay (redbox) sat behind the same check, though. If `sync` was delayed or lost, compile and runtime errors already reached the client state but no redbox was shown.

This PR keeps the indicator-readiness check only for the indicator UI, meaning the devtools indicator and its panels. The error overlay and the contexts it needs now render independently of it, so errors show as soon as they are known. When `sync` arrives normally, the indicator behaves the same as before.

#100628 removes the server-side cause of a delayed `sync` (waiting on the npm registry version check). This change is independent and protects the overlay from any other delay.

A regression test uses Playwright websocket routing to withhold only the `sync` message. For both the app and pages router, it checks that a module-not-found error still shows the redbox and that the devtools indicator stays hidden.

## Verification

Run locally with Turbopack dev and webpack dev:

- New `test/development/app-dir/dev-overlay-redbox-before-sync`: fails without this change (no redbox) and passes with it.
- `test/development/acceptance/ReactRefreshLogBox-builtins.test.ts`

`pnpm new-test` with the `unit` type now generates a flat `test/unit/<name>.test.ts` from a template, and nothing else.

(Minimal repro to attach: an App Router page using `next/font/google`, built twice with a persisted `.next/cache` and different `NEXT_DEPLOYMENT_ID` values.)
 
1. App Router project with a `next/font` font (for example `Inter` from `next/font/google`) and `deploymentId` set via `NEXT_DEPLOYMENT_ID` (as on Vercel with Skew Protection).

docs.title: turbopack: use Bitset in compute_chunk_group_info
docs.body:
Stacked on #100566, which adds `turbo-bitset`. Stack: #100566 → this → #100567 (`collect_graph`) → #100568 (`compute_merged_modules`) → #100630 (persisted chunk group sets).

## Summary

`compute_chunk_group_info` tracked each module's chunk groups with `RoaringBitmapWrapper` during its fixed-point traversal. The traversal checks "would `current |= parent` change `current`?" on every edge and then does the union; on Roaring's array containers both cost time proportional to the number of bits, which made this the slowest of the module graph passes on `bench/nested-deps-app-router-many-pages`.

It now uses `Bitset` for the working per-module sets, and converts them with `to_roaring()` when building the result. `ModuleToChunkGroups`, the batch types and production chunking still use `RoaringBitmapWrapper`, so persisted values are unchanged (#100630 switches those). The old code called `RoaringBitmapWrapper::is_proper_superset` (which actually computed `!parent.is_subset(current)`) and then `|=`. Now `current.union_with(parent)` does both in one pass and returns whether it added a bit. The separate first-visit `is_zero()` check plus `clone()` is gone too: `union_with` copies into a set that stores no blocks. This doesn't change the traversal, as a parent's set is never empty when its children are visited.

docs.title: fix: don't report an unhandled rejection for hanging promises created after the prerender aborted
docs.body:
### What

Under Bun, `next build` prints `CLIENT_HOOK_DYNAMIC` errors for routes that use client hooks with `cacheComponents: true`. Node prints nothing for the same app.

### Why

When the render signal is already aborted, `makeHangingPromiseWithError` returns `Promise.reject(error)` with no handler attached. The other branch of the same function attaches `.catch(ignoreReject)`, but this one didn't.

On Node, the global `unhandledRejection` filter drops these because `workUnitAsyncStorage.getStore()` returns the aborted prerender store. Under Bun the listener doesn't run in the async context that created the promise, so `getStore()` is undefined and the rejection gets printed.

### Fix

Attach `.catch(ignoreReject)` to the rejected promise in the aborted branch too, the same as the other branch. Anything that awaits the promise (e.g. React's `use`) still receives the rejection.

### Testing

- Reproduced with https://github.com/CodingDiego/next-client-hook-dynamic-bun on `next@16.5.0-canary.24` and Bun 1.4.4 (`bun --bun next build`): 4 `CLIENT_HOOK_DYNAMIC` errors before, 0 after.
- Added tests in `packages/next/src/server/dynamic-rendering-utils.test.ts`:
  - no unhandled rejection when the signal is already aborted
  - no unhandled rejection when the signal aborts later

docs.title: Turbopack: ignore fully dynamic alternatives when tracing file paths
docs.body:
## Summary

With Turbopack, a file read whose path is _either_ an unknown value _or_ a known file traced the **entire project** into `.nft.json`, including `public/`. It also printed "Dynamic filesystem access causes tracing of the whole project". Two examples:

- `readFileSync(options.path ?? path.join(process.cwd(), 'manifest.json'))`
- a default parameter `p = path.join(process.cwd(), 'manifest.json')` that is then read

The default-parameter form regressed in 16.4: #97867 models default params as "caller's argument or the default". The `??` form behaved like this before.

A bare unknown path (`readFileSync(p)`) is already skipped when `ignore_dynamic_requests` is on, as it is for Next.js server and client code. The mixed case slipped through because `has_constant_parts()` is true as soon as _any_ alternative is constant. The unbounded alternative then resolved to every file in the project.

### Approach

A new `Pattern::filter_non_dynamic()` in `turbopack-core` keeps only the top-level alternatives that have constant parts. When dynamic requests are ignored, the file-tracing handlers trace that filtered pattern. The handlers are: fs reads, `fs.readdir`, `path.join`, `path.resolve`, `child_process.spawn` (its file reference) and `child_process.fork`. As a result:

- the known file is traced, and the unknown alternative is ignored, just as a bare unknown path is;

docs.title: fix(app-router): support NextResponse.redirect from Middleware during Server Actions
docs.body:
### What?

Allows \NextResponse.redirect\ called inside Middleware to properly redirect client-side Server Actions.

### Why?

Fixes #65394
Fixes #58281

When Middleware intercepts an incoming Server Action request (\POST\ with \
ext-action\ header) and returns \NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/login', req.url))\, Next.js previously responded with a standard HTTP 307 redirect carrying a \Location\ header.

Because the browser's native \ etch()\ automatically follows 307 redirects, it re-sent the \POST\ action body to \/login\. docs.title: fix(app-router): use slot-specific error boundary for parallel routes
docs.body:
### What?

Resolves and attaches the slot's own `error.tsx` boundary to `LayoutRouter` for parallel routes instead of forcing the parent layout's error boundary onto all parallel slots.

### Why?

Fixes #69852

When a parallel route slot (e.g. `@slot`) defines its own `error.tsx` boundary and an error occurs inside a dynamic or nested route within that slot (such as `@slot/page/[id]/page.tsx`), Next.js previously caught the error using the parent layout's `error.tsx` boundary.

This caused the entire parent route UI to be replaced by duplicate instances of the parent error boundary (e.g. showing two "Home error" boundaries instead of "Home page" + "Slot error").

### How?

1. In `packages/next/src/server/app-render/create-component-tree.tsx`, inspect `parsedParallelRoute.modules.error` when rendering `parallelRoutes` for non-children slots.
2. If the slot defines its own `error` component, create its styles and scripts and pass `slotErrorComponent` to the slot's `LayoutRouter`.
3. If no slot-specific error boundary is defined, gracefully fall back to the parent layout's `ErrorComponent`.
4. Added an automated end-to-end test suite in `test/e2e/app-dir/parallel-routes-error-boundary` covering both client-side navigation and direct SSR rendering when a slot throws inside a dynamic route.

docs.body:
### What?

Adds an `instrumentationInject?: string[]` config option. Next.js compiles one module that runs every entry's `register` and `onRequestError`, then the project's own `instrumentation.{ts,js}` if it has one. This works like `instrumentationClientInject` does for the client.

```

```text
instrumentation slot
  → each instrumentationInject entry, in array order
  → then the project's instrumentation file, if there is one

Hosting platforms want to give every app default instrumentation, such as OpenTelemetry tracing. Today that means asking users to add an `instrumentation.ts` and a dependency to their project. docs.title: Turbopack: resolve dynamic new URL() requests to the matching asset at runtime
docs.body:
### What?

Turbopack now picks the asset for `new URL(<pattern>, import.meta.url)` at runtime when the pattern is dynamic or matches several files, for example `` new URL(`./${name}`, import.meta.url) ``. Each runtime request now gets its own asset. Before this change, every request was rewritten to whichever match came first.

### Why?

The URL code generation went through `ReferencedAsset::from_resolve_result`, which only returns the first placeable module. As a result, a dynamic `new URL()` was silently compiled to one fixed and possibly wrong asset. For example, a library's worker URL pointed at an unrelated `.mjs` file from the same directory. This came up while looking into #99674.

### How?

- **One code path:** every rewritten `new URL()` now goes through `PatternMapping::create_url`, which follows the pattern of `create_id`, `create_require` and `create_import`.
  - A request without dynamic parts is decided at build time.
  - A request with dynamic parts always becomes a `__turbopack_module_context__(map, 1)(key)` lookup, even with zero or one result, because the runtime value may not be one of the resolved requests. The request expression is still evaluated exactly once.
- **Map entries:** URL map entries contain only `module` (no `id`).
- **URL per mode:** each module entry produces the same URL its single-match equivalent would:
  - Relative mode: a relative URL.

docs.title: Fix Turbopack incorrectly folding `navigator.serviceWorker` checks
docs.body:
Fixes #100457

## What

Fixes a Turbopack analyzer bug that incorrectly evaluates `navigator.serviceWorker` as definitely truthy and non-nullish, causing valid runtime feature checks to be removed from compiled JavaScript.

The fix ensures that checks against `navigator.serviceWorker` remain in the output when its runtime availability cannot be determined at compile time. It also adds regression tests covering analyzer behavior, compiled execution, and the affected Next.js application scenario.

## Why

Turbopack models `navigator.serviceWorker` as a `WellKnownObject` to support service worker bundling. However, the analyzer's existing truthiness and nullishness logic treats every well-known object as definitely truthy and non-nullish.

Unlike objects that are guaranteed to exist, `navigator.serviceWorker` is an optional browser API and may be `undefined` at runtime. As a result, expressions such as:

```js
if (!navigator.serviceWorker) {
  return 'unsupported';
}
```

can be incorrectly evaluated as always false during compilation. The analyzer marks the branch unreachable, allowing subsequent optimization to remove the guard entirely.

This causes code that relies on the feature check to execute unconditionally and potentially throw when service worker support is unavailable. The issue is particularly relevant to iOS in-app browsers and insecure contexts, where `navigator.ser

docs.title: Only emit Next.request for requests that reach a render, and make middleware the root otherwise
docs.body:
### What?

When middleware runs separately from the render (e.g. when deployed) without trace context, the inserted `Next.request` root span is now emitted only for requests that continue to a render, and it covers the render too, instead of ending with the middleware. Direct responses, redirects, external rewrites, a user-set render `traceparent` and middleware errors no longer get a `Next.request` span: `Middleware.execute` is the root span instead.

### Why?

`adapter()` inserts `Next.request` as the shared parent of the middleware span and the render. It wrapped only the middleware handler, so the root ended before its child, the render, even started. Its duration covered only the middleware. For requests that never continue to a render (a redirect, a direct response, an external rewrite), the extra root added nothing: `Next.request` should only wrap requests that are rewritten or continue with `NextResponse.next()`.

### How?

- **Middleware:** reserves the root instead of starting it (`reserveRequestSpan`). It takes the IDs and the sampling decision from the OpenTelemetry SDK's tracer (`_idGenerator`, `_sampler`) and runs the middleware under a non-recording parent with those IDs.
  - No unended SDK root is kept. Leaving one open would retain an entry in `@vercel/otel`'s open-root map for every request.
  - An unsampled decision is reserved too, so the sampler doesn't run

docs.title: Turbopack: Fix race condition with late dependents of async modules
docs.body:
Fixes #100385

### What

Fixes a race condition in Turbopack's async module runtime where a module that does not contain top-level `await` can be imported before its asynchronous dependencies have fully completed evaluation.

The runtime previously relied on forwarding dependency queues for modules without top-level `await`, leaving a window in which a dependency had resolved but the module's own exports had not yet been registered. A module first loaded during this window could proceed without waiting and access incomplete exports, resulting in runtime errors or silently incorrect values.

This change ensures that late dependents wait for the module to finish evaluating when necessary, while preserving the existing evaluation order and microtask timing for dependents that were already waiting.

### Why

Turbopack's async module runtime uses queues to coordinate module evaluation and ensure that dependent modules do not access exports before their dependencies are ready.

Modules containing top-level `await` have their own queue, but modules without top-level `await` previously relied solely on their dependencies' queues. Once a dependency's queue resolved, a newly loaded dependent could observe no unresolved queue and execute immediately, even though the intermediate module's continuation was still pending.

`output: 'standalone'` no longer turns `supportsImmutableAssets` off when an adapter (`adapterPath`) is configured. Standalone builds without an adapter behave as before.

Some self-hosted platforms run the standalone server and also configure an adapter (for `modifyConfig` and `onBuildComplete`). docs.title: turbo-persistence: make batch_get callback-oriented
docs.body:
## What?

`TurboPersistence::batch_get` no longer returns an ordered `Vec<Option<ArcBytes>>`. It now reports each key to a callback:

```rust
pub fn batch_get<K: QueryKey + Sync>(
    &self,
    family: usize,
    keys: &[K],
    on_result: impl Fn(usize, Option<ArcBytes>) -> Result<()> + Sync,
) -> Result<()>
```

- `on_result` gets the index of the key in `keys`, and its value, or `None` when the key is missing or deleted.
- On success it has been called exactly once per index, including each occurrence of a duplicate key. The calls are in no particular order and may run concurrently on the scheduler's threads: for batches above the parallel threshold, the callbacks run inside the parallel chunks.
- A read error or a callback error is returned. Other callbacks may already have run, and some indices may never be reported.
- `on_result` runs while the database holds its internal read lock, so it must not call back into the database.

The turbo-tasks backend is updated the whole way down:

- `TurboKeyValueDatabase::batch_get`, `TurboBackingStorage::batch_lookup_data` and `restore_task_data_batch` take the same kind of callback.
- `batch_lookup_data` decodes `TaskStorage` inside the callback.
- The batched restore in `prepare_tasks_with_callback` stores each decoded result in its `TaskRestoreEntry` directly. The entry's result fields are now `OnceLock`s, so the writes stay safe.

docs.title: Turbopack: use flat module context ids for dynamic requests
docs.body:
## Summary

A request with a dynamic part (``require(`./dir/${x}`)``, `require.resolve(...)`, ``import(`./dir/${x}`)``) created its context inline from an object with an `id` and a `module` function per entry, repeating each id twice:

```js
__turbopack_context__.f({ "./dir/a.js": { id: () => "<id>", module: () => __turbopack_context__.r("<id>") }, ... })(key)
```

When every entry is a module (or ignored), it now uses the flat `[key, id, ...]` form that `require.context()` uses (#100526), plus a mode that says how the modules are loaded:

```js

__turbopack_context__.f(["./dir/a.js", "<loader id>", ...], 2).import(key)  // import() via async loaders

Ignored and dropped entries are `undefined`. So the object form is gone from both codegen and runtime, and behavior is unchanged, except that a dropped entry (a target the module graph removed as unused) now requires to `{}` instead of `0`.

docs.title: Do not warn about unexpected cache misses in draft mode
docs.body:
### Fixing a bug

- Related issues linked using `fixes #number`
- Tests added

Fixes #100680

## What

In draft mode, every request that reaches a `'use cache'` function from a Cache Components route logged `Unexpected cache miss after cache warming phase during prerendering…`, once per cached function, although the render itself was fine.

## Why

When draft mode is enabled, the use-cache wrapper deliberately never saves cache entries (unpublished content must not be cached). The prospective prerender therefore cannot warm them, and the final prerender then treated the miss as a sign of a non-deterministic cache key and warned. In draft mode the miss is expected.

## How

Skip the warning when `workStore.isDraftMode` is set. The miss still becomes a dynamic hole exactly as before, so draft content is rendered at request time; only the misleading warning goes away.

Verified on the reproduction from the issue (next 16.5.0-canary.25 with this change applied): the draft-mode request now logs 0 warnings instead of 2, and the page body is unchanged (`name:nav`, `draft=true`).

Added `app/draftmode/use-cache/page.tsx` to the `cache-components` e2e fixture and a test in `cache-components.draft-mode.test.ts` that enables draft mode, renders the page, checks the cached value and the draft flag, and asserts that no "Unexpected cache miss" line was logged.

### What?

Fixed ISR entries that are prerendered at build time never revalidating when the build output files have an mtime of `0` (the Unix epoch), using the default `FileSystemCache` implementation.

### Why?

Reproducible build tools normalize file mtimes to the Unix epoch. For example, Bazel `rules_js` writes every file of a `js_image_layer` with `time=0`.

Routes rendered for the first time at runtime revalidated normally.

### How?

- Treated an epoch mtime as the time the server started (`performance.timeOrigin`) when reading App Page, App Route and Pages Router entries from disk in `FileSystemCache`.
- The entry is now regenerated in the background once it

docs.body:
## Fix startup hang caused by symlinked files not emitting `aggregated` events

### What?

Fixes a startup hang in the Next.js development server when files are reachable only through a symlinked directory.

Watchpack does not emit `aggregated` events for files that are only reachable through a symlinked directory. When these files are included in `initialPageFiles`, the startup wait loop can block indefinitely while waiting for an event that never arrives.

This change prevents symlinked files from incorrectly blocking startup and adds a deadline-based fallback to ensure that the initial scan cannot permanently stall the server.

### Why?

The development server relies on Watchpack's `aggregated` event to determine when the initial file scan has completed.

The startup hang occurs because the initial file snapshot can include files discovered by following a symlink, even though Watchpack does not report those files through the expected event mechanism.

As a result, the startup wait loop continues waiting for files that never become known to Watchpack. Although an initial scan deadline exists, it was only checked inside the `aggregated` event handler. If Watchpack emits an event at startup and the handler returns early, no subsequent event may arrive to trigger the deadline check.

This can leave `next dev` unresponsive to requests until another file change t

docs.body:
### What?

When an application uses parallel route slots where one slot has a catch-all route (e.g. `@modal/[...catchAll]`) and another parallel slot has static segments at that level (e.g. `children` containing `items/[itemId]/view`), URL matching traverses through the static sibling. Because the static branch matches the requested URL, parameters for the catch-all dynamic segment in the parallel slot are not resolved and are absent from `resolvedParams`.

Previously, `reifyRouteTree` fell through to inheriting `parentPartialVaryPath` when a parameter was missing from `resolvedParams`. This produced an incomplete vary path for the parallel slot that omitted the catch-all parameter. Because the server response keys on the actual parameter value, the client never marked the prefetch task satisfied, repeatedly re-requesting the segment in an infinite prefetch loop.

This change returns `null` from `reifyRouteTree` when encountering an unresolved dynamic parameter and propagates the `null` result upward through child slot iteration. In `matchKnownRoute`, a `null` reified route tree cleanly bails out to server resolution.

### Why?

Fixes #100055.

docs.title: perf(turbopack): canonicalize async loader availability
docs.body:
### What?

Canonicalize async-loader availability before constructing loaders for dynamic `import()` and `next/dynamic`, so parents that make the same modules available share loader tasks instead of creating them once per page.

Lazy-compilation proxies keep their activation paths stable; their actual targets still use canonicalization when their closures contain no further lazy proxies.

### Why?

`AsyncLoaderModule` and `async_loader_chunk_item` are keyed by `AvailabilityInfo`. Both the available chunk groups and `entry_group` carry per-parent information. On v0 there are about 196K `async_loader_chunk_item` tasks for a few hundred targets.

Intersecting availability with reachable groups alone isn't enough: a module shared with every page, such as `react/jsx-runtime`, keeps that intersection different per page.

### How?

- **Precompute observed sets in `compute_chunk_group_info`.** Build a chunk-group graph from async, shared/shared-merged and collected references, then close over it per strongly connected component. For each async target, record the distinct chunk-group sets tested during chunking, their union, and whether it needs `entry_group`. Store this in a keyed cell on `ChunkGroupInfo`.

docs.title: Turbopack: add minServerChunkSize and maxMergeServerChunkSize options
docs.body:
### What?

Adds two experimental options under `experimental.turbopackChunking`:

- `minServerChunkSize` — the minimum chunk size used by Turbopack's production chunker for Node.js server-side JavaScript.
- `maxMergeServerChunkSize` — the size above which a Node.js server chunk is never merged with other chunks.

Both apply only to the Node.js server chunking context (production builds only). Edge chunking is unchanged and not configurable.

### Why?

`minChunkSize` / `maxMergeChunkSize` only affect client-side chunking. The Node.js server context used hardcoded thresholds, so there was no way to tune server chunking (e.g. to trade fewer, larger server chunks against duplication).

Edge is intentionally left out: Edge functions have a much smaller size limit, so its existing hardcoded thresholds (min `20000`, no max merge limit) are kept as-is.

### How?

- The options follow the same path as the existing client thresholds: config type + zod schema → `TurbopackChunkingConfig` / `TurbopackChunking` in `next-core` → `Project` → `ServerChunkingContextOptions`, used by both the regular and the `_with_client_assets` Node.js variants.
- When unset, the previously hardcoded Node.js values are used (min `4000`, max merge `100000`), so default output is unchanged.
- Only the ECMAScript chunk type is affected; client chunking, CSS chunking and the edge chunking context are untouched.

docs.title: fix(metadata): add trailing slash before hash in metadata URLs
docs.body:
### What?

Fix trailing slash handling for metadata URLs with hash fragments when `trailingSlash: true` and `metadataBase` is set.

Right now, `/foo#bar` becomes `/foo#bar/` instead of `/foo/#bar`. Even `/foo/#bar`, which already has the slash, gets changed to `/foo/#bar/`.

### Why?

The current code checks the full URL for a trailing slash and appends one at the end, without accounting for the hash.

I reproduced this on `next@16.5.0-canary.27` with `next build`. Both canonical and `og:url` in the generated HTML are affected.

### How?

Use `parsePath()` to separate the path, query, and hash. The trailing slash check now looks at the path, and the slash is added before the hash.

Previously, a `?` inside the fragment was treated as a query, so `/foo#bar?baz` got no trailing slash at all. It now becomes `/foo/#bar?baz`.

### Tests

Added tests for URLs with fragments, existing trailing slashes, query strings, `URL` objects, and `trailingSlash: false`.

I ran `resolve-url.test.ts` with Jest 29.7.0 outside the monorepo setup (21/21 passing). One new regression test fails without the fix.

I also checked the generated HTML using a compiled Next.js test app with the patched resolver.

Prettier passes. I haven't run the full monorepo checks or e2e tests locally.

`BailoutToCSRForNextDynamic` now only uses `ReactDOM.browser` when it exists. Otherwise it falls back to the existing `BailoutToCSRError` path.

### Why?

With `experimental.reactBrowserBailout` on (#96826), `next/dynamic` with `ssr: false` calls `browser()` from `react-dom`. Unlike the other `browser()` call sites, this component also renders in the browser.

When React is shared with another app at runtime (module federation, remote-components), `react-dom` can resolve to an older React that has no `browser`, for example a host on an earlier Next or on npm `react-dom` 19.2. Rendering the lazy component then throws:

```
TypeError: (0 , o.browser) is not a function
```

We hit this in [remote-components](https://github.com/vercel/remote-components) with a Next 16.5 canary App Router remote on Pages Router, Vite and older App Router hosts. Client-side module federation between apps on different Next versions would hit the same thing.

### How?

Feature-detect `browser` alongside the flag. The other `browser()` callers (`dynamic-rendering-client.ts`, `render-in-browser.ts`) only run on the server with the app's own bundled React, so they're unchanged.

Added a unit test that removes `browser` from `react-dom` and checks the children still render. Checked by hand against `react-dom@19.3.0-canary-da9325b5-20260417`, which has no `browser`: the origin

docs.title: Turbopack: fix trailing-slash package root resolution
docs.body:
### What?

Fix trailing-slash package-root resolution in Turbopack, including dynamic CommonJS requests with an empty runtime suffix.

### Why?

The package-root result could be keyed as a bare package request even when the request included a trailing slash. Dynamic module contexts then lacked the slash-root key and threw `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` for a valid package entry. Exact trailing-slash requests could also resolve the same folder twice through overlapping root and relative-subpath paths.

### How?

Resolve matching package roots once while preserving distinct bare and trailing-slash request keys. Only use relative-subpath resolution for patterns that can match deeper paths, leaving package-exports handling unchanged.

Add keyed Rust coverage for main/index fallback, exports and dynamic patterns, plus a loader-free execution fixture that distinguishes the package main from index and checks real and missing subpaths.

### Verification

- Confirmed the execution regression fails on the unfixed resolver and passes with the correction.
- `cargo nextest run -p turbopack-tests --test execution -E 'test(resolving)'` — 33 fixtures passed.
- `cargo test -p turbopack-core --lib` — 198 passed; 2 existing ignored benchmarks.

docs.title: eslint: check alt only on Image imported from next/image
docs.body:
Fixes #75482

### What?

Adds `@next/next/image-alt-text`, a rule that requires an `alt` prop on `<Image />` components imported from `next/image` or `next/legacy/image`. It's enabled as `warn` in `eslint-config-next`.

### Why?

`eslint-config-next` currently checks `next/image` alt text by mapping the JSX name `Image` onto `jsx-a11y/alt-text` (`img: ['Image']`). That matches by name, not by import, so it gets two cases wrong:

- **False positives:** any component named `Image` is flagged, including ones from `lucide-react`, `expo-image` or a local `const Image = ...`.
- **False negatives:** `next/image` imported under another name (`import NextImage from 'next/image'`) is never checked.

The new rule resolves the element to its import, so it checks the default export of `next/image` and `next/legacy/image` whatever the local name is, and ignores same-named components from elsewhere.

### How?

- **Rule (`packages/eslint-plugin-next`)**
  - Follows the import binding: default imports, aliases, `{ default as X }`, and `<NS.default />` from `import * as NS`. A local binding that shadows the import is ignored.
  - Reports `missingAlt` when `alt` is absent, and `invalidAlt` for a bare `alt`, `alt={undefined}`, `alt={null}` or `alt={false}`.
  - `alt=""` is allowed for decorative images.
  - A non-empty `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` counts as a label, match

docs.title: Fix draft mode rendering with Cache Components
docs.body:
PR #77141 made `'use cache'` bypass cache-handler reads and cache persistence when draft mode is enabled. Later changes, including #98005, made cached navigations reuse the static RDC. The additional postponed-state lookup for self-hosted RSC navigations and Server Actions did not check draft mode, so those renders could reuse published values.

Draft mode HTML page loads already bypassed the response cache. Both document and navigation responses could still generate an embedded runtime prefetch with Partial Prefetching. Its final prerender expected RDC entries that draft mode deliberately did not save, which caused unexpected cache miss warnings.

This change skips the additional postponed-state lookup for draft mode requests and disables cached-navigation rendering for their document and navigation responses. Server Actions that enable draft mode discard the published RDC before the subsequent render.

Dedicated runtime-prefetch requests still use their existing renderer. PR #98533 proposes disabling client-initiated prefetches in draft mode. That work remains separate and may continue in a replacement PR.

The tests cover fresh draft mode documents and navigations, actions that enable and disable draft mode, and form submissions without JavaScript.

Fixes #100680
Closes #100685
Closes #100697

docs.title: App Router sends no requests on iOS Safari when crypto.subtle.digest never resolves (16.4 cache-busting hash)
docs.body:
No minimal repro yet. It happens on one production app, only on one real device (see below). Details and a one-line workaround are below.
 

**Current (16.4.2, still the same code in 16.4.3 and 16.5.0-canary.27):** on an iPhone in Safari, while logged in to our app, client navigation stops working. `<Link>` taps and `router.push` show the pending state forever: the old page stays dimmed and the new route never loads. A full reload works. Logged out on the same phone, everything works.

**Expected:** navigation works, as it did on 16.2.1.

### What we found

The `?trace=1` overlay in our app records every `fetch()` the page makes, plus the segment-cache scheduler's state. During the stall:

- the prefetch scheduler sat at **4 requests in progress** (the `inProgressRequests < 4` cap) with **0 response bodies being read**;
- **no `fetch()` was ever made** for those 4 requests, so no prefetch or navigation request went out at all;
- no JS errors and no unhandled rejections.

Every router request runs through `setCacheBustingSearchParam`, which awaits `computeClientCacheBustingSearchParam` before calling `fetch`. Since the SHA-256 change, that function calls `crypto.subtle.digest('SHA-256', …)` whenever `crypto.subtle` exists:

docs.title: Optimize persistence CPU
docs.body:
A few small optimizations from profiling

* Replace SmallVec with Vec for our encoding buffer
    - During persistence these are pooled and preallocated so we never benefit from the inline storage
    - SmallVec places branches around core operations which complicate codegen
* Avoid temporary allocations during encoding via a new 'filtered collection encode primitive'.  This allows us to guess a size and fix it later by overwriting the varint.
* Expand the SST Writer output buffer to 256K to reduce the number of `write` syscalls by about 90%
* Update to the new bincode-fork location in vercel-labs, which also picks up a small varint encoding win

Altogether these saved about 10% cpu time and 25% wall time for v0 persistence

docs.title: Add a CLI for reviewing agent feedback
docs.body:
## Why

Agent Feedback reports are created inside coding environments that often cannot launch a local browser. The previous instructions made the final handoff depend on the agent finding and invoking host-specific browser tooling. In headless, sandboxed, or remote sessions, that step could fail even when the anonymized report itself was valid, leaving the maintainer without a usable review link.

This happened in practice when an agent could not share its feedback and had to be told to run a browser command manually. Browser control should not be part of the Agent Feedback reporting contract.

## What changed

- add the hidden `next internal agent-feedback [report]` command as the supported handoff for an encoded v5 Agent Feedback report
- keep the command internal because it is protocol machinery, not a public semver-covered CLI surface
- accept the report as a positional argument or through stdin, validate the complete v5 schema, and always print the review URL before attempting to open the default browser
- preserve the printed URL when browser launching is unavailable or fails
- bound stdin to 16 KiB and a five-second read deadline using Node's async iterator and `AbortController`
- support `--dry-run` for validation and URL generation without opening a browser
- update the Agent Feedback protocol and evals to use the internal CLI instead of host-specific browser commands

docs.title: Render complete HTML documents after MPA Server Actions
docs.body:
MPA form submissions to Cache Components pages could return only the continuation of a prerender. The action executed, but the response omitted the HTML document and did not render the returned `useActionState` value.

This change renders a complete document for MPA form submissions while retaining the RDC supplied by the prerender. This preserves ordinary `'use cache'` values on deployments where the default handler has no prerendered entries in memory. The action handler also prepares the render phase for MPA form submissions that do not revalidate data. Ordinary not-found responses include the root layout.

The diagnosis and reproduction in #99981 identified the self-hosted case. This fix also handles postponed state supplied by Vercel before the action body, without changing how that body is decoded.

The tests cover plain and stateful forms, both postponed-state variants, submission before hydration, cache reuse, invalidation, blocking routes, and ordinary and global not-found responses.

Fixes #99756
Closes #99981

docs.body:
## Summary

App Router can briefly remove the document title during navigation even when the destination's head is already renderable.

The empty placeholder originates at [`cachedRsc = ''` in `render-tree.ts`](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/7748e532a1abeb4387a722b0f1665bd53218f51a/packages/next/src/client/components/render-tree.ts#L1181-L1201). When optimistic routing encounters a partial head, this intentionally supplies an empty renderable fallback so a pending viewport does not block navigation. That value is subsequently assigned to `prefetchRsc`.

Previously, [`Head` passed this fallback as the initial value to `useDeferredValue`](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/7748e532a1abeb4387a722b0f1665bd53218f51a/packages/next/src/client/components/app-router.tsx#L193-L202), rendering an empty head even when the final head was already renderable. Removing the existing `<title>` during that commit causes the tab to briefly show the URL before the final title is committed.

Render the final head first and use the prefetched head as a Suspense fallback when it suspends. This preserves the empty placeholder for a pending head while allowing an available final head to render immediately. Add a metadata navigation regression that observes intermediate document titles.

docs.title: fix(eslint-plugin-next): recognise Head and Script import aliases
docs.body:
## Summary

The existing ESLint rule relies on hard-coded component names (`Head` and `Script`) to detect violations. It misses aliases such as `NextHead` and `NextScript`, and can incorrectly report third-party components with the same names. The underlying problem is that it does not associate the local names with the modules they were imported from.

The fix first scans import declarations and uses two Sets to record all local names default-imported from `next/head` and `next/script`, supporting both `import X from '...'` and `import { default as X } from '...'`. When checking JSX, it looks up the parent and child names in the corresponding Sets. This bases the decision on the import source rather than a fixed name. It only corrects the lint rule and does not change Next.js runtime behaviour.

## Verification

The regression tests cover aliases, multiple imports, third-party components with the same names, and both default-import forms. Five tests in the initial regression set failed against the original implementation. With the fix, all 245 plugin tests pass, along with the plugin build, type checking and formatting checks. Full scope/shadowing analysis is outside this change, and the whole repository has not been fully validated.

docs.title: Use fixed encoding for our 'id' types
docs.body:
Varint encoding works well for things like lengths/indicies which are naturally 'zero biased' but many of our 'id' types are not like that

Switch them to use a fixed encoding

This includes: 

* `TaskId` mostly 5 bytes before, now 4 bytes always
* `CellId` always 5 bytes before, now 4 bytes always
* `RawVc` always 9 bytes before, 8 bytes now
* `FunctionId` mostly 3 bytes before, now 2 bytes
* `ValueTypeId` mostly 3 bytes before now 2 bytes
* `TraitTypeId` transformed to a `NonZeroU8` so it always takes the fixed int encode path naturally

In principle it is possible that we might still benefit from varint encoding if most of the uses of these ids were biased towards smaller values, but at least in practice this isn't the case.

### Results

Measured on a large app comparing to canary

| | canary | this PR | change | per-round range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Cache size after cold build** | 2.646 GB | 2.546 GB | **−3.8%** | −3.8 to −3.7% |
| **Cache size after warm build** (compacted) | 2.628 GB | 2.527 GB | **−3.8%** | −3.9 to −3.7% |
| **Warm build user CPU** (mostly decoding) | 43.8s | 42.2s | **−3.7%** | −5.1 to −2.3% |
| Cold build user CPU | 482.6s | 483.0s | +0.1% | −1.4 to +1.0% |

docs.title: turbo-tasks-backend: resolve task priority when creating child contexts
docs.body:
### What?

`ExecuteContext::child_context()` in `turbo-tasks-backend` now reads the current task priority on the calling thread. The resulting `ChildExecuteContext` stores a priority that is already known, instead of an optional one.

### Why?

Both users of `child_context()` hand the child context to `scope_bounded` helper threads:

- the parallel path of `connect_children` (≥10k new children)
- the parallel invalidation of output dependents

Before this change the child context copied an override that is usually unset. On a helper thread, `get_current_task_priority()` then fell back to the task-local task state. That state only exists on the thread running the task, so helper threads got `TaskPriority::initial()`. Tasks scheduled or made dirty from those chunks (e.g. via `make_task_dirty_internal`) therefore got a priority that depended on which thread ran the chunk.

### How?

The priority is resolved in `child_context()`, on the thread that creates the context. An explicit override still wins; otherwise the task-local priority is read before the work moves to another thread. Making the field non-optional means a child context can no longer carry an unresolved priority.

Putting the fix in `child_context()` covers both parallel users, and any future one. Neither user relied on the late lookup, because the child context always runs on another thread. Paths that don't go paral

docs.title: [lts-maintenance] Backport synchronous Flight ping recovery
docs.body:
## What?

Backport React's synchronous render-phase ping recovery to Next.js 15's maintenance renderer.

Refs react/react#37830 and react/react#37805. The original React correction is react/react#36134 (`c0d218f0f3`), which Next.js already adopted on canary through #91905. The React DOM builds pinned by Next.js 15.5.28 still lack that correction.

## Why?

A production navigation can receive its complete Flight response but remain stuck on the previous content. When a pending Flight chunk receives its model row during React's render yield, it can remain `resolved_model` until React subscribes. Flight then initializes the chunk and invokes the ping callback synchronously.

If the root is already suspended with delay, the old render-phase branch neither restarts the render nor records the pinged lanes. The render subsequently marks those lanes suspended again, leaving no retry scheduled. An unrelated state update can unblock the transition.

## How?

- Apply the existing upstream correction: record render-phase pinged lanes so `markRootSuspended` preserves the opportunity to retry.
- Keep the pinned React versions and unrelated fixes intact. Persist the correction in two pnpm package patches and regenerate the ten affected normal/experimental React DOM bundles.
- Add a deterministic production browser regression using the real Flight decoder and lazy chunk initialization. Assert

docs.body:
Fixes #100769

### What?

`no-head-element` now only skips files that are actually inside the project's `app` directory.

### Why?

The rule checked whether the absolute filename contained `app/`. Any checkout whose path happened to contain that substring — `webapp/`, `my-app/`, or `/app/` inside a container — was treated as App Router code, so the rule silently reported nothing.

### How?

Resolve the filename and compare it against `<root>/app` and `<root>/src/app`. `getRootDirs` is used so `settings.next.rootDir` keeps working for monorepos.

Added regression tests for files under `webapp/`, `my-app/` and `/app/`, plus a valid `src/app` case.

docs.title: fix(eslint-plugin-next): accurately detect app directory in path resolution
docs.body:
### What?
Fixes an issue where ESLint rules `@next/next/no-head-element` and `@next/next/no-before-interactive-script-outside-document` were silently skipped when linting files in repositories whose path contains `app` (such as `my-app`, `webapp`, or Docker `/app`).

### Why?
The rules previously checked whether `context.filename` contained the substring `app/` or `app\`. When checked out under directories containing `app` (e.g., `.../my-app/pages/index.jsx` or `/app/pages/index.jsx`), this substring check falsely matched parent folder names instead of the Next.js App Router directory, causing rule enforcement for `pages/` files to be bypassed.

### How?
1. Added an `isInAppDir(context)` helper in `packages/eslint-plugin-next/src/utils/get-root-dirs.ts` that resolves file paths relative to `getRootDirs(context)` and tests for a leading `app/` or `src/app/` segment.
2. Updated `no-head-element` and `no-before-interactive-script-outside-document` to use `isInAppDir(context)`.
3. Added unit tests for both rules covering parent paths containing `app` segments.

Fixes #100769

### What?

`collectSegmentPrefetchResponses` in the `segment-cache/vary-params-base-dynamic` suite now starts from a new page, `/link-accordions`, instead of `/`. The new page renders only the two `LinkAccordion`s.

### Why?

The helper reveals an accordion link inside `act`, which expects at least one router request to start.

#91737 added visible navigation links to `/` for the back/forward cases. They point to the same routes, and they can trigger prefetches for them when they enter the viewport, before `act` starts. Whether this happens depends on how long the browser takes to get from hydration to `act`, so the suite is flaky on slower machines. docs.title: turbo-bitset: make block storage pluggable
docs.body:
### What?

`turbo_bitset::Bitset` can now use different storage for its blocks. A new public `BlockStorage` trait defines what that storage must support.

- `Bitset` is now `Bitset<S: BlockStorage = Vec<usize>>`, so every existing user keeps `Vec<usize>` storage.
- The trait is implemented for `Vec<usize>`, `SmallVec<[usize; N]>` and `ArrayVec<usize, N>`. `turbo-bitset` now depends on `smallvec` and `arrayvec` unconditionally.
- All `Bitset` methods and operators, plus `Encode`, `Decode` and `ShrinkToFit`, work with any storage. Set operations require both sides to use the same storage. The `turbo-tasks` integrations remain on the default `Bitset`.
- The encoding doesn't depend on the storage, so bytes written with one storage decode into any other.
- With `ArrayVec`, operations that would need more than its capacity of `N` blocks panic. Decoding a set that doesn't fit returns a `DecodeError`.
- `shrink_to_fit` only touches the storage when that frees capacity. An `ArrayVec` or an inline `SmallVec` is left unchanged.

### Why?

This lets small sets use inline storage where that helps, without making every `Bitset` user change its storage type.

### How?

- **Bounded storage:** when an operation would exceed an `ArrayVec`'s capacity, empty blocks at either end of the storage are dropped first. This fixes a case where an insert at the back panicked although the bits fit, because

docs.title: Turbopack: add build cache portability e2e test and fix location-dependent tasks
docs.body:
### What?

Adds an e2e test that checks whether the Turbopack filesystem build cache survives moving the project to another directory. It also fixes the first portability problems the test found.

It relies on the `executions` counter in turbo-tasks task statistics, added in #101025.

### Why?

A restored build cache should still be valid when the project sits at a different absolute path. That happens with CI checkouts, Docker build contexts, and caches restored into another workspace. Today, moving a project makes many tasks re-execute even though nothing changed. This PR adds a way to measure that and removes some of the causes.

### How?

**Test** (`test/e2e/app-dir/turbopack-portable-build-cache`, Turbopack production builds only, not deploy):

- Each case runs a cold `next build`, a warm build in the same directory, then moves the whole project root (including `.next`) and runs another warm build.
- Every build writes turbo-tasks task statistics (`NEXT_TURBOPACK_TASK_STATISTICS`) to a temporary file outside the project. The test collects the functions with `executions > 0`.
  - `cache_miss` isn't enough: it only counts newly created tasks, while a restored task that re-executes after an invalidation counts as a cache hit. #101025 adds the `executions` counter.
- Inline snapshots record the sorted executed function names for the same-dir and moved builds. All `NextConfig`

docs.title: Persist storage cache in Docker environments
docs.body:
### What?

Next.js now persists its server-side storage cache in Docker environments, the same as other environments. This covers the RSC / Server Actions encryption key, preview-mode keys, and the development Chrome DevTools workspace identifier.

### Why?

The shared storage-directory helper previously disabled `.next/cache` persistence whenever Docker was detected. As a result, Docker environments could not reuse cached RSC encryption secrets across separate key-generation processes.

### How?

The shared helper now always resolves the cache directory beneath the configured dist directory. Because storage is always available, each consumer drops the now-unreachable fallback path and uses the existing cache read/write flow directly. Existing key validation, expiry-based rotation during builds, and `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` precedence are unchanged.

Telemetry is intentionally unchanged: it has its own storage-location logic for CI and Docker, which already stores telemetry configuration in `.next/cache` there.

### Verification

- Ran a focused probe against the updated source with Docker detection mocked. It confirmed RSC encryption-key cache write and reuse, expired-key handling for runtime and builds, explicit encryption-key precedence, and preview-key cache write and reuse.
- `pnpm --filter=next types`
- Not run: full Next.js integration tests.

docs.title: fix(next/image): return 400 for malformed percent-encoded local `url`
docs.body:
### What?

When `url` is a local path containing malformed percent-encoding such as `/%`, a `URIError: URI malformed` is thrown and the request fails with a 500. Every other invalid `url` (e.g. one starting with `file://` or `//`, or one that is too long) returns a 400, so I made this case return a 400 with `"url" parameter is invalid` as well.

### Why?

In `validateParams` in `image-optimizer.ts`, the absolute URL branch wraps `new URL()` in a try/catch and returns `"url" parameter is invalid`, but the `decodeURIComponent` call in the local path branch is outside any try/catch. So when `/%` is passed, the `URIError` escapes `validateParams` and skips the usual path, where `validateParams` returns `{ errorMessage }` and the caller (`next-server.ts`) turns it into a 400. The error is also neither `ERR_INVALID_URL` nor a `DecodeError`, so the 400 mapping in `base-server.ts` doesn't apply either, and the request ends up as a 500.

### How?

I wrapped the `decodeURIComponent` call in the local path branch in a try/catch, so it now returns `{ errorMessage: '"url" parameter is invalid' }` when decoding fails. I used `return` rather than `throw` because every other check in `validateParams` reports errors by returning `errorMessage` instead of throwing. The message is the same one the absolute URL branch uses for an invalid URL, so no new message is added.

When the dev server answers the Chrome DevTools workspace request (`/.well-known/appspecific/com.chrome.devtools.json`) and there's no persisted UUID yet, it now creates `<distDir>/cache` before writing `chrome-devtools-workspace-uuid`.

docs.title: turbo-tasks-backend: fan out large aggregation update job and removal batches
docs.body:
### What?

An aggregation update queue now runs large batches in parallel instead of one
by one:

- **Jobs:** when it holds at least 4096 `jobs`, all of them run in parallel.
- **Edge removals:** when at least 4096 edge removals are due, all of them run
  in parallel. Removals are due when no job, aggregation number update or
  balancing is pending; this is the same rule #100892 uses to process
  removals one by one.

How the parallel batch runs:

- Each chunk runs on a child execution context and pushes the work its jobs
  generate into a private buffer queue. Buffers are never processed.
- After all chunks finish, every buffer is merged back into the queue:
  - generated jobs are appended to `jobs`;
  - generated removals are appended to the deferred removals, FIFO;
  - aggregation number updates go through the same done-map-aware merging as
    regular pushes;
  - balance and find-and-schedule work stays deduplicated;
  - scheduled tasks keep their highest priority;
  - optimizations respect the queue's cap and budget. Refused optimizations
    set `optimization_pending`, as before.
- GC queues, fan-out buffers and contexts with a GC collectible callback never
  fan out.

docs.title: [testmode] Fix compressed HTTP responses with test proxy
docs.body:
## Summary

Fix compressed responses received by Node HTTP clients when `experimental.testProxy` is enabled. Requests outside a test context and proxy `continue` responses now use native HTTP passthrough, preserving the original compressed bytes and headers.

Normalize stale `Content-Encoding` and `Content-Length` headers when serializing fetched responses with supported compression encodings, including cloned fetch responses. Preserve explicitly constructed mock responses as supplied, including deliberately compressed bytes. Handlers that construct a response with a modified body must update its headers themselves. Preserve bodyless responses such as HEAD so their representation metadata remains available.

Add regression coverage for chunked responses and compressed bodies whose decoded length is shorter or longer than the upstream content length, across native passthrough, proxy continue, fetched responses, and modified responses. Also cover explicitly compressed mocks, fetched-response clones, unsupported encodings, and HEAD metadata.

## Verification

- All 36 testmode integration tests passed in development mode with webpack, using the published native binding because the local native build has an incompatible lockfile API.
- Confirmed the standalone gzip reproduction fails against the unchanged build and passes with native passthrough.

docs.title: Add model metadata to Agent Feedback
docs.body:
## Summary

Agent Feedback currently records the coding harness but not the model that produced a report. In a recent sample, 61 of 108 reports named only a harness such as Claude Code, opencode, or Codex. That prevents us from comparing production friction with eval results by model, harness version, or reasoning effort.

This updates the Agent Feedback protocol to schema version 6 and asks reporting agents to include structured:

- harness version
- model identifier
- reasoning effort

Agents use `unknown` when their environment does not expose a value instead of inferring it. Existing schema v4 and v5 report links remain valid.

- https://github.com/vercel/front/pull/94097 updates the nextjs.org review UI to parse v6 reports and show the harness, harness version, model, and reasoning effort under **Attached to this report**.

The receiver must support v6 before this protocol change lands. The Front change makes the added metadata visible during report review but does not block receipt of v6 reports.

docs.title: turbo-tasks-backend: wait for a late add instead of panicking after MAX_RETRIES
docs.body:
### Why?

Large Turbopack builds crash at random with this panic:

```
inner_of_upper_lost_follower is not able to remove follower ... as it doesn't exist as upper or follower edges
```

The `inner_of_uppers_lost_follower` and `inner_of_upper_lost_followers` variants show up too. In a large monorepo's CI (an app of about 20M tasks), it fails 1 to 2% of production builds, and some changes fail several times in a row. Retrying the same commit usually passes. This is the same panic as #90053 and #89950.

### What?

A lost-follower job that runs before its matching add retries and requeues itself. After `MAX_RETRIES` (60,000, about a minute) it panics, assuming the edge is missing for real. With this change, such a job keeps waiting while any aggregation update queue is still processing work, because that work may hold the add. It waits without spinning, and it still panics once no queue is working.

### How?

**What led to the fix.** We instrumented the retry loop in that build so it logged instead of panicking. Every stuck removal eventually found its edge: the matching add was still queued behind other work. Typically that work is one queue re-balancing all the edges of an aggregating task with thousands of followers, which took over two minutes in one trace. Prevents `Error: spawn E2BIG` when applications running in standalone output mode spawn child processes, by passing standalone configuration via `globalThis` and avoiding giant serialized JSON strings in `process.env.__NEXT_PRIVATE_STANDALONE_CONFIG`.

When running with `output: 'standalone'`, the generated `server.js` set `process.env.__NEXT_PRIVATE_STANDALONE_CONFIG = JSON.stringify(nextConfig)`.
