docs.title: Fix blocking revalidation for `fetch` and `unstable_cache`
docs.body:
> [!TIP]
> This PR is best reviewed with whitespace changes hidden.

With Cache Components enabled, a page that uses cached `fetch` calls or `unstable_cache` can return a 500 during on-demand revalidation, including blocking regeneration after `expire`. Both wrappers skip the incremental cache lookup, so the final prerender cannot reuse the data computed by the prospective pass. It repeats asynchronous work and fails with `NEXT_STATIC_GEN_BAILOUT`.

The incremental cache now reads the Resume Data Cache (RDC) during on-demand revalidation before it bypasses persisted entries. Both `unstable_cache` and cached `fetch` calls use this path, so the final prerender can reuse the prospective pass's result.

This extends the fix proposed in PR #100895 to cached fetches and preserves the forced-refresh behavior introduced in PR #48516. The incremental cache continues to apply its tag invalidation checks before it returns an entry.

Fixes #99866
Closes #100895

docs.title: Honor explicit experimental.cpus when capping build workers
docs.body:
### What?

Makes `next build` honor an explicitly configured `experimental.cpus` instead of capping the worker count at the number of route entries.

### Why?

With an explicit `experimental.cpus`, `next build` could use far fewer workers than configured. In the repro, `cpus: 16` with one `generateStaticParams` route returning 2,000 paths logged "Generating static pages using 4 workers". Adding 20 extra routes made it use 16.

The cause is `getNumberOfWorkers(config, maxTasks)` in `packages/next/src/build/index.ts`, which caps workers at `maxTasks + 1`. The caller passes `maxTasks` as the number of route entries (pages + app), not the number of paths to prerender. The same capped count also sizes the shared static worker pool used for page-data collection and static generation.

This affects apps with few routes but many paths. The reporter's app has about 61k paths from a single route, and the build took about 15 minutes on 4 workers of a 96-core machine. This change restores the configured behavior; how much faster a given build gets depends on the machine and the app.

### How?

- An explicit `experimental.cpus` is now tracked and skips the cap.
- The default and `memoryBasedWorkersCount` paths still use the cap, so small apps don't spawn unnecessary workers.
- `getNumberOfWorkers` is only used by `next build`, so the dev server isn't affected.

docs.title: Docs: import.meta.glob with base changed its result keys in 16.4 — breaking change shipped without a changelog note or upgrade guidance
docs.body:
### What is the documentation issue?

In Next.js 16.4.0, import.meta.glob(..., { base }) (Turbopack) started returning keys relative to
  base instead of relative to the importing file. Code that parsed the keys broke silently after
  upgrading: no build error, no runtime error, no warning. The data just stopped showing up.

  The change came from #96557. Its title presents it as a bug fix ("resolve ../ and /-rooted
  import.meta.glob patterns"). The key-format change appears only in the PR description, and in the
  release notes it is one line among several hundred in the auto-generated changelog. The 16.4 blog
  post, the upgrade guide (version-16.md) and next upgrade --agent do not mention it.

  

### Is there any context that might help us understand?

#### What happened to us

  We auto-discover config modules in a sibling directory and group them by their first folder:

  const modules = import.meta.glob('./**/config.ts', { eager: true, base: '../plugins' });

  const group = tail.split('/')[0];

  On 16.4 the /plugins/ segment is no longer in the key, so every module resolved to group ''. The

docs.title: [ci] Resolve the PR to comment on from the workflow run alone
docs.body:
`PR CI Comment` trusted the artifact from an untrusted producer: the workflow on a PR.

While the PR comment is informative only, it was still subject to vandalism and phishing.

The artifact is gone, along with the `pr-ci-metadata` job that produced it and the download step. The target is resolved from `head_repository` and `head_branch`, which GitHub mints into the `workflow_run` payload: `GET /pulls?head={owner}:{branch}`, preferring open pull requests and falling back to any state only for a pull request whose head is the exact commit the run reported on.

The obvious alternatives were checked against the live API first, because they do not work:

| source | fork PRs |
| --- | --- |
| `commits/{sha}/pulls` | returns `[]` |
| `workflow_run.pull_requests` | empty, and sometimes empty for branch PRs too |
| `pulls?head={owner}:{branch}` | resolves |

That is why the artifact existed in the first place.


### Behavior changes

- Runs that ran no jobs (`cancelled`, `action_required`, `startup_failure`) are skipped. They previously resolved no pull request and silently did nothing. Now that fork runs resolve, they would otherwise post an empty `## Failing CI jobs` report. This also fixes that happening today on branch PRs, where a force push leaves a `cancelled` run that rewrites the comment that way.
- A run that comes back completed after a new commit reache

docs.title: fix: preserve IPv6 address in getHostname from the Host header
docs.body:
What?

getHostname() returns the wrong value for an IPv6 address passed in the Host header. For a host like [::1]:3000, it returns [ instead of [::1].

Why?

To drop the port, the function did host.split(':', 1)[0]. That works for example.com:3000, but an IPv6 literal in a Host header is wrapped in brackets and full of colons ([::1]:3000), so splitting on the first colon leaves just [. The function’s other code path — when it reads from a parsed URL — already returns [::1] correctly, so the same function gave two different answers for the same host. This affects i18n domain-locale detection and routing, which rely on getHostname.

How?

When the host starts with [, keep everything up to and including the closing ] instead of splitting on :. This matches what URL.prototype.hostname returns, so both code paths now agree. Added IPv6 cases to the existing get-hostname.test.ts.

Always minify ecmascript chunk items one by one when minification is enabled, and remove `experimental.turbopackMinifyBeforeChunking` together with the whole-chunk minification path.

docs.title: Add injectInstrumentation for adapter-supplied instrumentation
docs.body:
Add an `injectInstrumentation` config option. When the project has no
instrumentation file, Next.js compiles one module that runs every entry's
`register` and `onRequestError` in array order. An entry that throws does
not stop the others; errors are rethrown once all have run. A deployment
adapter sets the option from `modifyConfig`; a project instrumentation file
always wins.

webpack uses `next-instrumentation-inject-loader` on a stub entry. Turbopack
generates the same CommonJS module as a virtual `instrumentation.inject.cjs`
at the project root, so every entry resolves from the project.

docs.title: Fix navigations receiving a fallback shell on a cache miss
docs.body:
A client navigation to a `generateStaticParams` path crashes with React error #412 when its cache entry is missing, for example with a custom `cacheHandler` that starts empty or has evicted it. These paths have a `prefetchDataRoute`, so the navigation is handled as a static RSC request and receives the route's fallback shell, which doesn't have complete Flight data. Without Partial Prefetching the concrete entry is never written either, so every navigation to that path crashes.

A navigation now blocks on a prerender of the concrete path, which also writes the entry. This also keeps the navigation on the client with the default cache, where the same miss (for example after `revalidateTag(tag, { expire: 0 })`) gets a 404 and a full page load because the shell has no `rscData`.

A navigation can still receive an incomplete entry, by joining a concurrent document request that is serving the shell, or when the page is no longer fully static after the build (#98555). It now gets the same 404, so the router falls back to a document navigation instead of crashing. Both cases are covered by tests.

Fixes #99861

docs.body:
Placeholder images are SVGs with small 8px-wide webp/jpeg/avif/png/etc images inside and a Gaussian blur filter applied (using SVG).

In prod, we eagerly generate blurred placeholder images during codegen and inject them as base64-encoded URIs. That's important because it lets us show the placeholder as soon as the HTML is ready. In that case, the `next/image` component wraps it in an svg itself.

In webpack dev, we lazily generate the blurred placeholder image inside of an svg by pointing it to the image optimization route (`/_next/image?url=…&w=8&q=70`). There are some reasons why `next/image` can't easily wrap a raster image in an SVG itself that isn't really relevant to this PR, but what's important is that the SVG wrapping happens on the server.

docs.body:
### What?

Fixes an issue where interception rewrites (and other query-less rewrites) send an empty `x-nextjs-rewritten-query: ""` header under `next start`, causing the client-side router to incorrectly reuse cached intercepted segments across different search parameters.

### Why?

When using parallel and intercepting routes, RSC requests carry internal routing flags (such as `_rsc`) in the request search string. Previously, `resolve-routes.ts` compared the full incoming request search against `parsedDestination.search` (which is empty for interception rewrites). 

Because they didn't match, Next.js stamped `x-nextjs-rewritten-query: ""` onto the response. The client router interpreted this empty string as an explicit signal that the page was rendered with no search parameters, leading to stale modal states and cached route reuse for up to 300 seconds.

### How?

- Updated `packages/next/src/server/lib/router-utils/resolve-routes.ts` to compute the actual query the page renders with by merging the request query with the rewrite's query, while properly stripping internal Next.js bookkeeping keys (`_rsc`, `nextInternalLocale`, and `nxtP`/`nxtI` prefixed keys).
- If the resulting query matches the request query, the header is omitted (falling back to the URL). If it differs, the header correctly carries the full merged query.

docs.title: Assert no ERROR spans in successful OpenTelemetry e2e traces
docs.body:
## Summary

This PR adds a test-only invariant check to the OpenTelemetry e2e suite. After each test in the main `opentelemetry - $name` block, it fails if a trace whose request succeeded (root `BaseServer.handleRequest` span with `http.status_code` < 400) contains any span with an ERROR status. The check lives in a small helper, `assertNoErrorSpansInSuccessfulTraces`, which has its own unit tests.

## Motivation

The OpenTelemetry e2e tests check traces by matching against expected span trees with `expectTrace`. That catches the spans a test names. It does not catch an ERROR status on a span the test didn't write an expectation for, or a span that only shows up in `getAllSpans()` (for example, `next.bubble` spans that `getSpans()` filters out). If a change starts marking spans as failed on a request that actually succeeded, the existing tests can still pass.

That is easy to get wrong in the tracer. `recordSpanError` in `packages/next/src/server/lib/trace/tracer.ts` sets `SpanStatusCode.ERROR` for any thrown error unless it is a `BubbledError` with `bubble` set. So any new control-flow throw, or any error that is caught and recovered from further up, will mark the span as failed unless someone handles it on purpose. People who export Next.js traces to an APM tool see these as false failures on healthy requests, which makes error-rate alerts noisy and less trustworthy.

Original description:

---

### What?

With cacheComponents on, useServerInsertedHTML output appears twice in prerendered HTML. CSS-in-JS registries, like MUI's AppRouterCacheProvider (Emotion), ship their whole stylesheet twice in .

### Why?

prerenderToStream passes one ServerInsertedHTMLProvider to both the prospective client prerender and the final client prerender. The prospective render is thrown away, but the callbacks it registered stay on the shared provider and run again when the final HTML is built.

The prospective client prerender now gets its own provider, the same way warmupClientModulesForStagedValidation and the validation renders already do. The final render keeps the provider that renderServerInsertedHTML reads from.

docs.title: Turbopack: don't split page entries into a facade
docs.body:
## Summary

Fixes an HMR bug in the Pages Router with Turbopack. When an edit added or removed a re-export in a page, Fast Refresh reported the update as done, but the page kept showing the old content until a later edit forced a full reload. Webpack does a full reload in this case.

With `follow_reexports`, whether a module has re-exports decides whether it is split into a facade and its locals module. For a page entry, an edit that added a re-export therefore changed the module the page entry points at. HMR doesn't follow that change.

Page entries are now never split. Next.js marks pages router entries `standalone`, a new property of `EntryReferenceSubType` (#101291 removed the Next.js entry kinds from turbopack-core). Turbopack keeps a standalone entry whole: it doesn't follow its reexports and doesn't split it into a facade or into module fragments, since either would make its identity depend on its reexports. Nothing imports a page entry's exports, so there is nothing to tree-shake. This is limited to page entries. Other entries, such as client components, are also imported by other modules. Those imports would still be split, so the module would be evaluated twice.

A stack in the dev overlay loses the extra frame the facade added (`ReactRefreshLogBox` "module init error not shown").

docs.title: Turbopack: keep loader source maps when merging modules
docs.body:
## Summary

In production builds, Turbopack merges modules into a single output, then composes each module's loader source map into the merged map. It matched each loader map to its module through the map's optional `file` field. Loaders rarely set that field, so their maps were ignored, and stack traces pointed at the loader output instead of the original source. When several modules had maps, their mappings could also mix.

Each loader map is now paired with the module it came from and composed one module at a time, so mappings stay with their own module.

## Verification

- New e2e test `test/e2e/app-dir/webpack-loader-source-maps` uses a small fixture loader that shifts a module down by 3 lines and returns a source map without `file`. On canary, `pnpm test-start-turbo` fails with both loader-mapped modules reported 3 lines low; with this change it passes.
- The same test passes with `pnpm test-dev-turbo`, `pnpm test-start-webpack` and `pnpm test-dev-webpack`.

docs.title: Turbopack: narrow async-module emptiness dependencies
docs.body:
### What?

Adds `ModuleGraph::has_async_modules()`, a narrow turbo-tasks accessor that reports whether the module graph contains any async module. The browser and Node.js chunking code now use it when deciding whether to include the async-module runtime helpers, instead of reading the full `AsyncModulesInfo` set just to check whether it is empty.

### Why?

`AsyncModulesInfo` is a keyed cell holding every async module in the graph. Awaiting the whole value makes the reading task depend on every set member, so adding or removing an async module re-ran the runtime/evaluate-chunk tasks even when the result could not change. These callers only care about the empty/nonempty transition.

### How?

The accessor is a memoized task returning a boolean cell. The whole-set read is isolated there; when the set membership changes but stays nonempty, the accessor recomputes the same boolean and downstream chunking tasks are not invalidated. Empty-to-nonempty and nonempty-to-empty changes still invalidate consumers.

The existing runtime inclusion rules are unchanged, including the shared-runtime short-circuits and always including the helpers for the inline browser development runtime. The name follows the existing async-module terminology because the set includes async externals, WASM modules and transitive importers, not only modules with top-level await.

docs.title: Turbopack: flatten transitive CSS Modules composes
docs.body:
### What?

With Turbopack, CSS Modules `composes` now expands transitively. Chained local and cross-file `composes` export every class name, and cyclic `composes … from` imports produce a warning instead of crashing at runtime.

Fixes #85296

### Why?

Turbopack only expanded `composes` one level deep:

```css
.a { text-decoration: underline; }
.b { composes: a; }
.c { composes: b; }
```

`styles.c` was `"c b"`, missing `a`. webpack produces `"c b a"`. This happened for both `.module.css` and `.module.scss`.

Cross-file `composes … from` was emitted as an eager runtime import of the other CSS module's exports. If two CSS modules composed from each other, the import cycle crashed with `TypeError: Cannot define property …, object is not extensible`.

### How?

The flattening now happens at code generation time, in a single root task over the module graph (`turbopack-css/src/module_composes.rs`). It reuses the graph's existing edges and traversals:

- All reachable CSS modules are collected, and their direct `composes` lists (`classes()`) are loaded together up front, so the traversal itself is synchronous.
- `composes … from` targets come from the module graph edges whose reference is a `CssModuleComposeReference`. Nothing is resolved again.
- Modules are flattened in postorder of `ModuleGraph::traverse_edges_dfs`, starting at the CSS modules and following only composes edges. A

docs.title: Turbopack: read block-scoping support during codegen
docs.body:
### What?

`supports_block_scoping` is now queried during code generation instead of during module analysis.

- `EsmModuleItem::code_generation` reads it from the chunking context's environment, like `supports_arrow_functions` and the ESM/CJS externals checks.
- The eager reads in `analyze_ecmascript_module` and in tracing-mode `cross_module_constants` are removed, along with the `supports_block_scoping` argument/field threaded through `create_graph`, the graph `Analyzer` and `EsmModuleItem`.

### Why?

The value is only used in one place: choosing `const` vs `var` when codegen lowers `export default <expr>`. Reading it before analysis made the analysis task depend on the target environment's runtime versions for no reason, and the tracing-mode read was never used at all (tracing doesn't generate code).

The value now comes from the chunking context's environment rather than the module's compile-time-info environment. For Next.js these are the same: the client, server and edge chunking contexts are built from the matching compile-time-info environments.

### How?

Output is unchanged. Existing snapshots cover both branches: `swc_transforms/preset_env` (`chrome 41`, emits `var`) and `preset_env_modern` and others (emit `const`).

docs.body:
### What?

Turbopack issue headers now name the file the reported location belongs to. Both issue formatters, the Turbopack CLI/test-snapshot formatter (`turbopack-cli-utils`) and Next.js `formatIssue`, follow the same rules:

- If the issue has a source, the header shows the source's file, plus a 1-based `line:column` when there is a range.

docs.title: Turbopack: warn when a traced package does not resolve to a file
docs.body:
### What?

Warn when a traced package resolves to `package.json` but no module file.

### Why?

When an `exports` or `main` target is missing, tracing can include only the package metadata. Existing resolution warnings are filtered out because they originate in `node_modules`, allowing the build to succeed while the deployed app fails at runtime.

### How?

Detect metadata-only resolution results in `traced_modules_for_entries` and attach the warning to the nearest project file outside `node_modules` that pulls in the package so it survives filtering. The warning identifies the affected package and the file that requires it.

Exclude the requesting package’s own `package.json` and deduplicate warnings per project file and package. Warnings do not fail the build.

docs.title: fix: reuse completed preparations for static routes
docs.body:
### What?

Reuse completed `experimental_prepare()` work when committing navigation to a static route.

### Why?

A prototype integration with the `experimental_prepare` api revealed that a prepare on mousedown and commit on subsequent release/click triggered two requests. Preparation had finished before release/click but Next wasn't actually reusing the prepared work.

### How?

Keep the completed route information on the preparation handle, so commit can reuse it even if the shared route-cache entry has expired. Page data stays in the existing cache, and reuse still respects context changes and cache invalidation.

The existing cached-route and optimistic-route paths stay intact. `consumeCompletedRoute` clears the saved metadata and returns it only when it can still be reused.

docs.title: Same-page hash link doubles the hash (#a#a) after the page was loaded with a hash
docs.body:
https://github.com/SamWylde/next-hash-doubling-repro
 
1. `pnpm install`, `pnpm build`, `pnpm start`.
2. Open `http://localhost:3000/#faq` as a full page load (address bar, then Enter).
3. Click "Go to details" (`<Link href="#details">`). The box in the top right shows `location.hash`.

The page is `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'`. A page served from its build-time prerender does not show it: its initial route entry is marked stale (`InliningHintsStale`) and dropped, so the navigation takes `navigateToUnknownRoute`, which stores the canonical URL without a hash. An ISR page does show it once it has been regenerated at runtime.
 
Current: `location.hash` becomes `#faq#details`. Loading at `#details` and clicking the same link gives `#details#details`. The scroll still happens, but the address no longer matches any element, so reloading or sharing it does not land on the target.

### Cause
`navigateUsingPrefetchedRouteTree` in `client/components/app-router-state` builds the canonical URL as

```js
const canonicalUrl = route.canonicalUrl + url.hash;
```

but `create-initial-router-state` stores the initial route entry with `discoverKnownRoute(..., canonicalUrl, ...)`, where `canonica

docs.title: Turbopack: preserve CSS source maps through PostCSS
docs.body:
## Summary

CSS source maps lose their original locations when a PostCSS plugin changes the layout of CSS. Turbopack does not pass an upstream loader map into PostCSS, and it forwards that old map instead of using the map PostCSS returns.

Pass the upstream map into PostCSS and use its composed output map. Preserve already-normalized source URLs during resolution and CSS map emission, so sources are not prefixed twice or resolved against the generated filename again. CSS maps then identify the original CSS or preprocessor file, including imported sources.

The regression uses a custom loader and a whitespace-only PostCSS plugin, with no added dependencies. It checks original lines and complete source URLs for the main source, an imported source, and plain CSS. No CSS optimization behavior changes.

docs.title: Fix doubled hash on same-page hash links after loading a URL with a hash
docs.body:
### What?

After a page is loaded with a hash, same-page hash links double it. Loading `/page#faq` and clicking `<Link href="#details">` leaves the URL at `/page#faq#details`, and loading at `#details` and clicking the same link gives `#details#details`. A full href to the current page (`/page?x=y#details`) does the same, and so does a server action that redirects to a URL with a hash. The scroll still happens, but the address no longer matches anything, so reloading or sharing it doesn't land on the target. We hit this in production on 16.4.1 (details and a repro in #101168).

### Why?

`navigateUsingPrefetchedRouteTree` builds the URL as `route.canonicalUrl + url.hash`. Route cache entries are meant to store a hashless canonical URL (`navigateToUnknownRoute` already does this on purpose), but the initial router state, the server action redirect and the tree-mismatch retry store it with the hash. When a later same-page navigation uses one of those entries, the new hash gets appended to the old one.

### How?

Strip any hash from the stored canonical URL before appending the target hash. That's the only place the stored hash causes a problem. The other readers of a route entry's `canonicalUrl` (the segment fetches and the `didCommitWrongUrl` check) only look at the pathname and search, so I left the callers as they are.

I added four e2e cases to `test/e2e/app-dir/navigation`:

## Summary

`test/e2e/app-dir/no-double-tailwind-execution` has failed on canary since 2026-11-04 21:43 UTC, in every test mode. It installs `@tailwindcss/postcss@^4` and `tailwindcss@^4`, which now resolve to 4.3.4. That release's `@tailwindcss/node` `require()`s the ESM-only `magic-string@1.x`, so on Node.js 20.9.0 the PostCSS plugin fails to load and the page doesn't render:

```
Error: require() of ES Module …/magic-string@1.4.5/node_modules/magic-string/dist/index.mjs not supported.
    at …/@tailwindcss+node@4.3.4/node_modules/@tailwindcss/node/dist/index.js
    at …/@tailwindcss+postcss@4.3.4/node_modules/@tailwindcss/postcss/dist/index.js
```

This is the same break #101061 fixed for create-next-app. This test only hit it now because isolated test installs apply the repo's 48-hour `minimumReleaseAge`, and `@tailwindcss/postcss@4.3.4` was published 2026-11-02 at 21:31 UTC.

docs.title: Turbopack: retry chunk loads that failed with component chunks
docs.body:
## Summary

With `experimental.turbopackChunking.generateComponentChunks` enabled, a dynamic `import()` whose chunk fails to load (for example because the network drops) never loads again until a full page reload. Calling the same `import()` again after the network is back rejects immediately with the same `ChunkLoadError`, and no new chunk request is made. With the flag off, the retry refetches the chunk and resolves.

**Cause:** with component chunks enabled, async-loader chunk data carries `moduleChunks`, so loading goes through `loadComponentChunksOrWhole` in the browser runtime (`runtime-base.ts`). That function caches the load promise in `availableModuleChunks` for each component chunk. A rejected promise was never evicted, so on retry every component looked "available" and the split path just re-awaited the cached rejections. Without component chunks, the chunk data is a plain path that goes straight to the DOM backend, and the backend already drops failed loads.

**Fix:** the runtime's base-layer load caches (`availableModules`, `availableModuleChunks`, `splitChunkPromises`) now add entries through a small `cacheLoadPromise` helper. It stores the original promise, so in-flight/successful dedup and the promise identity React relies on are unchanged. It removes the entry when the promise rejects, but only if the entry still holds that same promise. The `ChunkLoadError` it

## Summary

With Cache Components, `next dev` reported sync IO that the user's code never did whenever a render closed a file:

- A server component that calls `fs.readFileSync(path)` without an encoding gets a false error in dev on every Node.js version: "Next.js encountered the unstable value `Date.now()` while prerendering", pointing at the `readFileSync` line. `next build` prerenders the same page without errors.

docs.title: Turbopack: process the WebAssembly loader as the module
docs.body:
## Summary

Turbopack's WebAssembly module was a wrapper around a generated ES module, the loader, which loads the `.wasm` file and instantiates it, or only compiles it for a `?module` import. The wrapper forwarded its references, exports, async-module info and code to that loader. Keeping the two graph identities in sync is what #99115 had to work around with `chunk_item_content_with_code_from` and borrowed exports.

The loader is now the module itself, processed like any other ES module, so exports, async-module handling, side effects and code generation come from the normal path. The wrapper is removed:

- The single-chunk (service worker) error moves to `RawWebAssemblyModuleAsset`, which already has the chunking context.
- The wasm file is now emitted only by `RawWebAssemblyModuleAsset`. The wrapper emitted it too.
- The loader is named after the WebAssembly source and keeps its query, so a `?module` import and a plain import of the same file show up under distinct names.

docs.title: fix(api-utils): guard against null-prototype headers in checkIsOnDemandRevalidate
docs.body:
### What?

Replaces direct `headers.hasOwnProperty(...)` with `Object.hasOwn(headers, ...)` in `checkIsOnDemandRevalidate`.

### Why?

In Node.js, `IncomingHttpHeaders` can be a null-prototype dictionary (`Object.create(null)`), such as in `node:http2` and strict proxy adapters. Calling `headers.hasOwnProperty(...)` throws `TypeError: headers.hasOwnProperty is not a function`, failing on-demand revalidation checks.

`Object.hasOwn` safely checks property existence without assuming inheritance from `Object.prototype`.

### How?

- Use `Object.hasOwn` instead of `headers.hasOwnProperty` in `packages/next/src/server/api-utils/index.ts`.
- Add unit tests in `test/unit/check-is-on-demand-revalidate.test.ts` verifying both standard and null-prototype headers.

docs.title: Keep 4xx status when there is no /_error page in App Router-only builds
docs.body:
### What?

In an App Router-only app (no `pages/` directory), client errors that Next.js generates itself come back as 500 in production.

| Request | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /items/%E0%A4` (malformed param) | 500 | 400 |
| `POST /hello.txt` (public file) | 500 | 405 |
| `Range: bytes=500-600` on a 6-byte public file | 500 | 416 |
| `If-Match: "nope"` on a public file | 500 | 412 |

Route handlers that return a 4xx themselves were already fine. 404 was also fine, because it has `/_not-found`.

### Why?

`renderErrorToResponseImpl` in `base-server.ts` looks for a page to render for the status code. `STATIC_STATUS_PAGES` only contains `/500`, so every other code falls back to `/_error`. App Router-only builds have no `/_error`, so it throws `missing required error components`. The `catch` block then sets `res.statusCode = 500`.

That error is a `WrappedBuildError`, which is not logged. So the server output shows nothing.

### How?

When no error page is found and the status is 4xx, return the standard status text (`Bad Request`, `Method Not Allowed`, ...) as `text/plain` and keep the status. 5xx still goes through the existing path.

Added `test/e2e/app-dir/app-router-client-error-status`. It covers 400, 405, 412, 416, a route handler returning 403, and a normal 200.

docs.title: [Pages] fix: interpolate query-only navigation when asPath has a query string
docs.body:
Fixes #84942

### What?

In the Pages Router, a query-only `router.push({ query })` or `<Link href="?…">` on a route with a dynamic segment followed by a static one (e.g. `/[id]/detail`) keeps the old segment when the current URL already has a query string.

```
current URL: /b/detail?fromId=a
router.push({ query: { id: 'c', fromId: 'b' } })

expected: /c/detail?fromId=b
actual:   /b/detail?id=c&fromId=b
```

This is a regression from 15.5.0, introduced by #82236.

### Why?

`resolveHref` (`packages/next/src/client/resolve-href.ts`) decides whether the current page was rewritten by running the anchored route regex against `router.asPath`. `asPath` includes the query string, so `^/([^/]+?)/detail(?:/)?$` never matches `/b/detail?fromId=a`. The page is then treated as rewritten, and the query is never interpolated into the path.

Routes like `/[id]` only appeared to work because the segment pattern happened to swallow the query string.

### How?

Match the regex against the pathname only, using the existing `parsePath` helper.

### Tests

Added a `dynamic-mid-path/[id]/detail` page and two cases (`router.push` and `Link`) to the `test/e2e/use-router-with-rewrites` suite from #82236.

Both new cases fail on canary (expected `b`/`c`, got `a`). All 11 tests in the suite pass with the fix in Turbopack dev, webpack dev, and production builds with both bundlers.

docs.title: Keep Content-Encoding and Content-Length on Route Handler responses
docs.body:
## What?

Scopes the recent `Content-Encoding` / `Content-Length` header stripping in Route Handlers to only the case that needs it: responses proxied from `fetch()`. All other Route Handler responses keep their headers.

## Why?

The security fix that strips `Content-Encoding` and `Content-Length` from every Route Handler response was only needed for one case. When a handler returns a response from `fetch()`, the body has already been decompressed, but the original headers are still attached, so they no longer describe the body.

Stripping them from **every** response caused regressions in ordinary apps:

- **Pre-compressed responses break.** A handler that returns gzip data with `Content-Encoding: gzip` now sends compressed bytes with no encoding header. The browser can't decode them, and the app errors.
- **Downloads lose `Content-Length`.** There's no progress indicator, and PDF viewers can't do range or progressive loading, so the whole file has to download before the first page renders.

## How?

1. **Strip headers only when they're stale.** Headers are removed only when the response came from `fetch()` and carries a `Content-Encoding`. Every other response keeps these two headers.
2. **Keep the security guarantee.** If a response's `Content-Length` doesn't match the actual body length, the connection is closed. No extra bytes get written past the declared length, which i

docs.title: Automatically compress route handler responses if not already compressed
docs.body:
Route handler responses were never compressed when self-hosted.

`NodeNextResponse.appendHeader` stored every header value as an array, even a single value. The compression middleware checks `Content-Type` with the `compressible` package, which only accepts strings, so any response sent through `sendResponse` (all app route handlers, including prerendered ones served from the cache) failed the content-type filter and skipped compression. `appendHeader` now keeps a single value as a plain string, matching Node's own `appendHeader` semantics.

Fixes https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/101120
Closes https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/101201
We must strip CE and CL headers from `Response` returned from route handlers due to https://github.com/vercel/next.js/security/advisories/GHSA-pc58-hwjq-p385. A `Response` from `fech()` is indistinguishable from a synthetic one. Any provenance can get lost via `clone` or manual reconstruction based on headers and body.
Instead, the responses from route handlers should be returned uncompressed and be compressed by the outgoing server: now `next start` or your hosting provider e.g. Vercel.

Route handlers should not return a `fetch()` without processing the body as this needlessly adds CPU overhead due to `fetch()`'s automatic decompression. Use a dedicated proxy library for that instead.

- moved dev-only comp

docs.title: Fix: Wait for Pages Router hydration before rendering route changes
docs.body:
### What?

Fixes a Pages Router race condition where a route change requested before the initial hydration render starts ends up performing that hydration with the next page's props, resulting in a hydration mismatch

Fixes #95367

### Why?

`hydrate()` in `client/index.tsx` creates the router, which makes `window.next.router` usable right away. The initial render only starts after a few more awaits: `router._initialMatchesMiddlewarePromise`, and in development `beforeRender` (`displayContent` in `client/dev/fouc.ts`), which waits for `requestAnimationFrame`.

If `router.push()` is called in that window and its data loads first, the router's `subscription` calls `render()` for the new route. No React root exists yet, so `renderReactElement` calls `hydrateRoot` with the new page's element against the old page's HTML.

Development makes the window much wider. Chrome doesn't run animation frames in background tabs, so a background tab never starts its initial render. That's what the issue's repro encounters. That also explains why one tab or `page.goto()` doesn't reproduce it.

### How?

- `client/index.tsx`: route-change renders from the router's `subscription` and waits until the initial render settles (its promise resolves on commit, or rejects if the render is canceled or fails). The router state and URL update as before; only the render waits.
- `client/dev/fouc.ts`: `display

docs.title: experimental_prepare: Don't refetch on commit due to stale inlining hints
docs.body:
## Summary

Fixes a narrow case where committing a prepared navigation (`router.experimental_prepare()`) fetches the route a second time.

It only happens when the route wasn't already in the route cache when the prepare started, and the page was prerendered at build time. Build-time prerenders are marked with `InliningHintsStale`, which causes the client to write their route cache entry already expired. So when the commit looks up the route, it misses the entry the prepare just wrote, and fetches the route again.

To fix this, the prepare saves the result of its route request on the preparation record, and the commit uses it instead of making a new request. It's subject to the same checks as taking over an in-flight request.

This is a workaround for `InliningHintsStale`. Once that mechanism is removed, this can be too.

Alternative to #101163; test cases adapted from that PR.

## Verification

- Not run: `pnpm test-start-turbo test/e2e/app-dir/prepare-navigation/prepare-navigation.test.ts` (left to CI)

## Problem

The `should handle a fetch action initiated from a static page` test relied on a module-level `let counter = 0` in `client-static/actions.js` and expected `#count` to go `0`, `1`, `2`. That only holds when one server process handles every request. With two instances behind a round-robin proxy, the two clicks hit different instances and the count reads `0`, `1`, `1`.

## Change

- `actions.js`: `incrementCounter` now returns `crypto.randomUUID()` instead of an incrementing module-level counter.
- `app-action.test.ts`: after each click, the test asserts that `#count` has changed from its previous value (initial `0`, then a new value, then another new value). The test no longer depends on how many instances serve the requests.

## Testing

- `app-action.test.ts` and `app-action-node-middleware.test.ts`: the test passes on a single server (webpack, start mode).
- Two instances behind a round-robin proxy ([repro](https://github.com/k-taro56/next-static-action-counter-repro)): before the change, `check` gave `[1,1]`; after it, it gives two distinct UUIDs.

## Note

`incrementCounter` is now a slightly misleading name. I left it unchanged to keep the diff small and can rename it (including the import in `page.js`) if maintainers prefer.

Fixes #101149

docs.title: Lint against new `as any` casts and require a reason to disable it
docs.body:
### What?

Adds two internal lint rules and turns them on:

- `@next/internal/no-as-any` reports `x as any` and `<any>x`. The error lands on the `any` keyword, so a disable comment above that line covers the cast even when the expression spans several lines.
- `@next/internal/require-disable-reason` requires a reason when `no-as-any` is disabled. The reason goes in comment lines directly above the disable comment:

  ```ts
  // React's Flight client exports this as `any`.
  // eslint-disable-next-line @next/internal/no-as-any
  ```

  A trailing `// eslint-disable-line` has no line above it, so there the reason goes after ` -- `. The rule rejects reasons made only of filler words ("TODO fix this", "needed for types"). It also rejects disabling `no-as-any` for a range of lines or a whole file, and a bare `// eslint-disable-next-line` that names no rule, since that hides casts too.

Both rules apply to `packages/**`, `test/**/*.test.{ts,tsx}` and `test/lib/**`.

Every existing cast in that scope gets a baseline marker, so new casts fail lint while the old ones stay easy to find:

```ts
// TODO(as-any): pre-existing cast, not yet reviewed
// eslint-disable-next-line @next/internal/no-as-any
```

`AGENTS.md` describes the rule, the reason format, and the workarounds to avoid (`as unknown as T`, `@ts-expect-error`).

Follow-up to the discussion in [this Slack thread](https

docs.title: turbo-tasks-fs: write outputs directly and verify them on apply
docs.body:
### What?

`DiskFileSystem::write` now atomically writes each output to its final path during the write task. The emitted effect no longer contains file content: applying it verifies that the write task's file is still on disk, or invalidates the writer so it writes again.

The effect protocol is also simplified. The separate capture phase is removed, and `Effect` exposes `key`, `identity`, `apply`, and a lazy `content_hash`.

### Why?

Write effects previously retained every output's full content in stable `ReadRef`s so they could be applied consistently after execution settled. Every output had to stay in memory until apply, and every write computed a content hash up front.

Direct writes move expensive file IO into the write task and keep only small effect data until apply. Content hashing is limited to paths that have multiple writer tasks.

An earlier revision of this PR wrote to a scratch directory and moved files into place on apply. That approach introduced scratch-file consumption, ownership reuse, and isolation problems, so it has been replaced.

The trade-off is a wider consistency window. Individual files are replaced atomically, but readers may observe a mix of old and new files while recomputation is in progress. Write tasks also rewrite their file on each execution, even when the content is unchanged. Benchmarks are still needed before claiming memory or wall-tim

docs.body:
Fixes #101111

### What?

Since `experimental.validateRSCRequestHeaders` is on by default (#93367, 16.3), a proxy that overrides a request header the client's `_rsc` search param is a hash of breaks every client-side navigation it does that on, in `next dev` and on self-hosted servers. The server answers each RSC request with a 307 to the `_rsc` value it computed, the client replays the request with its own value, and so on until the client's redirect limit of 20. On the reporter's reproduction I count 21 pairs of 307/200 responses per click, with the `Cannot write to a CLOSED writable stream` console errors from #97918; in their app the navigation falls back to a full page load about 8 s later.

The client computed `_rsc` from the values it sent, so the two only agree when the proxy leaves those headers alone. The check guards CDNs that key their cache on the URL alone, and those CDNs see the client's headers, so the hash has to be verified against the client's values. docs.title: Fix Node HTML stream error propagation and cancellation
docs.body:
### Summary
Fix error propagation and cancellation in fresh and resumed Node HTML streams.

Previously, the HTML transforms were connected with plain .pipe() calls, which do not forward upstream errors or automatically cancel upstream work. A fatal renderer or transform failure could leave the HTML stream open and the request hanging. The Flight stream could also continue running after HTML rendering failed or the client disconnected.

### Fix
This connects HTML transforms with `stream.pipeline()` (https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#streampipelinestreams-options) so failures propagate through the entire chain and cancellation tears down upstream work. I also tried to clean up the syntax of the pipelining with a helper method.
Flight errors are seen immediately, even before the first HTML chunk, and they destroy the Flight stream when its inject transform is destroyed.
When the attached destination fails or closes prematurely, it settles renderer readiness promises and aborts pending renders.
Already failed streams / premature closes are handled with `stream.finished()`, rather than waiting for events that may have already fired.
I am fairly confident that all the transform orders, buffering, backpressure, and general streaming behavior have been maintained. This also keeps node packages out of edge bundles, since that's still important for a time.

docs.title: Exclude native packages built for another libc from the build trace
docs.body:
On Linux, node_modules holds both the glibc and the musl build of any native package, because the `os` and `cpu` fields of an optional dependency say nothing about the C library. File tracing follows the package root and copies both into the traced output, even though only one of them can ever be loaded.

For `sharp` and `@swc/core` together that is roughly 77 MB of files that cannot execute, which is enough to push `output: 'standalone'` past a platform size limit such as AWS Lambda's 250 MiB unzipped ceiling.

`sharp` is already dropped from the server trace, but only when `hasNextSupport` is set, so self-hosted builds keep every variant.

Add `getCrossLibcIgnores()`, which returns ignore globs for the musl-targeted packages when the build runs on Linux with glibc. On a musl host, and on platforms where the target libc is unknown, it returns nothing and behaviour is unchanged.

docs.title: Fix Turbopack tracing of dynamic package subpaths
docs.body:
## Why the old code was wrong

Brought up by https://github.com/vercel-labs/next-safe-image-optimization/pull/12.

A computed platform-package request leaves a subpath pattern consisting of a wildcard followed by the static `/package.json`. The wildcard cannot consume the leading slash, but it can match nothing while the slash belongs to the following constant. Rejecting `/` as a prefix prevents metadata resolution and consequently omits the worker located through `dirname`, `join` and `existsSync`.

The same issue applies beyond slashes: a character forbidden to a wildcard can be explicitly present in the following constant. That constant can also begin before the wildcard's maximum allowed stopping position. For example, `DynamicNoSlash + 'st/worker'` matches `test/worker`, so `test/wo` must remain a possible prefix.

## How the fix works

Check whether an input suffix, starting anywhere the wildcard is allowed to stop, is a prefix of the following constant. Scan backwards at UTF-8 character boundaries and consider only suffixes no longer than that constant. This replaces the slash exception without relaxing wildcard-consumption restrictions or changing complete-match behavior.

docs.title: Turbopack: project package.json fields for fine-grained resolve dependencies
docs.body:
### What?

Resolving now depends only on the `package.json` fields it actually reads, instead of the whole parsed file.

- New `package_json_fields` task in `turbopack-core/src/package_json.rs`: a plain struct whose fields (`name`, `exports`, `imports`, `browser`, `main`, `module`, `types`) are separate `ResolvedVc<PackageJsonFieldValue>` cells. Field names outside that set (alias/main field names are configurable via `ResolveOptions`) go through a small per-name task. `package_json_field(source, name)` picks the right cell.
- Migrated every resolve consumer in `resolve/mod.rs`: alias fields (`apply_in_package`), main fields (`resolve_into_folder`), `exports_field`, `imports_field`, `find_self_reference` and `find_context_file_or_package_key`. None of them reads the whole `package.json` anymore.

### Why?

`apply_in_package` runs inline in the resolve tasks and awaited the whole `read_package_json` result, so every resolve that checks the `browser` field depended on the entire file. Editing `version`, `scripts`, `dependencies`, … re-ran those resolves. The projection still re-runs on every edit, but its field cells only change when that field's JSON changes, so readers of other fields are not invalidated.

### How?

- The field cells are created in a fixed order, so their identities are stable and the parent struct compares equal across re-executions.
- `PackageJsonFieldValue`

docs.title: Fix route handler cookies() not seeing proxy cookies on the same request
docs.body:
### What?

If `proxy.js` sets a cookie with `response.cookies.set()`, a Server Component can read it with `cookies()` on that same request, but a Route Handler can't.

```js
const response = NextResponse.next()
response.cookies.set('from-proxy', 'fast')
return response
```

For a request with `Cookie: session=1`, a page's `cookies()` returns `session=1` and `from-proxy=fast`. A Route Handler's `cookies()` returns only `session=1`, in both the Node.js and Edge runtimes. So if a proxy refreshes a session cookie, the page and the route handler read different values on identical requests.

### Why?

The `x-middleware-set-cookie` merge in `request-store.ts` checks the header with `in` and bracket access. That works on the Node headers that pages get, but Route Handlers pass Web `Headers`, so the merge doesn't happen. #93499 left a TODO about this.

### How?

For Web `Headers`, add the `name=value` part of each proxy cookie to the `Cookie` value when creating the request cookies. They aren't recorded as modified, so no extra `Set-Cookie` is added to the response. `request.cookies` and `headers().get('cookie')` still reflect only the `Cookie` header.

Prevent prerenders from changing foreground response status
docs.body:
When a navigation reused cached data from a stale partial prerender, Next.js could render its Flight response while regenerating the prerender in the background. Both renders had access to the same HTTP response. A background redirect could change the foreground response's status before its headers committed and force a document navigation. The shared status also caused problems in the other direction: a prerender could observe the stale document response's 404 status and include `noindex` in otherwise successful regenerated content.

This builds on the header isolation in PR #100960 and extracts the independent prerender output work from PR #100472. That draft explores a broader separation between App Router rendering and HTTP transport. We extract this part so the ownership change can be reviewed and landed independently of its action, cookie, and lifecycle refactors. The existing foreground/background scheduling remains intact, as it did in PR #100854.

Prerendering now receives an explicit initial status and owns its status throughout the render. Normal prerenders start at 200, while error-page routes establish their intended status. The shared rendering context exposes only status instead of the whole HTTP response, and prerendering returns its status through result metadata. Dynamic rendering continues to use the live response.

### What?

With Cache Components, `useParams()`, `usePathname()` and `useSearchParams()` inside a hidden `<Activity>` route now return the values that route had when it was hidden, instead of the active route's values. The hooks read router-wide contexts provided once in `AppRouter`, and `OuterLayoutRouter` doesn't provide them again per bfcache entry. docs.title: Fix slashed protocol detection in URL objects
docs.body:
## Summary

URL-object `href`s using `ws` or `wss` lose their protocol slashes and can concatenate the hostname and pathname. For example, `{ protocol: 'wss', hostname: 'example.com', pathname: 'socket' }` renders as `wss:example.comsocket` instead of `wss://example.com/socket`.

Match the complete protocol after colon normalization and include `ws:` and `wss:` among the slashed protocols. This also prevents custom schemes such as `sftp:` and `web+https:` from receiving slashes through substring matches. Dropping implicit `//` for these custom schemes is intentional and matches Node's formatter. Set `slashes: true` to keep the separator.

Extend the existing Link-rendering suite to cover WebSocket protocols with and without colons, existing slashed protocols, and custom schemes, including `news:`. The `sftp:` case covers explicit slashes with a host and port, a path, and a query.

## Verification

- All 14 Link-rendering tests passed using the modified formatter source compiled into an isolated Next.js `16.5.0-canary.42` runtime with React 19. Six regression cases failed with the original formatter.
- The formatter matches Node's `url.format` for 160 checked inputs covering protocol colons, host/hostname, pathname slashes, and explicit `slashes: true`.
- Both changed files passed formatting checks with the repository's pinned Prettier version and configuration.
- Full monorepo

docs.title: Expose full-route RSC prerender classification to adapters
docs.body:
PR #96080 scoped prerender classification to HTML and Route Handler responses. Full-route RSC outputs lack the metadata needed to select their own cache-miss policy.

HTML and RSC need independent classifications. An HTML shell with UI that finishes in the browser can have a complete static RSC payload. A complete generic HTML shell can also hydrate from static segment data while its full-route navigation response still requires concrete router parameters.

This change classifies full-route App Router RSC outputs using #101511's four-value contract. Complete reusable payloads use `complete/static`. Ordinary request-time RSC renders use `empty/dynamic`. Those renders can reuse cached data from postponed state, but that state is not an initial RSC response and does not make the output `resuming`.

Outputs for paths not generated at build time use `empty/static` when `ensureStatic = 'navigation'` guarantees static server output. Explicitly blocking parameter matchers use `empty/blocking`. They require a prerender before serving a cache miss, even when its result needs request-time rendering. That requirement persists after an on-demand entry expires or is evicted. Concrete built paths use their own output classification.

docs.title: Don't bundle Request Insights into production App Router entrypoints
docs.body:
**What:** `patch-fetch`, the `fetch` wrapper that every App Router route handler and page bundles, imported Request Insights at the top of the module. Request Insights only runs in the development server, but the import put it, the local span recorder and the span store into every production App Router entrypoint. With webpack, the server chunk that the App Router entrypoints share is 20 KB smaller. No behavior change. Development builds contain the same modules as before.

**Where it fits:** Independent change, based on `canary`. It has the same goal as #101313 and #101314 (less work when a server process starts and handles its first request) and does not depend on them.

docs.body:
**What:** The tracer (`server/lib/trace/tracer`) and the development span recorder (`local-span-recorder`) loaded the OpenTelemetry API when they were evaluated. docs.body:
**What:** In a route handler on Node.js 24, `new Request(request)`, `new NextRequest(request)` and `fetch(request, init)` throw `TypeError: Cannot read private member #state from an object whose class did not declare it`. The handler receives a `Proxy` of the request, and since Node.js 24 (undici 7) a `Request` keeps its state in private fields, which a `Proxy` does not have. The handler now receives the request itself. docs.title: Don't create an AbortController for every proxy request
docs.body:
**What:** The `handler` export of the proxy (middleware) module, which deployment adapters call, takes an optional `AbortSignal` for the request. When it got none, it created an `AbortController` for every request and constructed the request with that controller's signal, which nothing could ever abort. On Node.js a `Request` that is constructed with a signal follows it: it adds an abort listener to it and registers itself in a `FinalizationRegistry`, and both objects then live until a major garbage collection. The request is now constructed without a signal in that case.

**Expected impact:** A proxy that is called without a signal uses about 10 µs less CPU per request (of about 185 µs for an auth-style proxy, garbage collection included), and its handler call returns about 3 µs sooner at the median and 40 to 95 µs sooner at the 99th percentile. No behavior change: `request.signal` in the proxy is an `AbortSignal` that never aborts, as before. A caller that passes a signal gets exactly what it got before.

**Where it fits:** Standalone, based on `canary`. One of three independent changes to what the Node.js proxy does per request; the other two: #101337 stops copying the request headers when there is no trace context, and #101338 stops creating accessor functions for every request store.

docs.title: Don't copy the proxy request headers without a trace context
docs.body:
**What:** To forward a trace context to the request behind the proxy (middleware), the adapter keeps a copy of the request headers as the proxy received them. It made that copy for every request, before it knew whether there was a trace context, and dropped it when there was none. docs.title: Don't create accessor functions for every request store
docs.body:
**What:** `createRequestStore` returned an object literal whose lazy members (`headers`, `cookies`, `mutableCookies`, `userspaceMutableCookies`, `draftMode`) were accessors that close over the request. docs.title: turbo-tasks-backend: release unused capacity in task storage
docs.body:
## Summary

Task storage held more memory than its contents need because several of its collections never give capacity back:

- **The lazy field vec** (`TinyVec<LazyField>`) is shrunk to fit after each execution, but every field another task adds to a finished task later (cell dependents, aggregation edges, dirty state) doubled its capacity again. At the end of a large build it held ~1.75 slots per entry. Lazy fields are now pushed with `TinyVec::push_exact`, which grows by one slot, and `TinyVec` resizes heap buffers with `realloc` so the allocator can keep blocks in place.
- **Aggregation edges** (`upper`, `followers`, the aggregated dirty/collectible counters) move around constantly while the aggregation graph rebalances, and neither hash tables nor spilled lists shrink on their own, so they kept their peak capacity: `followers`' hash tables held 4.8x the bytes of their entries. `CounterMap` now calls `shrink_amortized` after removing entries, which shrinks once capacity exceeds 3x the length (3x rather than 2x, because a table right after doubling is already at ~2x).
- **Emptied lazy collections** kept an empty `LazyField` (137K empty `followers` on a large build). The generated `CounterMap` mutators now drop the field when it becomes empty, checked with an O(1) `is_empty` on the map they already hold; removing a lazy field shrinks the vec once at most half of it is used.

docs.title: fix(next/image): detect distortion using intrinsic proportions
docs.body:
## Summary

Make the `next/image` sizing warning detect distortion using the loaded image's intrinsic proportions. The previous check compared each rendered dimension with its prop and warned only when exactly one changed. This produced warnings for correctly cropped images, source dimensions that differ from the props, and fractional SVG sizes, while missing distortion when both dimensions changed.

Warn only when the computed `object-fit` is `fill`, since every other value crops or letterboxes instead of distorting. Then compare the rendered aspect ratio with `naturalWidth` / `naturalHeight`. The tolerance is the rounding error each dimension can carry: half a pixel for the rounded rendered size and one pixel for the truncated, density-corrected natural size. The `fill` prop keeps its existing behavior. The warning now describes an aspect-ratio mismatch and links to the `style` prop docs.

The browser regression covers the reported 820 × 720 → 680 × 720 crop, the neighboring 681 × 721 distortion, source/prop mismatches, fractional SVG heights, rounding on very wide and tall SVGs, density-corrected natural dimensions, proportional resizing, incorrect props, and the `fill` prop. Existing App Router and Pages Router assertions are updated for the new wording.

Reported in [agent feedback #6728](https://next-maintainer-agent.vercel.tools/agent-feedback/6728), independently reprod

docs.title: Fix only-generated revalidation of App Router paths without a cache entry
docs.body:
**What:** `res.revalidate(path, { unstable_onlyGenerated: true })` asks for a 404 when the path has no cache entry. The App Router page handler answers with `render404()`, which renders the not-found page through the same handler with the same request. A not-found page without a cache entry of its own called `render404()` again, in a loop that never returns to the event loop. When it did render, the handler threw `invariant: cache entry required but not generated` afterwards. `render404()` now removes the `x-prerender-revalidate-if-generated` header first, and the page handler treats the 404 as the complete answer.

**Expected impact:** An only-generated revalidation of an App Router path without a cache entry, or of a path without a route, now resolves. Under `next start` it never answered when the not-found page has no cache entry, and the server answered no other request. With a prerendered not-found page it rejected with `write after end` for a path that was never generated. In `next dev` it hung for every static App Router path. No change without `unstable_onlyGenerated`, for a route handler or a Pages Router path without a cache entry, or in minimal mode.

**Where it fits:** PR 1 of 2. A bug fix that stands alone, based on `canary`. #101342 is stacked on it: it fixes on-demand revalidation of dynamic routes in `next dev`, which makes this loop reachable for dynamic routes

## Summary

When a page component or root named parallel slot calls `notFound()`, use the root not-found file's metadata instead of retaining the page or layout title. Apply the convention metadata in recovery HTML and after hydration, and switch it during client navigation without leaving duplicate titles or reusing the 404 head for a known page.

docs.title: Fix RSC navigation and runtime prefetches in `next start`
docs.body:
With Cache Components enabled, `next start` served a generic fallback shell when a navigation to a prerendered path missed a custom cache. The incomplete RSC response crashed the client with React #412, as reported in #99861. Static paths that regenerated as partial were also served as static RSC, without the request data required by navigations and runtime prefetches.

PR #101125 addresses the navigation miss and returns a 404 when a navigation still receives incomplete output. The router then reloads the document. This alternative builds on that work and its regression cases to keep navigation on the client and handle runtime prefetches at their requested stage.

The handler derives the RSC miss policy from the classification introduced in #101511 and extended in #101309. RSC outputs classified as `static` or `blocking` wait for a coalesced prerender when their entry is missing or hard-expired. Other eligible RSC requests render independently while a coalesced background prerender populates the cache.

A concrete build-time entry takes precedence over its generic matcher. A built partial path therefore renders dynamically even when the matcher requires blocking for paths not generated at build time. Paths generated on demand retain their matcher's policy after expiration or eviction.

After a blocking prerender, the handler checks the actual result before serving it.

docs.title: Keep per-request functions out of V8's old generation
docs.body:
**What:** V8 allocates a function expression that is assigned to a property (`a.b = () => {}`) in the old generation until TurboFan has optimized the code around it, which takes thousands of calls. A minor garbage collection cannot free what such a function references. Next.js creates three kinds per request: `res.setHeader`, the globals `__next_require__` and `__next_chunk_load__`, and `reset` and `retry` of the error boundaries. Now the `res.setHeader` wrapper is in a variable with a second use, the globals get their handler as a function argument, and `reset` and `retry` are bound prototype methods. A variable with one use is not enough: the minifier puts it back into the assignment.

**Expected impact:** A page request leaves 4.6 KB less for a major garbage collection (72.2 → 67.6 KB on Node.js 22.23), from the first request of a process. With #101360, #101362 and #101338 (numbers in #101360) it is what lets a server action gain in a direct call of the route's `handler`: after 12,000 requests, garbage collection costs 132 µs per request without this PR and 16 to 18 µs with it. Under `next start` with its default compression that gain is absent (149 against 148 µs), because the compression middleware keeps per-request functions of its own. Cost: 48 bytes in every App Router browser bundle.

docs.title: Keep the promises of the request APIs on the work store
docs.body:
**What:** `cookies()`, `headers()`, `params` and `searchParams` hand out the same promise for every call during a render. At request time that promise was kept in a module-level `WeakMap`, keyed by the value it resolves with. The promise references its key, and V8's minor garbage collections treat such an entry as strongly held, so the promise and everything it references stayed until the next major collection. In Node.js 20 and 22 a promise references every async local store that was active when it was created: the whole request. The promises are now kept in a map on the work store and are dropped with it.

**Expected impact:** With #101360, #101361 and #101338 (numbers in #101360), this PR is what frees a page and a server action on Node.js 20 and 22: a page goes from 65.0 to 26.7 KB per request and a server action from 50.1 to 2.0 KB (22.23). Alone it frees nothing, and its map adds 0.2 to 0.8 KB per request. No gain on Node.js 24. Cost: about 5 ns per `cookies()` or `headers()` call in a page.

**Where it fits:** Independent, based on `canary`. One of four changes that stop the state of a finished App Router request from surviving minor garbage collections.

docs.body:
## Summary

A task type was an `Arc<CachedTaskType>` whose `arg` was a separately boxed `Box<dyn DynTaskInputs>`: two allocations per task, and every task cache equality check followed a second pointer to the argument.

`CachedTaskType` is now a dynamically sized struct with the argument as its last field, stored in a single allocation behind a one-word `CachedTaskTypeArc`:

```text
CachedTaskTypeArc ──► [ count | arg metadata | native_fn | this | arg ... ]
```

- The pointer stays thin (task storage and the task cache hold one per persistent task; a fat `Arc<… dyn …>` would push `TaskStorage` out of its 128-byte size class). - On a cache miss, `DynTaskInputsStorage::take_task_type` moves the stack-resident argument straight into the allocation, so it is never boxed. Already boxed arguments (decoded or resolved) are moved with a byte copy.
- The refcounting follows `Arc` (relaxed clone, release/acquire drop); freeing goes through `Box`, which drops the argument via its vtable. The header fields are private, so a `CachedTaskType` only exists inside a `CachedTaskTypeArc`.

docs.title: fix(next/image): match remotePatterns hostname wildcards per DNS label
docs.body:
Fixes vercel/next-js-mirror#292

### What

`matchRemotePattern()` compiled the hostname with picomatch. picomatch's `*` only stops at a `/` separator, and hostnames have no `/`, so `assets.example.*` also matched `assets.example.attacker.com`. The image optimizer allowlist accepted hosts the config should reject.

### How

- Add `makeHostnameRegex()` in `match-remote-pattern.ts`: `*` matches within a single DNS label, a label of exactly `**` matches one or more labels, and every other character is matched literally. In-label globs covered by the existing tests (`*1`, `*a*`, `ia*`) behave as before.
- Use it in `matchRemotePattern()` and in `writeImagesManifest()` (`build/index.ts`), which stores the hostname regex in the images manifest, so the runtime check and the manifest stay in sync, as the paired comments in both files require.

### Tests

Added cases to `test/unit/image-optimizer/match-remote-pattern.test.ts` covering the issue's table (`assets.example.*`, `cdn.*.com`, `*.example.com` against multi-label hosts). Verified locally by running the transpiled unit suite against the real picomatch: all 19 existing tests pass unchanged, the new test passes with the fix and fails without it.

docs.body:
## Summary

`AstPathTrie` nodes stored their `AstParentKind` inline: a 4-byte parent index plus the 24-byte kind (swc's outer node type, inner field, and a `usize` index for list fields), padded to 32 bytes. The tries live in the `CodeGens` cell of every analyzed module, so they are kept for the rest of the build.

Each trie now stores its distinct kinds once, in a table, and a node is two `u32`s: its parent and the index of its kind, 8 bytes. Most kinds repeat throughout a module (`Expr::Call`, `CallExpr::Callee`, ...); only the indexed ones (statement and argument positions) tend to be distinct. The builder interns kinds with an `FxIndexSet` and keys its children maps by the 4-byte kind index; the trie's API is unchanged.

### Results

Large Next.js app, cold `next build --experimental-build-mode=compile`, live heap sampled at the end of the build:

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AstPathTrie`s | 701 MiB (~23M nodes) | 269 MiB |
| Live heap | 13.55 GiB | 13.11 GiB |
| User CPU | 504–514 s | 506 s |

About 18% of nodes have a distinct kind, so the table costs ~94 MiB and the nodes ~175 MiB. The tries are serialized with the `CodeGens` cell, so the persistent cache shrinks too.

docs.title: Turbopack: don't emit the client entry's modules again in every Pages Router page
docs.body:
**What:** With Turbopack, the chunk group of every Pages Router page (the chunks it loads) contained the client entry's modules again, so pages downloaded modules that `/_app` had already loaded. This regression (#98685, first in `16.5.0-canary.27`) is in no stable release. A second defect is also in the stable release: with `async` scripts (`experimental.disableOptimizedLoading: true`) a page can fail to hydrate when its chunks run before those of `/_app`. Two changes: an entry module is a member of every chunk group that lists it, and a page other than `/_app` lists only its page loader as entry.

**What:** Experimental and off by default. With `experimental.turbopackDeferModuleEvaluation`, a production build with Turbopack evaluates a module of the Node.js server graph when one of its exports is first read, not when its importer is evaluated. This applies to an import that is only read inside functions, and only if Turbopack already removes an unused import of that module. docs.title: Keep what an API route gets for each request out of V8's old generation
docs.body:
**What:** V8 allocates a function expression that is assigned to a property (`res.json = (body) => {}`) in the old generation until TurboFan has optimized the code around it, and the pair of functions of an accessor property always. A minor garbage collection cannot free what they reference. For each Pages Router API request, Next.js assigns ten such functions to the response and defines four such accessors on the request. Now an object literal creates the functions and a helper assigns them, and a lazy property has one pair of accessors for all requests, which finds the request through its receiver.

**Expected impact:** A finished API request leaves 1.0 to 4.7 KB less for a major garbage collection. On Node.js 20.9, garbage collection on a direct `handler` call takes 4 to 5 µs per request instead of 23 to 41. On Node.js 22.23 that gain depends on when V8 optimizes the code that creates `res.setHeader`, which this PR leaves alone: one measurement shows 33 → 14 µs, a second 20.5 → 19.1. Set-up of a request is 3 to 5 µs faster on a direct `handler` call on Node.js 22.23; behind `next start` and in minimal mode on 22.23 it is inside the noise. The first read or write of a lazy property (`req.cookies`, `req.draftMode`) is 1.0 to 1.9 µs slower on a direct call and 0.1 to 0.4 µs behind a server. Cost: 498 bytes in the `pages-api` runtime, 410 in `app-page`.

docs.title: Turbopack: keep the evaluation order of modules when merging them
docs.body:
**What:** With scope hoisting, Turbopack merges modules into one function, and importing one module of a merged group runs all of them. So a merged group can run a module earlier or later than the source order says. The grouping did not check for that. This PR checks each group against the order in which every entry evaluates its modules, and splits it where the order would change.

**Why it matters:** The order only matters for a module that does something when it is evaluated: it sets a global, reads the environment, registers a plugin or fills a registry. For a module without side effects it makes no difference when it runs. But Turbopack only knows that a module has none when its package declares `sideEffects: false`, and an app's own modules and its set-up modules declare nothing. Those are the modules that run out of order today, in stable `15.4.1` to `16.4.5` and on `canary`:

- A set-up module calls `dayjs.extend(utc)` and is imported before a module that calls `dayjs.utc()` at module scope: `next build` fails (`16.3.8`, `16.4.5`, `canary`).
- Environment set-up is imported before a config module: the config reads the unset value.
- A registry that modules fill at import (auth, logging, rate limit, CORS) is filled in another order.

The smallest case needs no `require()`: route `a` imports `a1`, `s1`, `a2`, `s2`, and route `b` imports `s1`, `s2`. Today route `a` runs `a

docs.title: fix(dev): time out the dist-tags fetch in getVersionInfo so a hanging registry cannot stall next dev
docs.body:
### What?

Adds an explicit 5 second timeout to the npm registry request that `getVersionInfo` (`packages/next/src/server/dev/hot-reloader-shared-utils.ts`) makes for the dev tools' version indicator.

### Why?

`getVersionInfo` fetches `${registry}-/package/next/dist-tags` without an explicit timeout. Its inner `try` catches a fetch that rejects, which is what happens on an offline machine, and returns `staleness: 'unknown'`. A registry that accepts the connection and never answers does not reject, so the promise never settles:

- **webpack:** `HotReloaderWebpack.start()` awaits it (`this.versionInfo = await this.tracedGetVersionInfo(startSpan)`), so `next dev` never reaches "Ready".
- **Turbopack:** the request is started lazily, but each HMR connection's first `sync` message awaits `getVersionInfoCached()`. A browser connecting during a hang gets no sync.

I hit this during npm's incident on 2026-10-22 ("Degraded Package Install and Publishing"). Every CI job that started `next dev` (15.5, webpack) for Playwright timed out waiting for the server, for about 3.5 hours. The version indicator is the only thing that uses this response.

There is no issue for this, and no option to turn the check off.

### How?

The fetch gets `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(VERSION_INFO_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS)`, 5 000 ms. A healthy registry answers well inside that, and a slow mirror still has time. On ti

docs.title: turbo-tasks: pack CellKey into one word
docs.body:
## Summary

`CellKey` was an enum of a `u64` key hash and a `u32` provisional id, so it took 16 bytes, and a keyed cell dependency `(CellRef, CellKey)` took 24. Keyed dependencies are stored twice per edge: once in the reader's `cell_dependencies_keyed` and once in the cell owner's `cell_dependents_keyed`. Some apps have millions of these edges. In the app measured below, a single `nft.json` task holds 5.5M dependents.

`CellKey` is now one `u64`, and its top bit tells the two kinds apart:

- `CellKey::hash(h)` keeps the low 63 bits of the key hash. A collision on the dropped bit only causes over-invalidation: a dependent is recomputed when a sibling key changes. A stale read is not possible.
- `CellKey::provisional(id)` sets the top bit above the 32-bit id.
- `CellKey::kind()` returns a `CellKeyKind::{Hash, Provisional}` to match on. `is_provisional()` replaces the old `matches!` checks.

Each entry now takes 16 bytes. `CellKey` is encoded at its fixed 8-byte width; it was a varint, which took 9 bytes for a full-width hash. This changes the persisted format, and the persistent cache is versioned by commit.

### Results

v0 chat, cold `next build --experimental-build-mode=compile`, task storage memory report and sampled live heap at the end of the build:

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cell_dependents_keyed` | 415.0 MiB (41.3 B/entry) | 282.2 MiB (28.1 B/entry) |

docs.title: turbo-tasks-malloc: move shrinking reallocs so shrink_to_fit frees memory
docs.body:
## Summary

mimalloc's `realloc` keeps a block where it is whenever the new size is at least half the old size ([`alloc.c`](https://github.com/microsoft/mimalloc/blob/dev3/src/alloc.c): "reallocation still fits and not more than 50% waste"). A collection grown by doubling is always at least half full, so `shrink_to_fit` on it does nothing, and its slack (up to 50%, about 25% on average) stays allocated for as long as the value lives. That defeats every `shrink_to_fit` we rely on to trim long-lived data. Examples:

- the call in `Rope::from(Vec<u8>)` and `Rope::from(String)`
- the `ShrinkToFit` applied to cell values
- the shrinking in the backend's `TinyVec` and `AutoMap` collections

`TurboMalloc::realloc` now handles shrinks that land in that window itself. When a smaller size class would fit, it allocates a new block, copies the bytes into it and frees the old one. Growing reallocs, shrinks below half and over-aligned blocks still go to mimalloc as before.

### Results

v0 chat, cold `next build --experimental-build-mode=compile`, single runs, sampled live heap at the end of the build:

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| sampled live heap | 8.19 GiB | 7.50 GiB (−8.4%) |
| ropes built from `Vec`/`String` | 2.30 GiB | 1.71 GiB (−26%) |
| peak RSS | 11.86 GB | 11.43 GB (−3.6%) |
| wall time | 43.9 s | 43.7 s |
