docs.title: fix: recover PPR resume params from host rewrites
docs.body:
### What

In minimal mode, a PPR resume request for a host-rewritten route can fail with E592 ("postponed state should not be provided when fallback params are provided").

Example: a request to `/article` is rewritten to `/sites/runtime.example/article` and matches `/sites/[domain]/[[...slug]]`. The fallback param recovery in `base-server.ts` matches the original public path (`/article`) against the route, so it can't recover `domain`. The params keep the placeholder `[domain]` and the resume throws.

### Fix

The existing param resolution still runs first. Only for a minimal-mode PPR resume request that went through a rewrite and still has no valid params do we retry the lookup with the rewritten pathname.

### Tests

Before: the two placeholder-query cases from the issue return 500 (E592).
After: all five cases return 200, and the existing cases still pass.

Thanks to @jenslys for the detailed repro and for pointing at the lookup in the issue.

Fixes #101144

docs.title: Turbopack: respect adjustFontFallback: false for next/font/google
docs.body:
## Summary

With Turbopack, `adjustFontFallback: false` on a `next/font/google` font was ignored. The metric-adjusted `<Font> Fallback` face was still emitted and added to the font stack, and the font files were marked as size-adjusted. Webpack respects the option.

This had two causes:

- `NextFontRequestArguments` (`crates/next-core/src/next_font/google/request.rs`) was missing `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]`. The swc transform sends the options object with camelCase keys, so `adjustFontFallback` was never read and always defaulted to `true`. It is the only multi-word field in that struct. The `next/font/local` request struct already has the attribute.
- Even with the option read correctly, `get_font_fallback` would still wrap the unadjusted metrics lookup in an automatic fallback face. When `adjustFontFallback` is `false` and no `fallback` list is provided, no automatic fallback is generated anymore, matching the webpack loader.

When `fallback` is set, the behavior is unchanged.

This also unblocks #100305. That PR keeps the adjusted fallback when `fallback` is set. Without this fix, `fallback` + `adjustFontFallback: false` would get the adjusted face too, because the option is never read. That's what fails the existing `next/font › preload › font without size adjust` test there.

Fixes #74134

It is the workload behind the numbers in a series of build-time prerendering PRs that follow, so they can be reproduced.

docs.title: Skip measuring leaf segments when computing prefetch hints (-11.5% prerender CPU)
docs.body:
## Summary

Prerendering an App Router page in `next build` gets cheaper: on a 4,000-page static site, static generation uses 11.5% less CPU and 11.9% less wall time. The generated output is byte-identical.

When a page is prerendered, `collectPrefetchHints` renders every segment of the route to a prefetch response and gzips it to learn its size. That size has exactly one use: deciding whether the segment is small enough to be inlined into the prefetch of one of its children. A leaf segment has no children, so its size is never read. The leaf is the page itself, usually the largest segment of the route, so every prerendered page paid for one extra Flight render and one gzip of most of its data to produce a number nothing consumes.

This change measures a segment only if it has children. Segments with static prefetching disabled were already skipped the same way. The computed hints do not change.

## Verification

Paired benchmark on Vercel Sandbox VMs (8 vCPU x86, Node 24.22.1), base `ec8ddcd7a52`:

- Workload: `bench/static-isr-site` (#101398), 4,004 pages, 4 workers. The fixture is compiled once per arm with `next build --experimental-build-mode compile`, then `--experimental-build-mode generate` passes are timed, so only prerendering is measured.
- Design: both builds run in the same VM with passes interleaved A B B A; one delta per VM; mean and 95% interval across 8 VMs; p

docs.title: Measure segment gzip sizes with zlib directly (-4.9% prerender CPU)
docs.body:
## Summary

Prerendering an App Router page in `next build` gets cheaper: on a 4,000-page static site, static generation uses 4.9% less CPU, 5.4% less wall time and 2.6% less peak memory. The generated output is byte-identical.

When a page is prerendered, `collectPrefetchHints` gzips the prefetch response of each segment to learn its size, which decides whether the segment is inlined into a child's prefetch. `getGzipSize` did that by copying the buffer into a `Blob`, piping the Blob's stream through a `CompressionStream` and collecting the result with a `Response`: two copies of the data and three web streams for every measurement, to produce one number.

In Node.js, `CompressionStream('gzip')` is zlib's gzip with the default options behind a web stream. This change calls `zlib.gzip` on the buffer directly. The size is the same, so the hints are the same. The edge runtime keeps the web-stream implementation: the `node:zlib` require sits in the `else` branch of a `process.env.NEXT_RUNTIME === 'edge'` check, so it is not part of edge bundles.

Relation to #101399: that change stops measuring leaf segments, which are the largest measurements. The two are independent and both apply, but they overlap, so their effects do not add up fully. Together with #101406, all three were measured against `canary` as one: static generation wall time -22.4%, CPU -14.0%.

Prerendering a page with `cacheComponents: true` gets cheaper when the page has dynamic holes: on a 2,000-page site where 60% of the pages are partially prerendered, static generation uses 5.3% less CPU and 7.8% less wall time. - Full prelude (the normal case): only "dynamic metadata while nothing else is dynamic". The first report with a Suspense boundary above it settles that.

docs.body:
## Summary

Includes #101401; only the last commit is new. It will be rebased once #101401 lands.

Prerendering a partially prerendered page with `cacheComponents: true` gets cheaper again: on top of #101401, static generation of a 2,000-page site where 60% of the pages have dynamic holes uses 8.7% less CPU and 10.4% less wall time. The generated output is the same, and failing builds print the same errors.

Why it was still slow: after #101401, validating the static shell of a page with a full prelude still reads one component stack, which React builds by calling every function component on the stack again. That stack answers one question: is a dynamic hole inside the metadata boundary while nothing else is dynamic (the "`generateMetadata` depends on request data while the rest of the route does not" error)?

What the change does: React's postponed state already records where every hole is. The new `mayHaveDynamicMetadata` searches the postponed state for the metadata boundary's name (`__next_metadata_boundary__`). If it is not there, no hole is inside the metadata boundary, the metadata is not dynamic, and `trackDeferredAllowedDynamicAccesses` returns without reading a stack.

docs.title: Share one abort reason across prerender aborts (effect alone below the ±1.1% noise floor)
docs.body:
## Summary

Prerendering with `cacheComponents: true` creates fewer exceptions. Measured alone on a 2,000-page site against `canary`, static generation uses 0.9% less CPU and 1.2% less wall time, which is below what 16 VMs resolve (±1.1% on CPU). The generated output is the same. One thing a developer can observe changes; see "Behaviour change" below.

Why it was slow: `AbortController.abort()` without an argument constructs a new `DOMException` with a stack trace as the reason. A prerender ends each of its renders by aborting controllers, about ten per page in `prerenderToStream`, plus several per page in segment collection (`collectSegmentData`, `renderSegmentPrefetch`). In a profile of the benchmark, constructing these exceptions was 1.65% of the JavaScript CPU time of static generation.

What the change does, in two commits:

1. Segment collection: its aborts pass one shared `DOMException('This operation was aborted', 'AbortError')`, the kind `abort()` would have created. Nothing reads the reason of these aborts and user code cannot see it. This part also applies without `cacheComponents`.
2. `prerenderToStream`: the expected aborts that end the prospective and the final renders pass one shared reason of the same kind, created on first use (`getPrerenderAbortReason`).

docs.title: Balance static generation across workers with smaller batches (-7.1% prerender wall time)
docs.body:
## Summary

`next build` finishes static generation sooner when routes differ in cost: on a 4,000-page static site with 4 workers, static generation takes 7.1% less wall time. CPU time is 2.7% higher and peak memory is unchanged there. The generated output is byte-identical on that site, and which worker renders which page is as reproducible as before.

Which worker renders which page still depends only on the export paths and the number of workers, as on `canary`: the batches are dealt out to the workers in turn, and nothing is decided by which worker happens to be free. That matters for a page whose Flight row order depends on what its worker rendered before (for example a second request that resolves without I/O because another page of that worker already put the response into the data cache). docs.body:
## Summary

With `cacheComponents: true`, `next build` serializes and compresses the resume data cache of a partially prerendered page once instead of twice. Measured alone on a 2,000-page site against `canary`, static generation uses 1.0% less CPU and 1.2% less wall time, which is below what 16 VMs resolve (±1.1% on CPU). The generated output is the same, including the fallback shells that are seeded from these strings.

Why it was slow: a partially prerendered page serialized its resume data cache twice. The render does it for the postponed state that is written to the `.meta` file. Then `exportAppPage` in the export worker did it again, with `stringifyResumeDataCache` and `deflateResumeDataCache`, for the copy that seeds fallback shells. Each time, every cache entry is read from a teed stream, base64 encoded, stringified and deflated. The two results are the same string.

Why it is safe: it relies on the postponed state being built from the same cache that the render returns as `renderResumeDataCache`, with the same `experimental.disableResumeDataCacheCompression` setting. That holds at all four pla

docs.title: Capture one stack per `use cache` timeout error (effect alone below the ±1.0% noise floor)
docs.body:
## Summary

Every call of a `"use cache"` function captures one stack trace instead of two. Measured alone on a 2,000-page `cacheComponents` site against `canary`, its effect on static generation is below what 8 VMs resolve (CPU -0.5% ±1.0%). The generated output is the same, and a build that fails with a cache timeout prints the same error with the same stack.

Why it was slow: `cache()` in `use-cache-wrapper.ts` creates a `UseCacheTimeoutError` for every call of a cached function, so that the error points at the caller if the function hangs. The error is almost never used. Its constructor captured a stack trace, and the next line, `Error.captureStackTrace(timeoutError, cache)`, replaced that trace with one that starts at the caller of `cache`. Capturing is the expensive part of creating an error, and it happened twice. The benchmark site makes about 8 such calls per page.

What the change does: `Error.stackTraceLimit` is set to 0 while the constructor runs and restored right after, so only the second capture happens. The constructor only builds a message string, so nothing else runs while the limit is 0. The stack that is kept is the one that was shown before.

Behaviour change: none. This path runs for every `"use cache"` call, at build time and at runtime, in development and in production.

docs.title: Escape inline Flight data in one pass over UTF-8 bytes (+8.7% req/s on a docs-style page)
docs.body:
## Summary

Rendering an App Router page on the Node.js server gets cheaper, most where the page sends a lot of data to the client. On the documentation-style page of `bench/basic-app` (`/docs`: a 616 KB document, 523 KB of it inline Flight data), `next start` serves 8.7% more requests per second and median latency drops 6.3%. A dashboard-style page gains about 3%; a blog index is within noise. The HTML is byte-identical.

Every batch of Flight data is inlined into the document as the body of a `self.__next_f.push(...)` script. To build that script, `pullFlightData` in `stream-ops.node.ts` ran each batch through `JSON.stringify`, a slice, the `htmlEscapeJsonString` regex replace, `Buffer.byteLength` and a UTF-8 write. Each of those walks the whole payload and most allocate a payload-sized string; byte chunks were decoded to a string first. The inline scripts are 56% to 85% of the document on the benchmark pages, so this was 16.4% of main-thread CPU on `/docs`.

This change escapes the UTF-8 bytes directly, in one table-driven pass, into a reused output buffer (`encodeInlineFlightScript`). It produces the same bytes because every character that `JSON.stringify` and `htmlEscapeJsonString` escape is a single ASCII byte, except U+2028 and U+2029, which are matched as their three-byte sequences, and no byte of a multibyte UTF-8 sequence is an ASCII byte. docs.title: Reuse settled client chunk loads across renders in production (-1.4% dashboard page latency)
docs.body:
## Summary

Server-rendering an App Router page with many client components gets slightly cheaper. On the dashboard-style page of `bench/basic-app` (`/dashboard`, dozens of client component modules), median latency under `next start` drops 1.4% and throughput rises 1.6%. The effect is small, and it was measured twice. Rendered output does not change.

During SSR, React asks for every chunk of every client reference on every render: about 1,500 `__next_chunk_load__` calls per `/dashboard` request. Each call went through the client component load tracker (an `AsyncLocalStorage` lookup) into the bundler runtime, where Turbopack's `loadChunkAsync` runs a regex over the chunk path before it finds the chunk in its own cache and returns an already settled promise. Outside of development a chunk that has loaded stays loaded, so all of that work produces a promise the previous render already had.

This change remembers the settled promise per chunk, per page entry, and returns it directly (`installGlobalModuleLoadingHandlers`). It is the same promise object the bundler returned, because React relies on its identity. The old path is kept when:

- the dev server is running (`__NEXT_DEV_SERVER`): chunks can be replaced there, so nothing is remembered;
- a render is measuring client component loading, that is its span is recording or `NEXT_OTEL_PERFORMANCE_PREFIX` is set: every load then go

docs.title: Fix OpenTelemetry treated as enabled when no tracer provider is registered (+3.2% route handler req/s)
docs.body:
## Summary

Bug: in a Turbopack production build, Next.js treats OpenTelemetry as enabled when no tracer provider is registered. Every `trace()` call made from the bundled server code of an app (route handlers, pages) then starts a noop span, enters a context scope and chains promises, on every request. Nothing is recorded, so responses are the same, but the work is paid for. With the fix a trivial route handler under `next start` serves 3.2% more requests per second.

`isOpenTelemetryEnabled()` in `server/lib/trace/tracer.ts` decides whether a provider is registered by comparing the name of the provider delegate's class with `'NoopTracerProvider'`. The tracer is also bundled into the app's server output, together with `@opentelemetry/api`. Turbopack minifies that copy and emits the provider as an anonymous class expression (`b.NoopTracerProvider=class{...}`), so `constructor.name` is `''` and the check answers "enabled". The unbundled copy in `next/dist` keeps the name and answers correctly, which is why only code in the app bundle was affected. Webpack builds have the bug too: their minifier mangles the class name (`b.NoopTracerProvider=e`).

The fix also compares the delegate's class with the API's own noop provider class, taken once at module load from a `ProxyTracerProvider` without a delegate. The name check stays, so nothing that was detected as noop before is treated di

docs.title: Reuse a route module's loaded manifests between requests (+6.8% route handler req/s)
docs.body:
## Summary

A request to the Node.js server does less work before it reaches user code. A trivial route handler under `next start` serves 6.8% more requests per second and its median latency drops 3.9%. Responses are identical.

`RouteModule.prepare()` calls `loadManifests()` for every request, which loads fourteen manifests. Outside of development each of them is read once and then served from the manifest cache, but every request still joined each manifest's path, looked each one up in the cache and rebuilt the interception route patterns, to arrive at the same objects as the request before.

This change keeps the result of the previous load on the route module and returns it while the page, the project directory and the dist directory are the same. Otherwise it loads as before. The old path is always taken in development, where manifests change between requests, and in the Edge runtime, where they come from globals.

Behaviour change: the object `loadManifests()` returns is now the same object for consecutive requests in production, including the values that used to be created per request: the empty fallback used for a missing manifest and the array of interception route patterns. Code that mutated them would now affect later requests. A search of the callers found none.

docs.title: Send small route handler bodies with Content-Length, uncompressed (+24.5% req/s)
docs.body:
## Summary

Behaviour change: on `next start` and `next dev`, a route handler response whose body is under 1024 bytes and already in memory is now sent with a `Content-Length` and is no longer gzipped. This changes behaviour that #101220 ("Automatically compress route handler responses if not already compressed") introduced three days before this work, and it edits two expectations that PR added to `test/e2e/compression/compression.test.ts`. The author of #101220 should confirm that this is wanted.

It applies when all of these hold: the `compression` middleware is active on the response, the body arrives as a single chunk of fewer than 1024 bytes, and the body's stream closes in the same tick. That covers bodies made from a string, an `ArrayBuffer`, a typed array, `Response.json()` / `NextResponse.json()`, and a cached route handler body. 1024 bytes is the middleware's default `threshold`, which is how the router server sets it up.

What a client sees, for `GET /api/app` in `bench/basic-app` (body `{"name":"John Doe"}`):

| request | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `Accept-Encoding: gzip` | `Content-Encoding: gzip`, `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, 39 body bytes | `Content-Length: 19`, 19 body bytes |
| no `Accept-Encoding` | `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, 19 body bytes | `Content-Length: 19`, 19 body bytes |

docs.title: Remove five per-request overheads from request handling (+9.6% route handler req/s)
docs.body:
## Summary

Five small pieces of work that the Node.js server repeated for every request are done once or not at all. Together they make a trivial route handler under `next start` serve 9.6% more requests per second, and one with a dynamic segment 11.0% more. Responses are identical. Each is its own commit; they were measured together because each alone is below what the benchmark resolves.

1. **`structuredClone` of the parsed URL** (`server-utils.ts`). `handleRewrites()` deep-cloned the parsed URL for every request that reaches a route module. `structuredClone` serializes and deserializes, about 3 µs for an object this small. A parsed URL holds strings, `null`, and a query of strings and string arrays, so those are copied directly. Any other value still goes through `structuredClone`.
2. **Middleware lookup for every request** (`base-server.ts`). `handleNextDataRequest()` awaited `getMiddleware()` before checking whether the request is a `_next/data` request at all. The result is only used to normalize the trailing slash of a data request. The lookup now happens there.
3. **`process.env` read in every `trace()` call** (`tracer.ts`). `getLocalSpanRecorder()` read `process.env.__NEXT_DEV_SERVER` first. In the unbundled server that variable is not inlined, so each read is a call into Node.js (about 0.2 µs, a dozen times per request). Only the dev server registers a recorder, so

docs.title: Build route definitions once outside development (0.63x minimal-mode CPU per request)
docs.body:
## Summary

In minimal mode, a request costs much less CPU to route. On the minimal server of `bench/next-minimal-server`, a trivial route handler takes 0.63x the CPU per request and serves 1.66x the requests per second; a route handler with a dynamic segment takes 0.69x and serves 1.54x. `next start` is not affected: there the router server has already matched the request and this code does not run. Responses are identical.

Since #94157 ("Remove server route matcher stack"), a request that the server matches itself goes through `getRouteMatch()` in `base-server.ts`, which calls `getRouteDefinitions()`. That rebuilds every route definition from the manifests (`normalizePagePath`, `normalizeAppPath` and a `path.join` per route), then sorts the dynamic routes and compiles a route regex for each dynamic route it tests. All of it is repeated for every request, and the cost grows with the number of routes. In the benchmark app, which has a dozen routes, it was 34% of the minimal server's CPU on the trivial route handler.

Outside of development the manifests do not change. This change keeps the definitions, their sorted dynamic subset and the compiled matchers for as long as `pagesManifest`, `appPathsManifest` and `appPathRoutes` are the same objects, and rebuilds them when one is replaced. Development rebuilds them for every request, as before.

docs.body:

Includes #101411 and #101413; of its twelve commits the last ten are new. docs.title: Let scavenges reclaim a prerender's React requests after it is done (-6.4% prerender CPU)
docs.body:
## Summary

Prerendering App Router pages in `next build` uses less CPU: 6.4% less on a 4,000-page static site in the default configuration (4.5% less wall time), and about 2% to 4% less on a 2,000-page site with `cacheComponents: true`. The generated output is identical. The gain is garbage collection: objects of a finished prerender used to survive every young-generation GC and were only freed by a full GC.

Why they survived. React aborts a render through the `signal` it is given: `attachAbortSignal` in Fizz and in the Flight server calls `signal.addEventListener('abort', listener, { signal: lifetime })`, where `lifetime` is React's own signal that fires when the render ends, so that the listener is removed then. Node.js implements that `signal` option with a weak listener: a `WeakRef`, a `FinalizationRegistry` entry and a `WeakMap` entry whose value reaches its key. A scavenge treats all three as strong references. The listener closes over the render's request, so the request and everything it holds (its tasks, its table of written objects, the model) is copied by the next scavenge, promoted by the one after, and freed only by a full GC. Per prerendered page that was about 330 KB in the default configuration and 290 KB under `cacheComponents`.

docs.body:

Moves Turbopack onto the fixed-width integer support added in vercel-labs/bincode-fork#21. It is used for a few usecases

- **Identifiers.** `TaskId`, `RawVc`, `CellId`, `ValueTypeId`, `FunctionId` and `TraitTypeId` now get fixed-width encoding from bincode's own fixint encoder/decoder adapters. The hand-rolled `turbo_bincode::fixed_width` helper is removed.
- **Persisted hashes and millisecond timestamps.** These are now encoded at fixed width:

    - `outputs_hash` and `sources_hash` in `routes_hashes_manifest`

docs.body:
## Summary

Prerendering App Router pages with `cacheComponents: true` in `next build` uses about 2% to 3% less CPU on a 2,000-page site: -2.1% and -3.1% in two paired benchmarks of this change alone, with 7 of 8 VMs agreeing in each. docs.title: Create the request store as a class instance so scavenges can free it (alone below ±1.1% noise floor)
docs.body:
## Summary

Every App Router request leaves less behind for the garbage collector. On a trivial route handler under `next start`, what survives a scavenge drops from 2.3 KB to 0.5 KB per request and the scavenge pause from 1.85 ms to 0.81 ms. On its own, against `canary`, the change does not move CPU per request or throughput on a warm `next start` route handler beyond the ±1.1% a 32-VM paired benchmark resolves; what survives a scavenge drops 4.7% there (Verification). Its effect shows on top of the other route handler changes, where the request store is a larger share of what survives (below). Responses are byte-identical.

The request store (`createRequestStore`) was an object literal with five getters (`headers`, `cookies`, `mutableCookies`, `userspaceMutableCookies`, `draftMode`), created for every request. V8 allocates the accessor pair of a getter in an object literal in the old generation, and the pair references the getter's closure. A scavenge treats every pointer from the old generation as a root, so each store kept what its getters close over (the request's `Headers`, the lazily created cookies, the implicit tags) alive until the next major GC, long after the response was sent.

docs.title: Skip three conversions for plain requests in request handling (part of +13.4% route handler req/s across 5 PRs)
docs.body:
## Summary

Three per-request conversions are skipped when their result is known. Together with four sibling changes (#101425, #101427, #101423, #101424) route handlers serve 13.4% more requests per second from a freshly started server and use 0.855x the CPU per request once it is warm (after 30,000 requests). Responses are byte-identical. Three independent commits:

1. `NextRequest` converted all request headers to a Node.js headers object for the `NextURL` it creates, which sorts and combines them. `NextURL` reads one header from it: `host`, to detect a domain locale, also after `clone()`. It now gets an object with only the host. `Headers.get('host')` returns the value the converted object held: the values joined by `, `, and nothing when the header is absent. This applies to middleware too.
2. `decodePathParams` splits the pathname, decodes every segment, escapes path delimiters with a regular expression compiled per segment, and joins the result. A pathname without `%`, `#`, `?` or a backslash comes out unchanged (nothing to decode; an encoded delimiter needs a `%`), so it is returned directly. It cannot throw a `DecodeError` either.
3. `normalizeCdnUrl` parses `req.url`, strips routing params from the query and formats the URL again. For an absolute path of unreserved characters (letters, digits, `-`, `.`, `_`, `~`, `/`) without a query, a hash, a leading `//` or a `.`/`.

docs.body:
## Summary

Includes #101414; only the last commit is new. It will be rebased once #101414 lands.

A request no longer waits for the registration of `instrumentation.ts` again after it has completed. Together with four sibling changes (#101425, #101426, #101423, #101424) route handlers serve 13.4% more requests per second from a freshly started server and use 0.855x the CPU per request once it is warm (after 30,000 requests). Responses are byte-identical.

`RouteModule.ensureInstrumentation` runs twice for every request (from the route template and from `prepare`). Each call awaited a dynamic import of the instrumentation globals and then the registration promise, long after both had settled: four trips through the microtask queue and 2.6 KB per request.

The route module now remembers that registration completed and skips both awaits from then on. Registration is a single promise per process that is never replaced, so awaiting it again after it fulfilled does nothing, and `ensureInstrumentationRegisteredWithDeferredSpans` returns `undefined` once registration has started. The flag is only set after a successful await: while registration is pending, callers still wait for it, so the hook still completes before the first handler runs, and when it failed every request still rethrows.

## Summary

An app with rewrites pays for them again on every request that reaches a page or a route handler: 4 to 5 microseconds of CPU per rewrite per request on a warm server, whether or not a rewrite matches. docs.body:
## Summary

Every request to a `next start` server does four small things again that it had already done, or that give the same result each time. Without them a trivial route handler allocates 2.7 KB less per request (113.6 KB to 110.8 KB). Together with three sibling changes (#101433, #101435 and the last commit of #101416) a warm server uses 0.937x the CPU per request on that route, which none of the three siblings touches. The four, one commit each:

docs.title: Compile the value patterns of `has` and `missing` once, not per request (-134 B allocated per rule per request)
docs.body:
## Summary

A `headers`, `redirects` or `rewrites` rule, or a middleware matcher, with a `has` or `missing` item that carries a `value` cost every request that reached the item a `RegExp` compilation: 134 bytes and about 0.6 microseconds per rule per request under `next start`, whether or not the rule applied. The pattern is now compiled once per process. An app without such rules is unchanged. Responses are byte-identical, and so is the client bundle.

Why it was slow: `matchHas` (`prepare-destination.ts`) ran `new RegExp('^' + value + '$')` for every item with a `value` whose header, cookie, query key or host was present on the request. It is called for every rule whose source matched the path: by the router (`resolveRoutes`), by the route module when it walks the rewrites again (`handleRewrites`, the only walk behind a deployment adapter), and by the middleware matcher.

What the change does: the compiled expression is kept in a `Map` by its source. The values come from the configuration, so the map has as many entries as the configuration has distinct values. The expressions have no flags, so `String.prototype.match` with a kept one gives the same result and leaves no state behind. A value that is not a valid pattern throws on every request, as before: nothing is stored for it.

docs.body:
## Summary

Includes #101401, #101402 and #101403 (the first four commits); only the last commit is new. It will be rebased once they land. This is a change to how a page is prerendered with `cacheComponents`, and it needs a decision from the maintainers of that path; what it changes for a page author comes first.

What the prospective HTML prerender does today. With `cacheComponents`, `prerenderToStream` renders a page to HTML twice. The first render (over the prospective Flight result) is thrown away. It has two jobs, both for the benefit of the final render, which runs in two back-to-back tasks (render, abort) and turns whatever is still waiting at the abort into a hole:

1. Loading. It makes every client module of the page load: client reference chunks, async modules, `import()` inside client components. It is kept alive until the process-wide module loading signal is idle (`trackPendingModules`, `cacheReady()`). Without it, a module that takes longer than a task would leave a hole where static HTML belongs.
2. Evaluating. It is the first render to evaluate the page's client modules, and synchronous IO does not stop it (its store's controller is not the one React listens to). So `Date.now()` or `Math.random()` in the scope of a client module runs there, once, and not in the final render, where synchronous IO is an error (`cache-components-errors/module-scope.test.ts`).

docs.body:
## Summary

In an app with `i18n`, `next start` prepared a locale redirect for every request, although only the root path can be redirected. For every other path that work is now skipped: a request allocates 1.2 KB to 1.7 KB less. CPU per request does not change measurably. An app without `i18n` is unchanged. What the change does: the router server makes that same test first and only then resolves the domain, parses the URL and calls `getLocaleRedirect`. A request target that does not start with `/` (absolute-form, `*`) still goes through `parseUrl`, which throws for some of them today and keeps doing so.

Where it applies: `next start` and standalone output only. A deployment adapter does not run the router server.

This change has no CPU effect of its own: a paired benchmark of it alone reads 0.997 ±0.036 and 0.998 ±0.026. In a profile the URL parse that was skipped here showed up again in the next parse of the same request (`resolveRoutes`), at the same cost. What it removes is the allocation.

docs.title: Copy the request headers in IncrementalCache only for a cache handler that can keep them (-11 KB allocated per request with 32 headers)
docs.body:
## Summary

`next start` copied all request headers twice per request. It now copies them only for a cache handler that can keep them. With the 32 request headers a hosting platform adds, a route handler request allocates 11.2 KB less (243.2 KB to 232.0 KB on `/api/app`). Its CPU effect alone is below what the benchmark resolves (0.950 ±0.050 CPU per request on `/api/app`, 6 VMs). Responses are byte-identical.

Why it was slow: `base-server.ts` constructs an `IncrementalCache` in `handleRequestImpl` and another in `renderToResponseWithComponentsImpl`, each with `requestHeaders: Object.assign({}, req.headers)`. A copy costs more as the header count grows: 5.6 KB per copy with those 32 headers. docs.body:
## Summary

`next start` removes Next.js's internal headers from every incoming request. It did so by comparing every request header with the list of internal names, so the cost grew with the number of headers a request carries. It now asks the headers object for each of the twelve names. The same headers are removed. Alone it saves about 3 microseconds per request in a profile, with no measurable allocation; that is below what a paired benchmark resolves (CPU per request 1.008 ±0.065 and 0.993 ±0.067 with the 32 headers a hosting platform adds, 4 VMs). Why it was slow: `filterInternalHeaders` (`server/lib/server-ipc/utils.ts`) ran `for (const header in headers)` with `INTERNAL_HEADERS.includes(header)`: every header times a scan of 12 names.

The `for...in` also skipped own non-enumerable properties, which a Node.js request's headers object never has (every header is a plain assigned property); if one existed it would now be removed too.

Where it applies: the router server, so `next start` and standalone output only. A deployment adapter does not run it.

docs.title: Preserve Content-Encoding on Route Handler responses in send-response
docs.body:
## What

Stop stripping `Content-Encoding` from Route Handler responses, and keep the header stripping in `sendResponse` scoped to the only case that needs it: responses proxied from a decoded `fetch()`.

## Why

`packages/next/src/server/send-response.ts` copies response headers through a `FORBIDDEN_HEADERS = ['content-length', 'content-encoding', 'transfer-encoding']` check that applies to every response, on the assumption that the body was transparently decompressed by `fetch`. That assumption only holds for decoded fetch responses. For the dominant App Router case (a handler returning a manually built `Response`) nothing decoded anything, yet the header is still dropped.

The concrete failure, verified on 16.4.5 stable and 16.5.0-canary.45: a handler returning a gzip body with `Content-Encoding: gzip` sends the compressed bytes intact but without the header (raw `1f8b` magic declared `text/plain`). Under 1 kB the compression middleware does not kick in, so the response ships with no encoding at all; over 1 kB the middleware re-compresses the already-compressed body (double gzip confirmed by double decompression) and clients decompressing once read gzip-in-gzip.

## How

Keep stripping `content-length` (Node recomputes it at piping time) and `transfer-encoding` (hop-by-hop), but preserve `content-encoding` as-is. For decoded fetch responses, losing `Content-Encod

Fix deployed RSC responses after static-to-partial revalidation
docs.body:
After a fully static Cache Components route regenerated as partial, adapter deployments returned empty RSC responses. The platform supplied new postponed state, but the handler still trusted the build-time `prefetchDataRoute` and stripped Flight headers. Navigations failed with React #412 and fell back to document loads. Runtime prefetches and runtime shells also failed to receive their request data.

The handler now uses supplied postponed state to select dynamic RSC rendering in minimal mode. That state takes precedence over the build-time static RSC signal. The handler preserves Flight headers so the renderer honors the caller's router state and requested prefetch stage. It produces fresh RSC and can reuse the Resume Data Cache from the supplied state.

PR #101357 addresses this same static-to-partial revalidation case for `next start` as part of its broader RSC cache handling changes.

The deploy regression suite uses real router interactions to cover navigation, runtime prefetches, and runtime shells after revalidation, including caller-specific cookies and prefetch stage boundaries.

docs.body:
## Summary

Every `NextRequest` parsed the request's `cookie` header when it was constructed, whether or not the handler ever reads `request.cookies`. The cookies are now parsed when they are first read. What the change does: the constructor only keeps `this.headers.get('cookie')`, the string the parser would have been given at that moment. docs.title: Release fetch cache locks when origin fetch throws synchronously
docs.body:
Adopts #101380. Closes #101380.

Cached fetches can leave a cache lock held when `originFetch` throws synchronously. The deduplication wrapper constructs a `Request` before returning a promise, so malformed URLs and invalid request options can throw before the existing `.catch` handler is attached. Subsequent fetches for the same cache key then wait indefinitely, which can make static generation time out even when the page catches the original error.

This change calls `originFetch` inside a promise callback so synchronous throws become rejections and reach the existing handler that releases the lock. The regression test covers two pages fetching the same malformed URL and rendering their fallback content.

Fixes #101377.

docs.title: Turbopack: webpack-loader pool processes stay alive (and hold their heap) after compilation, through "Collecting page data" and "Generating static pages"
docs.body:
### What happens

During `next build` with `reactCompiler: true`, Turbopack starts one webpack-loader pool for the React Compiler's Babel transform, sized to `available_parallelism()`. The pool processes (`pool_entry-[turbopack-node]_transforms_webpack-loaders_ts_*.js`) each grow to about 370-560 MB RSS during compilation. Compilation ends ("Compiled successfully"), but the pool processes are not shut down: they stay alive and idle, holding that memory, until the whole build exits. Static generation then starts its own workers on top of them.

Measured in a Docker build (Linux VM, 8 CPUs, next 16.4.4, a production App Router app, process tree sampled every 2 s inside the VM):

| phase | loader pool | static workers (6) | `next-build` main |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| compile | 8 processes, about 3.4 GB | none | about 2.1 GB |
| static generation | still 8 processes, about 3.4 GB, idle | about 2.6-3.1 GB | about 2.5 GB |

The peak of the build is the sum of all three, about 8 GB. With `reactCompiler: false` (and `TURBO_TASKS_AVAILABLE_PARALLELISM=2`) there is no loader pool at all and the same build peaks about 3 GB lower. With the CPUs pinned to 2 (`taskset -c 0-1`), the pool is 2 processes, about 0.8 GB, still alive through static generation.

docs.title: Route Handler responses lose Content-Encoding in 16.4.5, so self-compressed bodies are sent without it
docs.body:
https://github.com/thedann/next-content-encoding-repro
 

1. `npm install && npm run build && npm start`
2. `curl -s -D - -o body.bin -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip' http://localhost:3000/gzipped`
3. Look at the response headers and the first bytes of `body.bin` (`xxd body.bin | head -1`).

The route handler gzips its own body and sets `Content-Encoding: gzip`:

```ts
import { gzipSync } from 'node:zlib'

export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'

export function GET() {
  const body = gzipSync('<?xml version="1.0"?><urlset></urlset>')

  return new Response(new Uint8Array(body), {
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'text/xml',
      'Content-Encoding': 'gzip',
    },
  })
}
```
 

**Current (16.4.5):** the `content-encoding` header is removed, but the body is still the gzipped bytes:

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: text/xml

00000000: 1f8b 0800 0000 0000 0013 ...
```

Clients receive binary data labelled `text/xml`. In production this broke our `sitemap.xml` for Googlebot and our uptime monitor.

**Expected (and the behavior in 16.4.3):** the header the handler set is kept:

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-encoding: gzip
content-type: text/xml
```

docs.body:
## Summary

`next build` with `cacheComponents` no longer logs `Unexpected cache miss after cache warming phase during prerendering` for a page that reads a short-lived `use cache` entry which another page of the same build already stored. The message blames non-deterministic arguments; here the arguments are fine. The prerendered output does not change.

When it happens: a `use cache` function with a short cache life (`cacheLife('seconds')`, `revalidate: 0`, or an `expire` under five minutes) whose arguments are the same on several pages, for example the stock of a product read by that product's page in every locale. The first page that reads it generates the entry and writes it to the cache handler. A later page prerendered by the same worker gets it from the cache handler, and that page logs the message, as an `Error:` with a stack, once per page.

Why. A static prerender leaves a hole for such an entry. In `cache()` in `use-cache-wrapper.ts`, the cache-warming render of the later page finds the entry in the cache handler, sees that it is too short-lived, and returns the hanging promise without recording anything in the page's resume data cache. The final render then has neither an entry nor a marker for the key, takes the "this is the final prerender, all caches should have been warmed" branch, and warns. Every other path that omits an entry records why: the page that gener

docs.title: next upgrade: only stop for an equivalent open pull request
docs.body:
The agentic `next upgrade` now stops only for an equivalent **open pull request**, not for any branch or commit that once attempted the same change.

**Why**

The duplicate check in `shared.md` told the agent to scan local and remote branches and commits and stop on any "equivalent work". In practice, a Future Defaults run that would enable `cacheComponents` stopped before changing any files. The only reason was a long-abandoned remote branch that had tried to adopt Cache Components once. No PR was open for it. Abandoned branches are common, so this check blocks real upgrades and gives users nothing to act on.

**Approach**

An open PR is the only signal that someone is actively shipping the same change. Limiting the stop condition to open PRs, and defining "equivalent" narrowly, should remove these false-positive stops while still preventing duplicate PRs.

- Removed the instructions to check local/remote branches and commits.
- An open PR is equivalent only if it carries this app's `next-upgrade` marker for the same upgrade type, or performs the same version update (to this target or newer) or adopts the same Future Defaults.
- Branches, commits, and closed/merged PRs never stop the upgrade. Partial overlap (older target, another app, a subset of the Future Defaults) is not equivalent. The agent mentions notable related work in its report and continues.
- Updated the handoff

Eleven eval fixtures (`agent-000`, `agent-021` through `agent-030`) pinned `ai@5.0.59` and `@ai-sdk/react@2.0.0-beta.28`, so an agent adding AI features inside them would start out on the deprecated route.

This moves those fixtures to `ai@7.0.166` and `@ai-sdk/react@4.0.170`. None of the fixture sources or `EVAL.ts` files import from `ai` or `@ai-sdk/react`, so no code changes are needed.

`@ai-sdk/react@4` has a peer dependency of `react@^18 || ~19.0.1 || ~19.1.2 || ^19.2.1`, and the fixtures pinned `react@19.1.0`, so `npm install` (which the eval runner uses) fails with `ERESOLVE`. `react` and `react-dom` move to `19.1.2` in the same fixtures, a patch bump in the same minor line.

AI SDK 7 requires Node 22 or newer.

Same change as vercel/workflow-examples#61.

## Testing

- Before the React bump, `npm install` in a copy of `agent-000` failed with `ERESOLVE` on the `@ai-sdk/react` peer range.

docs.body:
## Summary

With `cacheComponents: true`, `next start` serves a page whose static shell reads `use cache` data with 9% to 14% less CPU per request: a 1 MB page -12.9% under load and -12.6% under serial load, a 528 KB page -9.5% and -9.0%, their RSC requests (client navigations) -12.5% and -13.8%, -8.5% and -11.4%. None of it depends on the request: the state only changes when the page is revalidated.

docs.title: Drop the staged Flight replay buffer early (-0.8 MB kept per RSC request with cacheComponents)
docs.body:
## Summary

This is a memory change. With `cacheComponents: true`, an RSC request (a client navigation) served by `next start` no longer leaves its whole response payload behind for the old generation: the bytes of a request that survive a young-generation GC fall by 91.1% to 97.5%, from 0.8 to 0.9 MB to 0.02 to 0.07 MB (paired benchmark, 8 VMs, p < 0.001 in all four cells). CPU per request, throughput and latency are not shown to change. Responses are unchanged.

Why it happened. Under `cacheComponents` the Flight render of a request is staged, and its stream is read twice: once for the response and once by `countShellBytes`, which measures how many bytes belong to the static stage. Both readers come from one `ReplayableNodeStream`. That class keeps every chunk in `_chunks` so that a reader created later can replay what it missed. Here both readers are created before the source emits anything, so the buffer is never read, but it kept collecting every chunk of the payload for as long as the object lived.

docs.title: Resolve parallel route params from the URL when predicting routes
docs.body:
When the client predicts a route from a learned pattern, it matched the URL against the known-route trie and collected param values along the matched path. That path follows one parallel route branch, usually `children`. Other branches map the same URL onto their own segments, so a param that only exists in another branch, like a slot's catch-all, never got a value. The pattern's old value was kept instead, which produced a tree mixing params from two URLs:

```
URL: /de-de/f/herren

children:     [locale]=de-de / f / [slug]=herren
@desktopNav:  [locale]=de-de / [...catchAll]=f/women   <- learned from /en-de/f/women
```

The server then rendered a different tree, and the client retried the navigation with a second request. The retry could lose the scroll-to-top, because the slot leaf with no layout boxes held the scroll intent. This affects the documented `@modal/[...catchAll]` pattern for closing a modal on navigation, and the same stale value causes the prefetch loops traced in #98073.

Now the trie only selects the pattern. When the pattern is reified, each active branch reads its own params from the URL parts, using the same rules as route discovery. If a branch doesn't fit the URL, prediction falls back to the server. Inactive parallel routes become default segments, which is what the server sends for them; on navigation the client reuses the active segment in that slot.

### What?

When an `import { ... }` names an export that doesn't exist, Turbopack's "Export X doesn't exist in target module" issue proposes the closest export name ("Did you mean to import Y?"). It no longer proposes names that the same declaration already imports.

### Why?

The suggestion picked the most similar name among **all** exports of the target module, including ones the user had just imported in the same statement. For example, the `comptime/cross-module-strict` execution test imports every export of `other.js` plus `MISSING`, and the issue suggested `LONG_REGEX`, which is already part of that import. - Reading the import map only at render time leaves reference resolution and the ESM references' task inputs untouched, so caching is unaffected.
- Aliases are excluded by their original export name (`Kitten as k` excludes `Kitten`). Names imported by a *separate* declaration are still suggested.

docs.title: Turbopack: don't grow effect vectors inside the analyzer arena
docs.body:
The analyzer collects effects into bump-allocated vectors while it walks a module. A bump arena can't free memory, so every time one of those vectors grows, its old buffer stays allocated until the analysis finishes. Effect vectors grow constantly, so a large part of the arena ends up being abandoned buffers.

Collect effects in heap vectors instead, and copy each finished block into the arena at its exact size. The arena then only holds what is actually kept, as intended when effects moved into the arena in #94614.

No change in output. Measured on analyze_ecmascript_module alone, release build, 5 alternating rounds against the parent commit, as median paired changes:

| Input                 | Peak memory | Bytes allocated | Allocations | CPU   |
| --------------------- | ----------- | --------------- | ----------- | ----- |
| 8,000 modules         | -20.1%      | -8.4%           | +3.3%       | -0.9% |
| Generated stress      | -22.3%      | -14.9%          | +0.0%       | -1.0% |
| Four large benchmarks | +0.0%       | +6.7%           | +3.1%       | -4.1% |

Peak memory is the sum of each module's peak live allocations. On the 8,000 modules it goes from 7,652 MB to 6,118 MB. The CPU changes are within noise. The four large benchmark files gain bytes from the heap vectors' own growth and the final copy, without a change in peak.

Fixes a runtime error with Turbopack scope hoisting (module merging) when a module imports a named export that doesn't exist from a module that was merged into the same scope hoisting group:

docs.title: turbo-tasks-backend: keep the active count inline
docs.body:
## Summary

A task's activeness was an `ActivenessState` lazy field. The field was added when the task became active and removed when it became inactive, and tasks do that a few times per build: about 17.8M activations on a large app with 7.9M tasks. Every one of those added and removed a lazy field. The removals mostly happened long after the task completed, so each also left an empty 40-byte slot in the lazy field vec.

The state is now split:

- **The active count** lives inline in an `i16`. It fits in `TaskStorage`'s padding, so `TaskStorage` stays 128 bytes.
- **The lazy `activeness_state` field** holds the rarely needed rest: root and active-until-clean state, the clean event, and the count while it doesn't fit the `i16`. Only roots, tasks kept active until clean, and very widely shared tasks need it.
- **Activeness is unchanged in meaning:** a task is active while either is present, which covers a negative count during races.

Most activations are now just a counter update. The call sites go through an `ActivenessAccessors` trait (`is_active`, `has_positive_active_count`, `add_active_count`, …).

docs.title: turbo-tasks-backend: store task edges in flat EdgeSets
docs.body:
## Summary

A task's dependency edges were `AutoSet`s, which become hash tables above a few elements. In the task storage memory report at the end of a build, about half of each such table is slack: empty buckets, power-of-two rounding, control bytes and the boxed table header.

This replaces them with `EdgeSet`, a flat array of exactly its elements:

- **Lookups** (`contains`) scan it and never change it.
- **Inflating is implicit:** `insert` and `remove` switch an array of more than 32 elements to a hash table first, since more changes usually follow.
- **Flattening is explicit:** `shrink_to_fit` turns a hash table back into an exactly sized array. The callers know when a batch of changes is done.
- **`push`** adds an element the caller guarantees is new, without a lookup and without inflating.

Keeping completed sets sorted, for binary-search lookups, was considered but offered no compelling advantage.

### Forward edges: a task's own edges

These are `children`, `output_dependencies`, `cell_dependencies`, `cell_dependencies_keyed` and `collectibles_dependencies`. Only the owning task adds them, while it executes.

- Inserting while the task executes inflates a large set, and the existing `shrink_on_completion` flattens it on completion. A re-executing task keeps its previous edges in the current set (the `outdated_*` sets are a copy) and inserts again on repeated reads.

Turbopack: list compact re-export namespace keys in code unit order
docs.body:
### What?

Turbopack's compact re-export registration (`TURBOPACK_ESM_REEXPORT`) now defines namespace keys in ECMAScript code unit order, also when the names are re-exported from several modules.

### Why?

The spec requires a module namespace object's `[[OwnPropertyKeys]]` to return its exports sorted in code unit order. The compact registration emits one group per source module in import order, and the runtime defines the properties in list order, so the keys were listed module by module. For example, `export { 'has,comma', b } from './first'` plus `export { c } from './second'` gave `['b', 'has,comma', 'c']` instead of `['b', 'c', 'has,comma']`.

This was tracked by the expected-failure test `reexport-registration/__skipped__/mixed-encoding-namespace-key-order`, added during review of #101229.

### How?

The keys are sorted at build time in `build_compact_reexports`. The runtime is unchanged.

- Each group's pairs are sorted by their emitted key. The comparison uses UTF-16 code units, which matches the spec. Rust's `str` order is UTF-8 byte order and differs for characters outside the BMP.
- If the keys are already sorted across groups (the common case), the registration is unchanged, including import subsumption.
- If the sorted keys interleave across sources, the registration is split into runs of consecutive same-source keys, so a source can appear more than once. The gr

docs.title: Turbopack: discover snapshot fixtures with custom entries
docs.body:
### What?

The Turbopack snapshot suite now finds fixtures by their `input` directory, not by a hard-coded `input/index.js`. This means `swc_transforms/mono_transforms`, whose `options.json` sets `"entry": "input/packages/app/index.js"`, now actually runs, and its committed output is checked again.

### Why?

`tests/snapshot.rs` only created tests for `tests/snapshot/*/*/input/index.js`. A fixture with a custom `entry` and no `input/index.js` was silently skipped. Its snapshot could go stale, and the transform and resolution behavior it covers could regress without any test failing. `mono_transforms` was the only remaining fixture in that state. Its old output used the outdated chunk naming.

### How?

- The fixture glob now matches `tests/snapshot/*/*/input`, still excluding `node_modules`. The test resolves the fixture root as that directory's parent.
- The entry is still read from `options.json` and defaults to `input/index.js`, so every fixture keeps its configured entry.
- The generated test names change (`…__input__index_js` → `…__input`). No fixture was dropped: the only new test is `mono_transforms`.
- Regenerated the `mono_transforms` output. Its JSX in `packages/component` is transformed, the third-party JSX under `input/node_modules` is left as is, and no issues are reported. No other fixture output changed.

docs.body:
## Summary

Fixes [#101491](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/101491).

While using `--experimental-build-mode compile` and setting `output` to `standalone`, custom status pages like `/500` were mistakenly considered static in `staticPages`.

That fix makes sure that status pages aren't considered as static during compile mode to include server chunk data in the standalone output.

docs.title: Turbopack: wait for /_app chunks before evaluating Pages Router entries
docs.body:
### What?

With Turbopack, Pages Router pages now wait for `/_app`'s chunks before evaluating their entries. Before, hydration could fail with `Module X was instantiated because it was required from module Y, but the module factory is not available.` when an `/_app` chunk executed after the page's chunks.

### Why?

A page's client chunk group treats `/_app`'s modules as already available, so those modules aren't duplicated into the page's chunks. However, the browser runtime only waits for an entry's own `otherChunks` before it instantiates the entry's runtime modules. The page's entries include modules that live only in `/_app`'s chunks (e.g. the Next.js client main module). The only thing that ordered `/_app` before the page was the document order of `defer` scripts.

Whenever that order doesn't hold, the page instantiates modules whose factories haven't registered yet:
- `async` scripts: `experimental.disableOptimizedLoading` in production
- deferred or injected scripts
- WebView quirks: reported on iOS WKWebView in #98099

This affects both bootstrap modes: per-route evaluate chunks (the default) and the inlined bootstrap of `turbopackSharedRuntime`.

### How?

- **Turbopack:** `ChunkingContext::evaluated_chunk_group` gets a `parent_assets` input. These are the assets of another evaluated chunk group that is always loaded alongside this one, and whose modules the availabil

docs.title: fix: include /500 traced files in standalone output in compile mode
docs.body:
Fixes #101491

### What?

With `next build --experimental-build-mode compile` and `output: 'standalone'`, a custom `pages/500.js` fails instead of showing the custom 500 page. Opening `/?fail=1` on the standalone server returns a plain `Internal Server Error` with a `ChunkLoadError` for the 500 page chunk.

### Why?

In compile mode the static check returns early, so `ssgPages` stays empty and no page is prerendered. But `usedStaticStatusPages` still adds `/500` to `staticPages`, as if it will be prerendered to HTML. `copyTracedFiles` then skips every page in `staticPages`, so the traced files for `/500` never reach `.next/standalone`. The chunk exists in `.next/server/chunks/ssr/` and is listed in `.next/server/pages/500.js.nft.json`, but it is missing from standalone.

### How?

In `packages/next/src/build/index.ts`, do not add used static status pages to `staticPages` when `isCompileMode` is true. In compile mode nothing is prerendered, so `/500` is rendered on demand and its traced files need to be copied. A separate `generate` build is unchanged, since it runs with compile mode off.

Added a regression test in `test/production/standalone-mode/compile-mode-500/`. It builds in compile mode, checks the traced `/500` chunks exist in standalone, starts the standalone server, and expects `/` to return 200 and `/?fail=1` to return 500 with "Custom 500 page".

docs.title: Turbopack: replace MinifyType with extensible EmitOption chunking options
docs.body:
### What?

Replaces `MinifyType` / `MangleType` and `ChunkingContext::minify_type()` with an extensible `EmitOption` system. Each crate can now attach its own emit configuration to a chunking context. This adds `EcmascriptEmitOptions` (full SWC minify options, indentation, merged-module comments) and `CssEmitOptions` (minification, chunk-item comments).

This continues #92807, rebased onto current `canary`, with that PR's open review comments addressed.

### Why?

The minification enums in `turbopack-core` tied the core chunking abstraction to a few fixed minification strategies. Passing richer SWC minifier configuration through them would have required `turbopack-core` to depend on SWC. With a trait-object option bag, `turbopack-core` stays dependency-free and each language crate owns its emit settings.

### How?

- **Core:** `EmitOption` is a marker value trait. Chunking contexts return an `EmitOptions` list, and consumers look up the concrete type they need (the last match wins). Every chunking context implements `emit_options()` explicitly, with no trait default, so a context can't silently drop its configuration. `UseCacheContentHashChunkingContext` keeps its compact AST emission.
- **Ecmascript / CSS:** each crate has builders with minification presets and a non-allocating `get_or_default` lookup. Code generation now receives the ecmascript emit options directly instead o

docs.title: fix: don't classify static ImageResponse routes as dynamic under --debug-prerender
docs.body:
Fixes #101501

### What?

Under `next build --debug-prerender`, a static `ImageResponse` metadata route
(no dynamic APIs, no `dynamic`/`revalidate` exports) is intermittently
classified as dynamic (`ƒ`) instead of static (`○`), and no `.body`/`.meta`
is written. Identical cold builds flip between the two. Plain `next build`
always reports `○`.

### Why?

In `packages/next/src/server/og/cache-image-response.ts` the element tree is
serialized with `prerenderToNodeStream`, guarded by
`createHangingInputAbortSignal`. In the final prerender that signal aborts
after exactly one tick (`scheduleOnNextTick`). `--debug-prerender` runs the
prerender with the development React build, and the serialization sometimes
needs more than one tick to flush. When the abort wins, the code treats the
tree as if it were waiting on dynamic input and returns a hanging promise, so
the route is classified dynamic. The one-tick wait is a timing heuristic, not
proof that the input is dynamic.

### How?

Bound the serialization by the prerender's own `renderSignal` instead of the
hanging-input abort signal. A tree waiting on genuinely dynamic input still
suspends on a hanging promise that only settles when the render signal aborts,
so it is still classified dynamic through the same path. Finite rendering work
is allowed as many turns as it needs. No other callers of
`createHangingInputAbortSignal` are touche

docs.body:
The prerender classification introduced in #96080 uses `blocking` for both required prerendering and request-time rendering with no initial response. Those cases need different cache-miss policies.

This change adds `compute: 'dynamic'` for empty PPR outputs that permit request-time rendering without a separate prerender first. The `blocking` value now requires generation or revalidation before serving a response when no usable cached prerender exists. The generated result can still need request-time rendering. This requirement also applies after an on-demand prerender expires or is evicted.

Outputs for paths not generated at build time use `empty/static` when `ensureStatic = 'navigation'` guarantees static server output. Their response is empty because no fallback is available, but generation must produce static server output or fail validation. Concrete built paths retain the classification of their own output.

This prepares #101309's full-route RSC classification and #101357's request handling for the proposed update to nextjs/adapter-vercel#114. That proposal maps `static` and `blocking` to `onMiss: 'sync'`, and `dynamic` and `resuming` to `onMiss: 'dynamic'`. Turbopack client reference manifests now store each distinct client chunk list and SSR chunk list **once per manifest**. Before, the same list was repeated inline for every client reference that used it.

docs.title: turbo-tasks: capture effects on multiple workers
docs.body:
## What?

`take_effects` now captures many effects on several workers instead of polling all captures on one thread.

The workers are spawned with a new crate-private `spawn_in_current_task` helper. The spawned futures share the current task's state like local tasks do, so their cell reads are tracked as dependencies of the task that calls `take_effects`, and the task execution waits for them before it completes. Workers take the next effect from a shared counter and the results keep the original effect order, so dedup, conflict detection and retry behaviour are unchanged.

Context: #100250 (making `next build` scale beyond 16 cores).

## Why?

In a warm build (persistent cache) every effect is captured again, and a capture reads the effect cell and the content it writes. That data is not in memory yet, so each read restores it from the persistent cache synchronously on the reading thread. All captures were polled by one `try_join` in one task, so all restores ran one by one on a single thread.

On `bench/large-app-router` (5000 routes, ~200k output files) with 32 CPUs, a warm build's emit step had a ~4s window with one busy thread: ~200k captures with ~167k individual task data/meta restores. With this change the window is ~0.9s.

docs.title: Turbopack: scale default disk write concurrency
docs.body:
### What?

On Linux, Turbopack's default disk write concurrency now scales with available parallelism instead of using a fixed limit of 4. The Linux default is `clamp(available_parallelism, 4, 16)`, using `turbo_tasks::parallel::available_parallelism()` so CPU affinity and `TURBO_TASKS_AVAILABLE_PARALLELISM` are respected.

**macOS, Windows and all other platforms stay at the current fixed default of 4**, pending measurements on those platforms. Their limits (e.g. open file limits on macOS, metadata contention on NTFS) differ from Linux. `TURBO_ENGINE_WRITE_CONCURRENCY` still overrides the default on every platform.

### Why?

On larger machines, writing many small build outputs was throttled by the fixed limit. This is part of the build scaling work in #100250.

### How?

- The scaling default is gated with `cfg(target_os = "linux")`. Other platforms compile to the fixed default of 4.
- On Linux, 4 is the minimum and the fallback when parallelism can't be determined.
- On Linux, the cap of 16 limits open file handles and blocked tokio workers. A limit of 32 or 64 did not make builds faster in the sweep below.
- EMFILE retry handling is unchanged.

docs.body:
### What?

Removes `turbo_bincode::indexmap` and `turbo_bincode::indexset`. Every value that stored an `IndexMap`/`IndexSet` through them now stores an `OrderedAutoMap`/`OrderedAutoSet`.

### Why?

Without these helpers, `IndexMap`/`IndexSet` fields no longer derive bincode, so they can't be stored in cells. Cells use `OrderedAutoMap`/`OrderedAutoSet` instead:

- they keep the insertion order;

docs.body:
Stacked on https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/101638, which moves the `turbopack` marker and `<distDir>/package.json` writes into Turbopack.

### What?

With Turbopack, `next build` no longer deletes the whole dist dir before it starts. While Turbopack writes the final output, it removes every file in the dist dir that this build does not write. After the writes finish, it removes directories that are left empty.

- The dist dir ends up exactly as a clean build leaves it: no stale files remain. Unchanged files are kept rather than deleted and rewritten.
- These entries are kept as before: `cache`, `dev`, `diagnostics`, `lock`, `trace`.
- Only `BUILD_ID` is deleted upfront, so a failed build never leaves a startable mix of old and new output.

- Webpack builds, `cleanDistDir: false`, and generate mode behave as before.

The upfront clean ran synchronously on the JavaScript main thread. In a warm build of a large app it took about 8–11 s, mostly `unlink` calls, even though most output files do not change between builds. Part of issue #100250 (scaling `next build` beyond 16 cores).

### What?

In `next dev`, the server-side React Flight clients (SSR, `"use cache"`, encryption, segment data, instant validation) no longer give React a source map URL for the "fake functions" React creates for Server Component stack frames. This only happens when **no Node.js inspector is attached** and the frame's script is a **plain absolute POSIX path**, i.e. a chunk loaded from disk. Every other case keeps the existing behavior.

The change is in `findSourceMapURLDEV` (`packages/next/src/server/lib/source-maps.ts`).

### Why?

Part of #100250 (making Turbopack `next dev` / `next build` faster and scale beyond 16 cores).

For every Server Component stack frame it replays, React's dev Flight client `eval`s a fake function, padded with as many newlines as the frame's line in the chunk. With many frames this is a large amount of single-threaded work and memory on the SSR side.

docs.title: test: close lingering prerender-export server connections
docs.body:
### What?

Makes static-server teardown deterministic in `test/production/prerender-export/prerender-export.test.ts`.

### Why?

In a recent canary run, all three attempts of this suite passed both tests, then failed in its own `afterAll` with `Exceeded timeout of 120000 ms for a hook`.

The hook was waiting for `http.Server#close()`. That callback only fires after every client connection has ended, so a lingering browser or keep-alive/in-flight fetch connection can keep teardown open until Jest's hook timeout. The CI log doesn't show which client held the socket, so the fix doesn't depend on client socket state.

### How?

- Call `server.close()` first, so the static server stops accepting new connections.
- Then call `server.closeAllConnections()` and await the close callback.
- Import `Server` from `http`, which matches `startStaticServer()` and exposes `closeAllConnections()`.

There are no skips, retry-count changes, timeout increases or sleeps.

### What?

Fixes the flaky `should handle slashes in router push correctly` test in `test/e2e/repeated-slashes`, which regularly needed in-job retries in `test prod` jobs on canary.

### Why?

Several of the `router.push()` cases in this test target a missing page, which causes a hard navigation. docs.title: Turbopack: release freed memory right after project shutdown
docs.body:
## What?

After `project.shutdown()` resolves in a Turbopack `next build`, return the memory that was freed by dropping the turbo-tasks storage to the OS right away. Until now it stayed resident for another 6–10s.

Part of #100250.

## Why?

`TurboTasksBackend::stop` already drops the task storage (`storage.drop_contents()`). Even so, on a large generated App Router app (5000 routes, 32 CPUs) the main process stayed at **~12.5–13 GB RSS** once shutdown resolved. It only fell to ~1 GB in steps over the next 6–10s, while the static generation workers were already loading their page bundles. That overlap directly raises the peak memory of the build's process tree.

Root cause, found with RSS timelines, mimalloc commit stats and thread counts:

- mimalloc keeps each page in the heap of the thread that allocated it. A free from another thread only queues the block on that page, and the owning thread has to collect its heap before the page becomes free.
- Tokio scheduler workers collect on every park (`on_thread_park` → `TurboMalloc::thread_park`). **Blocking-pool threads have no such hook.**
- Many blocking-pool threads used to be scheduler workers that did compilation and persistence work. They handed their worker role to a new thread in `block_in_place` (used by `scope_bounded`) and own a large share of the heap. During shutdown the process grows from 44 to 75 threads.

Webpack dev no longer clears dev-overlay errors on a hot update that changes no modules.

## Summary

In `next dev`, the first request waits until the JS-side route discovery in `startWatcher` (`setup-dev-bundler.ts`) has run. Today that means waiting for **Watchpack's initial scan of the whole project** and then a full `aggregated` route pass, even though a `recursiveReadDir` snapshot of `app/` and `pages/` is already taken at startup. docs.body:
With content hashing, a source map's filename was hashed from the map's own content, so `<hash-a>.js` referenced `<hash-b>.js.map`. Tools that pair maps with their files by name (e.g. datadog-ci sourcemaps upload) could not match them.

docs.body:
> [!NOTE]
> Built on #101617 (merged). Alternative approach: #101506.

## What?

Turbopack now computes `.next/diagnostics/route-bundle-stats.json` itself and emits it as a normal production output asset. This removes the JS `writeRouteBundleStats` step.

- **Endpoint data:** In production, page endpoints expose their first-load JS inputs through `EndpointOutput::first_load_js`. These point to data the endpoint already computes:
  - **App Router:** client references, client reference chunks and shared client chunks. Entry chunks use the same CSS and component-chunk filtering as `entryJSFiles`, followed by the shared root chunks.
  - **Pages Router:** the page's client chunk group, plus the `/_app` chunks.
- **Per-route stats:** `route_bundle_stat` is one turbo-tasks function per route. It reads the first-load JS from all of the route's endpoints, then:
  - dedupes chunks by path in endpoint order;
  - sums their `Asset::size()` values.
- **Endpoint lists:**
  - Pages pages list their HTML endpoint followed by `/_app`.
  - Pages API routes list only `/_app`.
  - App routes list all of their HTML endpoints.
- **Chunk size:** the new default `Asset::size()` returns `Vc<Option<u64>>`, reusing `AssetContent::len()`. Missing files and redirects have no size, so they aren't counted.
- **Emission:** the asset is included in `output_assets_operation` for the full build or deferred phase

docs.title: fix: emit meta refresh for redirect when streamed render has no Suspense boundary
docs.body:
Fixes #101499

### What?

When `redirect()` throws during a streamed render and the page has no `<Suspense>` of its own, the response no longer goes out as a bare `200` with the redirect only in the RSC payload. The error document rendered by `renderToStream`'s recovery path now carries the redirect in its captured errors, so `makeGetServerInsertedHTML` emits the `<meta http-equiv="refresh">` tag, matching the behavior when the redirect happens inside `<Suspense>`.

### Why?

A redirect inside `<Suspense>` is a recoverable boundary error: Fizz reports it through the HTML `onError` handler, it lands in `allCapturedErrors`, and the meta refresh tag is emitted. Without a boundary, the same redirect thrown during a postponed/resumed render is a fatal shell error (`onShellError`), so it never reaches `onError` and nothing is captured. The recovery path then tries a real 307 with a `Location` header, but the prerendered shell already went out, so the header set is dropped and the status assignment has no effect. The recovery also rendered the error document with a fresh empty `serverCapturedErrors` array, so no meta tag was emitted either. Non-JS clients (curl, link checkers, crawlers) stayed on an empty `200` page. The meta tag is the only redirect mechanism left in that case, and it is the one the `redirect` docs promise for streaming contexts.

docs.title: turbo-tasks-backend: read collectibles and update the reader dependency atomically
docs.body:
### What?

Keep a task that reads collectibles from keeping stale collectibles when they change while it reads them. After `read_strongly_consistent()`, the reader now always reports the current collectibles.

Adds `collectibles_read_race`: 128 readers re-execute in each of 100 rounds and peek the collectibles of a shared root operation, which changes its collectibles in the same round. The readers don't wait for that operation, so the change races with their reads.

### Why?

`read_task_collectibles` read the source's collectibles and made the reader's collectibles dependency current under separate locks. A collectibles change in between still saw the dependency as outdated (not read yet), so `InvalidateDueToCollectiblesChange` made the reader dirty but not stale. The reader's execution then completed with the collectibles it read before the change, and its dirty flag was cleared.

### How?

`read_task_collectibles` locks the source and the reader together with `task_pair`, like output and cell reads already do. A task reading its own collectibles uses the single guard.

### Verification

On `canary` `bbd36623`, with 40 busy loops on a 32-vCPU machine. "Dirty handoff" is the follow-up fix stacked on this PR.

docs.title: [no-js-crawlers] Disable streaming SSR for crawlers not supporting JS
docs.body:
AI crawlers and agents fetch raw HTML without executing JavaScript, so Suspense boundaries that Fizz outlines into hidden divs (revealed later by client JS) are never perceived by them: the content sits in `<div hidden id="S:...">` waiting for the Fizz runtime to reveal it.

When `experimental.disableProgressiveLoadingForNonJsBots` is enabled and the request user agent matches the `experimental.nonJsBots` regex (has a [default with known AI crawlers](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/sebbie/non-js-bots-progressive-loading/packages/next/src/shared/lib/router/utils/non-js-bots.ts)):

- the request bypasses prerendered content (PPR shells, static prerenders, ISR fallbacks) and renders dynamically, since prerendered artifacts have progressive chunking baked in
- the render waits for all Suspense boundaries to resolve 
- `progressiveChunkSize: Infinity` is passed to React so every completed boundary is inlined at its position instead of outlined into hidden content

The flag is on in the Cache Components shard with the goal of removing `experimental.disableProgressiveLoadingForNonJsBots` and stabilizing `experimental.nonJsBots`.

non-JS bots are different than HTML limited bots. non-JS bots don't support any JS while HTML limited bots only understand `meta` tags in `head`.

The docs say this header ["cannot be overridden"](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/headers#cache-control) and that you can't set Cache-Control for these assets in `next.config.js`.
