docs.title: Apply config redirects to Pages client navigation with a matching Proxy
docs.body:
### What?

When a `next.config.js` redirect matches a Pages `_next/data` request and Proxy's matcher matches the path, `next start` and `next dev` now answer with the redirect status and `x-nextjs-redirect: <destination>`, without `Location`. The Pages client router then performs the redirect: it renders the destination and updates the address bar.

### Why?

The [redirects docs](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/docs/01-app/03-api-reference/05-config/01-next-config-js/redirects.mdx?plain=1#L41) say config redirects apply to client-side routing (`Link`, `router.push`) when Proxy is present and matches the path. Today the data request gets a plain 307 with `Location`. The browser's `fetch` follows it silently, so the client router never sees a redirect. In `next start` it renders the destination under the source URL. In dev it renders the source page.

Proxy's own redirects of data requests already use `x-nextjs-redirect` instead of `Location` (`packages/next/src/server/web/adapter.ts`), and the client router acts on that header (`getMiddlewareData` in `packages/next/src/shared/lib/router/router.ts`). Config redirects never did.

The routing gate test that caught it: [`docs-router-contract` › "applies Pages config redirects on client navigation only with a matching Proxy"](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/test/e2e/routing-server/router/docs-router-contra

With Turbopack, `next build` spawns the static workers (page-data collection and prerendering) from a small **fork server**: a helper process started before the in-process compile. The main process no longer forks them itself.

Turbopack compiles inside the `next build` process, so the main process holds a very large heap (~13 GB on a large app) by the time the static workers are created.

docs.title: Turbopack: return freed memory eagerly while shutting down the project
docs.body:
Based on canary: #101529 has been merged (ba894dd), and this PR is rebased onto it. #101623 is stacked on this PR: on mimalloc v3.6.1 it is needed for the post-shutdown release to reach ~1 GB again.

## What?

While `project.shutdown()` persists and drops the turbo-tasks storage, mimalloc now returns freed memory to the OS immediately instead of after its purge delay. The main process's RSS therefore falls progressively during persistence instead of staying at ~13 GB until the end.

## Why?

- On a large app, `next build` spends 20–30 s in `project.shutdown()`, mostly persisting the filesystem cache.
- Page-data collection (static workers) runs concurrently and loads its bundles meanwhile.
- The storage is freed during that time, mostly by threads other than the ones that allocated it. Those pages only leave RSS after mimalloc's delayed purge, so the main process held its full heap for most of the shutdown span. That overlap is often where the build's peak process-tree RSS comes from.
- Making mimalloc purge eagerly for the whole build costs much more system CPU (an earlier experiment measured +122 s), so this only applies during shutdown.

Part of #100250. A worker fork-server PR (#101586) will be benchmarked on top of this one.

docs.body:
### What?

In a production build, `whole_app_module_graphs` now waits for the module graph before it calls `scale_down_node_pool`. `whole_app_module_graphs_without_dropping_issues` does the same.

### Why?

`module_graphs_op.connect()` returns before the graph is computed, so the scale down ran before any Node.js process existed. The webpack loader and PostCSS processes then stayed alive until `next build` ended. Development already resolves the graph first.

On a docs site with 46 MDX pages (canary.47, 10 cores), 12 loader processes and about 20 child processes stayed alive through static generation. With this change they exit when the graph is done. On 16.4.2 these processes held about 2 GB, and the build was killed in a 3 GB container.

### How?

Await the connected `Vc` before the scale down. The new test uses a loader that writes its process id into a module, and the page checks during prerender whether that process is still alive. It fails on canary.47 and passes with this change.

docs.title: fix: app pages directory validation adjustment
docs.body:
### What?

Fix directory detection so that Next.js only recognises `app` and `pages` paths when they are actual directories, rather than accepting any existing filesystem entry.

Also added regression tests covering root-directory precedence, files with reserved directory names, fallback to `src/`, and directory symlinks.

### Why?

The currently existing `findDir()` implementation uses `fs.existsSync()`, which also returns `true` for regular files.

For example, if a project contains a file named `app` at its root and a valid `src/app/` directory, Next.js can incorrectly select the file instead of the directory.

### How?

Use `fs.statSync(..., { throwIfNoEntry: false })?.isDirectory()` to validate each candidate path.

This preserves the existing search order while ignoring regular files and continuing to recognise symlinks that resolve to directories.

**Testing**
- Added focused regression tests for the affected cases.
- Full Jest and TypeScript checks have not yet been run.
- CI results are pending review.

docs.title: turbo-tasks: avoid redundant aggregation roots and root-upper optimization cascades
docs.body:
## Summary

Two fixes in `turbo-tasks-backend` for cases where reading **already computed** tasks from a new root, or from a parentless `turbo_tasks::run` closure, restructures large parts of the aggregation graph. Context: #100250. The motivating pattern is a new root operation reading the existing endpoint outputs after the emit, like the route bundle stats in #101540.

### A: count all root uppers as one upper in `optimize_task`

`optimize_task` raises a task's aggregation number when `(uppers - 1) * followers` is too large. A root aggregates its whole subgraph, and raising the number never removes an upper edge to a root, yet root uppers were still counted.

So every additional root over an existing subgraph made large parts of it look like they needed optimization. The resulting raises cascaded into a rebalance of the subgraph without reducing upper edges. The old code already counted a `root_uppers` variable but never used it, and it also counted root *followers*.

The fix:
- Count only root **uppers**, persistent or transient.
- Treat them as a single upper when evaluating the threshold and seeding the search.

Behavior with at most one root upper is unchanged.

### B: parentless calls no longer make persistent callees aggregation roots

docs.title: turbo-tasks: don't make parentless transient tasks aggregation roots
docs.body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #101604, from [this review comment](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/101604#discussion_r4548045743).

#101604 stopped making parentless persistent callees, such as tasks called from a `turbo_tasks::run` closure, aggregation roots. This PR does the same for parentless **transient** callees.

The same argument applies to transient tasks:
- A parentless connect has no upper, so there is nothing to shield.
- Tasks that need to be roots already are:
  - Strongly consistent reads and collectibles reads are only allowed on `root` functions. The check is based on the task's function and applies to transient function tasks as well.
  - `root` functions are made roots when they are created, whether persistent or transient.
  - Top-level transient tasks (root and once tasks) are created with the maximum aggregation number.

Now `connect_child` only makes a task a root when a transient parent calls a persistent child. That rule shields the persistent graph from the transient caller and is unchanged.

The "already constructed root" shortcut is removed. It only applied to the parentless transient case, so it is dead code now.

## Verification

- `connect_child` unit test: a parentless transient child is not made a root. This test is flipped from the previous behavior.

docs.title: turbo-persistence: report batch_get misses from batch_lookup_entry
docs.body:
Follow-up to #100678, from a review comment there.

## What?

`batch_get` now reports missing keys while it walks the SST files of a shard, instead of doing a separate pass over the keys afterwards.

- `MetaFile::batch_lookup_entry` takes an `is_last` flag and an `on_miss` callback, next to `on_found`.
- On the last (oldest) SST file of the shard, it walks every key that is still unresolved and reports the misses through `on_miss`:
  - keys outside the file's hash range, without a lookup;
  - keys inside the range that miss the quick filter or the SST lookup.
- On every other file nothing changes: only the keys in its hash range are visited, and nothing is reported as missing, since an older file may still hold the key.
- `batch_get_chunk` passes `is_last` from the file's position in the shard. Its `on_miss` reports `None` for the key and counts `not_found`. A shard without any SST files reports all its keys as missing.

## Why?

The pass after the SST loop walked all keys of the chunk once more to find the unresolved ones. The last file already walks the keys, so it can report the misses itself.

## How?

- The lookup stops early once all keys of a chunk are found, as before; there is nothing left to report then.
- The `batch_get` contract is unchanged: every index is reported exactly once (found, `None` for a tombstone or a missing key), and callback errors are returned.

When dependency installation fails, `create-next-app` prints `Aborting installation. <pm> install has failed.` but exits with code **0**. Scripts and CI calling `create-next-app` therefore see a false success.

## Summary

Avoid app-wide export code generation when an unrelated `UnusedReferences` entry changes. Part 1 of a two-PR stack for #100250; the upper PR (#101627) stabilizes chunk-group numbering. Both fixes are independent of client-reference-manifest serialization (#101513, closed unmerged, and the items-64/65 stack).

`UnusedReferences` is already a keyed cell. `EsmExports::code_generation`, `build_compact_reexports`, and `PatternMapping::resolve_request` previously awaited the whole map before looking up a reference. One new import can consequently invalidate export code generation throughout the app. In an exploratory 1,000-route reproduction, the baseline lib-import build recomputed `EcmascriptModuleContent::new` 5,660 times and `precompute code generation` 9,881 times.

### What?

Turbopack now writes the two dist dir files that do not belong to any entrypoint itself, when the project is created:

- `turbopack`: an empty marker file that says the output was produced by Turbopack.
- `package.json`: `{"type": "commonjs"}`, so files in the dist dir use CommonJS handling even when the app's own `package.json` has `"type": "module"`.

docs.title: fix(app-page): keep a proxy rewrite status when the prerender status is 200
docs.body:
### What?

Keeps the status a proxy rewrite sets (for example `NextResponse.rewrite(url, { status: 410 })`) when the rewrite target is a prerendered page and `cacheComponents` is enabled.

### Why?

With `cacheComponents`, a prerendered page always stores a status of 200. Delivery in `app-page-runtime.ts` applies the selected entry's status unconditionally, so that 200 replaces the status the proxy already set on the response. In `next start`, a rewrite to a static page with `{ status: 410 }` or `{ status: 503 }` returns 200, while the rewrite's headers (`retry-after`) still arrive. Without `cacheComponents` the same app returns 410 and 503.

### How?

The entry status is applied only when it is not the plain 200 default, since 200 is what the response already has. Entries with a real status (404, 500, redirects) are applied as before, so a rewrite to a page that stores a 404 still returns 404.

A new production test (`proxy-rewrite-status`) rewrites to a prerendered page with a 410, with a 503 plus `retry-after`, and with an RSC request, checks a direct request still returns 200, and checks a rewrite to a `notFound()` page still returns 404. The 410 and 503 cases fail on canary without the change (200 instead) and all cases pass with it. The existing `prerender-output` suite still passes. `partialPrefetching` is set to `false` in the test so the non-PPR path is the one under t

docs.title: Read component stacks of aborted prerender tasks only when needed (-5.3% prerender CPU)
docs.body:
Replaces #101401, moved from the cramforce fork so the PRs on top of it can be stacked; the code is unchanged.

## Summary

Prerendering a page with `cacheComponents: true` gets cheaper when the page has dynamic holes: on a 2,000-page site where 60% of the pages are partially prerendered, static generation uses 5.3% less CPU and 7.8% less wall time. The generated output is the same, and failing builds print the same errors with the same component stacks.

Why it was slow: when the final HTML prerender of a page is aborted, React reports every task that is still pending, one per dynamic hole, through `onError`. The `onError` in `prerenderToStream` read `errorInfo.componentStack` for each of them to validate the static shell. React builds that string on first read by calling every function component on the stack again and formatting two stack traces per component, and its production build does not cache the result. In a profile of the benchmark this was 16% of the JavaScript CPU time of static generation.

The stacks are matched against five patterns whose results are only read by `throwIfDisallowedDynamic`, and what that reads depends on the prelude:

- Full prelude (the normal case): only "dynamic metadata while nothing else is dynamic". The first report with a Suspense boundary above it settles that.
- Empty prelude that is allowed (fallback shells, `instant = false`): nothing

docs.body:
Replaces #101413, moved from the cramforce fork so the PRs on top of it can be stacked; the code is unchanged.

## Summary

Behaviour change: on `next start` and `next dev`, a route handler response whose body is under 1024 bytes and already in memory is now sent with a `Content-Length` and is no longer gzipped. | request | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `Accept-Encoding: gzip` | `Content-Encoding: gzip`, `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, 39 body bytes | `Content-Length: 19`, 19 body bytes |
| no `Accept-Encoding` | `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, 19 body bytes

docs.body:
Replaces #101406, moved from the cramforce fork so the PRs on top of it can be stacked; the code is unchanged.

## Summary

`next build` finishes static generation sooner when routes differ in cost: on a 4,000-page static site with 4 workers, static generation takes 7.1% less wall time. Which worker renders which page still depends only on the export paths and the number of workers, as on `canary`: the batches are dealt out to the workers in turn, and nothing is decided by which worker happens to be free. That matters for a page whose Flight row order depends on what its worker rendered before (for example a second request that resolves without I/O because another page of that worker already put the response into the data cache). docs.title: [internal-skills] fetch CI status on demand instead of blocking on --wait
docs.body:
The `$pr-status-triage` skill prescribed `node scripts/pr-status.js [PR] --wait` as the default first step for CI triage, which blocks on `gh run watch` until the entire workflow completes before any triage begins. In practice this left the agent idle waiting for full workflow completion instead of triaging failures as they landed.

This updates the skill to fetch current status on demand (no `--wait`) and start triaging immediately from the jobs that have already finished, re-fetching as more results land. `--wait` is now reserved for cases where the final run state itself is needed: confirming an all-green run before handing back, or picking up results after retriggering jobs. The flaky-rerun loop uses a `--wait` re-analysis instead of a flat 5-minute sleep, and a new step makes push timing explicit: push once every result relevant to the fix is in, without waiting for the whole workflow to complete.

docs.title: Store "use cache" durability once per entry in server reference manifest
docs.body: With `durableUseCacheEntries: true`, the `durability` metadata of a `"use cache"` function was duplicated in every `workers[page]` entry of `server-reference-manifest.json`. It's now stored as a deduplicated list on the action entry, and each worker only references it by index. This makes the manifest quadratically smaller (it no longer scales with cache functions × pages). The values are usually identical across workers, but not always (e.g. an asset URL resolves differently in an App Page and a route handler), hence the list instead of a single value.

docs.body:
Adds a failing e2e test that reproduces #100431. This PR only adds the test. It's expected to fail until the bug is fixed.

### What?

New suite: `test/e2e/app-dir/optimistic-routing-redirected-prefetch-loop`. It runs in production mode only, because Known Routes prediction isn't used in dev.

The fixture copies the issue's reproduction:

- The home page has five `<Link>`s that share one `[...slug]` route: `/docs/one`, `/docs/two`, `/docs/three`, `/old/a`, `/old/b`.

The test stands in for the CDN with Playwright `page.route`. Requests for `/old/a` or `/old/b` that carry the `next-router-segment-prefetch` header get `307 Location: <target>`. This matches the issue's `scripts/proxy-307.mjs`. Everything else goes to the serve

docs.title: Fix `ImageResponse` prerendering with `--debug-prerender`
docs.body:
With Cache Components, `ImageResponse` uses serialized Flight output as the key for image bytes cached during the prospective prerender. Flight debug info can differ between the prospective and final passes, causing cache misses that can make static image routes dynamic under `--debug-prerender`.

The route-handler scheduling changes in #101593 let streaming Flight's immediate work finish within the prerender budget. The React fix react/react#38233 included in #101673 supports lazy decoding after EOF with the debug channel discarded. The image serializer can now use `renderToPipeableStream` and discard debug info through a separate channel, following the pattern in `encryptActionBoundArgs`.

The debug channel still leaves I/O debug chunk references in the main stream. However, React omits this info for work completed before the render's `startTime`. The warm final pass therefore drops records emitted in the prospective pass. A future `startTime` makes both passes omit those records and references.

The abort-signal change proposed in #101509 does not address the key mismatch. In the original reproduction, serialization completes in both passes, but the final cache lookup fails because the emitted debug info differs.

The metadata-image suite now runs with and without `--debug-prerender` and covers deferred trees, image variants, and request-dependent images.

Closes #101509

docs.title: Keep the registry lookup from slowing first dev compiles
docs.body:
### Why?

Since #95062, the dev version check runs `<pm> config get registry` when the first browser connects. Through corepack that is ~600 ms of CPU, competing with the compile of the first route the user navigates to. The dev soft nav benchmark regressed +32% in 16.5.0-canary.37. #100628 stopped `sync` from waiting on the check, but the CPU contention is still there.

### How?

Read `npm_config_registry` first, which package managers export to the scripts they run (`pnpm dev`, and `npm run dev` with a non-default registry). Otherwise run the subprocess at `PRIORITY_LOW` so it only uses idle CPU, which also covers running `next dev` directly. The resolved registry is unchanged for every `getRegistry()` caller.

Validation: added unit tests for the env shortcut and the priority; 2 of 4 fail without the change. In a local replica of the dev soft nav benchmark (10 interleaved cold runs each), canary.36 was 1205 ms, canary.48 was 1760 ms (+46%), and canary.48 with this change was 1176 ms (−2% vs canary.36).

docs.title: [static-gen] Add opt-in static generation profiling and a scheduler benchmark
docs.body:
Adds opt-in profiling for the static generation step of `next build`. It's the instrumentation for an adaptive static generation scheduler (stacked PRs follow). It doesn't change scheduling or rendering.

**Why**

Static generation splits pages into one equal slice per worker, renders each slice in fixed groups of `staticGenerationMaxConcurrency` (default 8), and never rebalances. To judge changes to that, we need per-worker numbers that `next build` doesn't report today: how long each worker sat idle, how far apart the workers finished (the tail), and how much memory they used.

**Approach**

With `NEXT_STATIC_GENERATION_PROFILE=1`:

- Each export worker records one entry per page: worker id, phase (`initial`, or `final` for Cache Components fallback shells), start and end time, pages in flight when it started, and whether it succeeded.
- Each worker samples `performance.eventLoopUtilization()`, RSS (`process.memoryUsage.rss()`), and heap in use (`v8.getHeapStatistics()`) every 100ms. It also records heap after each major GC and counts fetch cache hits and misses on its `IncrementalCache`. It takes one more sample when each export call ends, so a short call isn't reported as idle with zero memory.
- Records go to `.next/diagnostics/static-generation/worker-*.jsonl`. When static generation finishes, the parent writes `.next/diagnostics/static-generation-summary.json` and logs o

docs.title: [static-gen] Render static pages in a rolling window behind experimental.staticGenerationAdaptive
docs.body:
Adds `experimental.staticGenerationAdaptive` and, behind it, renders each worker's pages in a rolling window: the next page starts as soon as any page finishes, instead of rendering fixed groups of `staticGenerationMaxConcurrency` with `Promise.all`.

Stacked on #101688.

**Why**

`exportPages` renders `exportPaths.slice(i, i + maxConcurrency)` with `Promise.all`, then the next slice. Every group waits for its slowest page, so one slow page idles the other slots.

**Approach**

A small `mapWithConcurrency(items, limit, fn)` helper keeps up to `limit` calls running and starts the next item when any call settles. It returns results in input order, because `buildRDCCacheByPage` in `export/index.ts` picks the first matching resume-data-cache seed in result order. docs.title: [static-gen] Dispatch static pages from a shared queue with a worker-scoped incremental cache
docs.body:
With `experimental.staticGenerationAdaptive`, static generation now cuts pages into small chunks and lets idle workers pull the next chunk, instead of giving each worker one fixed slice. Each worker keeps its incremental cache across chunks.

Stacked on #101689.

**Why**

Today each worker gets one contiguous slice of `exportPaths`. When expensive pages sit next to each other, one worker gets all of them and becomes the long tail while the others go idle. On the vercel-front site app (next-benchmarks), one worker finishes about 92 s before the other in a ~190 s static generation step, and the idle worker sits at about 50% of the window.

**Approach**

- `export/index.ts`: when the flag is on, split the pages into chunks and run them through `mapWithConcurrency(chunks, numWorkers, …)`. At most `numWorkers` chunk calls are in flight, so `staticGenerationMinPagesPerWorker` still caps how many workers are used. jest-worker sends each call to an idle worker (calls without a worker key go into its shared FIFO queue, and a worker only takes a call when it has none running), so whichever worker finishes first gets the next chunk. Results are concatenated in chunk order, which keeps them in `exportPaths` order.
- Chunk size: `experimental.staticGenerationChunkSize`, or by default about four chunks per worker, clamped to between 1× and 3× `staticGenerationMaxConcurrency`. jest-worker run

docs.title: Optimistic routing rewrite prefetch loop
docs.body:
Adds a failing test for an infinite prefetch loop in optimistic routing.

When a link's route is predicted from a known pattern, the client skips the route tree request and fetches the link's segments directly. If the server rewrites (or redirects) the URL to a different param value of the same dynamic route, the per-segment response is written under the rendered pathname rather than the requested one. The predicted entry is never fulfilled, so the scheduler requests it again, indefinitely.

docs.body:
With `experimental.staticGenerationAdaptive`, each static generation worker now picks its own concurrency from its event loop idle time and memory headroom, and refuses pages when it's saturated. The parent sends work optimistically from live metrics, enforces a machine-wide memory budget, recycles workers whose memory baseline creeps up, and retries pages from a crashed worker instead of failing the build.

Stacked on #101690.

**Why**

After dynamic dispatch (#101690), the concurrency window is still fixed at `staticGenerationMaxConcurrency` (8). Pages that wait on I/O leave the CPU idle, and raising the knob by hand risks running out of memory. jest-worker also runs one call per worker at a time, so with #101690 each chunk drains to zero before the next one arrives.

- Each worker keeps a session for the whole `exportApp` run: shared setup, one incremental cache per phase (same scoping as #101690), and a local queue. A step call submits pages and resolves as soon as the worker could take more pages, while earlier pages keep rendering. So the worker never drains between chunks, even with one jest-worker call at a time.

With `output: 'standalone'`, `next build` copies `.env` and `.env.production` into `.next/standalone`, so `server.js` can load them at runtime. Adding `./.env` / `./.env.*` to `outputFileTracingExcludes` under `'/*'` does not remove them, and the docs did not explain why.

docs.title: turbo-tasks-backend: fix transient root test race
docs.body:
## Summary

Fixes a race in `parentless_calls_of_transient_tasks_are_only_roots_if_root_functions` (added in #101614).

The test created the transient `root` operation and made a parentless call to `transient_endpoint` in the same `tt.run` closure, then asserted that the endpoint had exactly one transient ref. The operation has no output yet, so it is scheduled right away, and `tt.run` doesn't wait for it to finish. When it runs, it calls the same `transient_endpoint` task (`TransientValue` arguments compare by value). `connect_children` then adds a second transient ref for that transient parent edge. Whenever the operation finished before the assertion ran, the test saw `left: 2, right: 1`.

The backend behavior is correct, since both refs are legitimate. The fix only reorders the test: it makes and checks the parentless endpoint call in its own `tt.run` before the operation exists, then creates the operation and checks that it is a root. All the original assertions are kept.

## Verification

- Original test under CPU load on 8 cores: 98/300 and 91/300 runs failed at `437:5` with `left: 2`, matching the canary CI failure.
- Fixed test: 0/300 failures idle and 0/1000 under the same CPU load.

docs.title: Keep the layout router context stable in hidden Activity routes
docs.body:
### What?

With Cache Components, components that call `useRouter()`, `useSelectedLayoutSegment()` or `useSelectedLayoutSegments()` inside a hidden `<Activity>` route no longer re-render when the active route changes.

Stacked on #101299, which does the same for `useParams()`, `usePathname()` and `useSearchParams()`.

### Why?

These hooks read `LayoutRouterContext`. `InnerLayoutRouter` created a new value object for it on every render, and the layout router renders the segments of hidden routes on every navigation. So every component reading the context in a hidden route re-rendered on every navigation, although the values the hooks use (the segment's tree and `bfcacheId`) don't change while a route is hidden.

### How?

- `InnerLayoutRouter` and `LoadingBoundaryProvider` memoize the context value, so it only changes when one of its fields does.
- The fields no longer change for a hidden segment:
  - The segment path and the params are memoized by value. The root params are a constant.
  - `url` was the active URL everywhere. An inactive bfcache entry now keeps the URL it was hidden with, stored in its `navigationState`.
- Whether a route is shown (`isActive`) moves out of `LayoutRouterContext` into a new `IsRouteActiveContext`, so hiding or showing a route doesn't change the layout router context either. Like the other per-entry providers, it is only rendered in the browser.

## Summary

Stacked on [#101703](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/101703), the adopted [#101628](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/101628), which lets a Proxy rewrite's status win over the status stored with a prerendered page.

Its two cases rewrite to a page stored with 200, which only fails on canary when Cache Components is on. These cases pin down the precedence with Cache Components off and on:

- A rewrite with `{ status: 410 }` to a page that calls `notFound()` (stored 404) returns 410. Canary returns 404.

- A direct request to the rewrite target still returns 200, so the rewritten requests leave the stored entry alone.

This is the precedence Vercel uses: the CDN applies a non-200 Proxy status over the status of the response it serves. The new cases pass in deploy mode.

docs.title: Keep a proxy rewrite status on RSC responses for stored redirects
docs.body:
## Summary

Stacked on [#101703](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/101703), the adopted [#101628](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/101628) plus test cases for stored 404 and redirect statuses.

When Proxy rewrites with a status to a page that redirected at build time, `next start` answered the router's RSC request with 200. For RSC requests to a stored redirect, the runtime sets the status to 200 because the payload carries the redirect, and that also replaced the status Proxy had set. The client then followed the redirect without seeing the Proxy status.

The 200 now only replaces the redirect status that the runtime applied from the stored entry. With a Proxy status, the RSC response keeps it, the router falls back to a document load, and the page still redirects. Without one, the response is still 200 and the client redirects without a document load.

This matches Vercel, where the CDN applies a non-200 Proxy status to RSC responses too.

## Verification

- New tests click a `<Link prefetch={false}>` and record the status of the router's RSC request:
  - Through a rewrite with `{ status: 410 }`: 410, and the browser still ends on the redirect target. Without this change it gets 200 in `next start`, with Cache Components off and on.
  - Without a rewrite: 200, as before.

`node scripts/pr-status.js` decided a run was clean by counting failed jobs and never looked at the run's conclusion. A finished run can have no failed jobs without passing: it can be waiting for a maintainer to approve a fork PR's workflows (`action_required`), cancelled before any job failed, unable to start because of a broken workflow file (`startup_failure`), skipped, or stale. docs.title: Next.js development high memory usage
docs.body:
**Before posting a comment on this issue please read this entire post.**

## Previous work

The past few weeks we've been investigating / optimizing various memory usage issues. Specifically geared towards production memory usage. In investigating these we were able to find there was one memory leak in Node.js itself when using `fetch()` in Node.js versions before `18.17.0` (you'll want to use `18.17.1` for security patches though). 

Most of the reports related to memory usage turned out to be reports of "it's higher than the previous version" rather than a memory leak. This was expected because in order to run App Router and Pages Router at the same time with different React versions two separate processes were needed. This has been resolved by reducing the amount of processes to two, one for Routing and App Router rendering, and one for Pages Router rendering. So far we haven't received new reports since the latest release.

In some issues there were reports related to Image Optimization in production, however no reproduction was provided so it could not be investigated adequately, if you have a reproduction for that please refer to this issue: #54482

docs.title: Loading state during navigation (not prefetching)
docs.body:
Would love a way to show instant feedback to the user when they navigate between routes that doesn't involve prefetching.

I don't think the point about 100KB loading states is a valid concern. Loading states are often just a spinner. If anything, the default approach should optimize for basic loading states and let people configure something special if they have a special 100KB loading state.

Let me know your thoughts, definitely want to understand how the Next team is thinking about this.

> I want to clarify how loading UI works in Next.js.
> 
> Routing in the App Router is "server centric". We need a network roundtrip to the server when doing route transitions. The client doesn't know what loading state to render, until it communicates with the server.
> 
> When we prefetch, we can retrieve both the route to navigate to _and_ the loading UI. Prefetching is what makes navigations feel snappy. If you prefetch the loading UI which does not have data fetching, then you can "instantly" show this loading state, followed by the dynamic content on the page being streamed in after. This is enabled through React Suspense and streaming server-rendering as part of the App Router.
>

docs.title: Loading with parallel routes only works on root
docs.body:
https://github.com/bananashell/nextjs-parallel-route-loading-issue 

1. next dev
2. hard reload localhost:3000 (loading of header is done as expected)
3. hard reload localhost:3000/a
4. loading of header is skipped and entier page results in being sync 

If a loading.tsx is added to the root of a parallel route it only uses that suspense boundary on the root level.

Give this tree

```
/ (root)
    @header
        page.tsx
        default.tsx
        loading.tsx
    /a
        page.tsx
        loading.tsx
    /b
        page.tsx
        loading.tsx
```

-   navigating to `/` will use the loading.tsx if `@header/page.tsx` is async
-   navigating to `/a`directly would not use the loading.tsx for `@header` and prevent streaming from happening

The only solution I've found for this is to manually add a Suspense boundary to `default.tsx`

```tsx
// @header/default.tsx
import HeaderSlot from "./page";
import { Suspense } from "react";
import Loading from "./loading";

export default function DefaultSlot() {
    return (
        <Suspense fallback={<Loading />}>
            <HeaderSlot />
        </Suspense>
    );
}
```

docs.title: Middleware rewrites are network-proxied when using `next start -H 127.0.0.1`, causing EPROTO 500 behind TLS-terminating proxies
docs.body:
https://github.com/Vorshim92/next-loopback-rewrite-repro
 

1. `npm install && npm run build`
2. Start with an explicit loopback hostname: `npm start -- -H 127.0.0.1 -p 3000`
3. Simulate a TLS-terminating reverse proxy (nginx): `curl -i -H 'X-Forwarded-Proto: https' http://127.0.0.1:3000/a`

The app contains a minimal proxy (middleware) that rewrites `/a` → `/b`, the way i18n routing libraries (next-intl, next-i18n-router) rewrite localized pathnames:

```ts
export default function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
  if (request.nextUrl.pathname === "/a") {
    return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL("/b", request.url));
  }
}
```
 

**Current:** the request fails with **500** and the server logs:

```
Failed to proxy https://localhost:3000/b Error: write EPROTO ... SSL routines:tls_validate_record_header:wrong version number
```

The rewrite is treated as an *external* rewrite and proxied over the network back to the server itself — with the `https` scheme inherited from `x-forwarded-proto` — against the plain-HTTP port, so the TLS handshake fails.

Related observations:

- With `-H 127.0.0.1` but **without** `x-forwarded-proto: https`, the rewrite is still silently network-proxied back to the server (an extra internal HTTP hop on every rewritten request); it just happens to succeed. docs.title: `next start`: client abort during a cold image transform permanently hangs that `/_next/image` URL for all future requests (coalesced generator never settles)
docs.body:
https://github.com/wine-hound/next-image-optimizer-abort-hang
 

The linked repository is a single blank page + `repro.sh`; `npm install && npm run build && ./repro.sh` reproduces end-to-end. Manually:

1. `next build && next start` with a large source image in `public/` (a ~12 MB JPEG makes the timing window easy to hit locally; we originally hit it with a 484 KB JPEG on a slow 2-core CI runner).
2. Abort a **cold** (not yet disk-cached) transform request mid-flight:
   ```bash
   curl -m 0.02 'http://localhost:3000/_next/image?url=%2Fbig.jpg&w=640&q=75'
   ```
3. Request the **same URL** again with a generous timeout:
   ```bash
   curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} in %{time_total}s\n' -m 15 \
     'http://localhost:3000/_next/image?url=%2Fbig.jpg&w=640&q=75'
   ```

Output of the reproduction script (`next@16.3.0-canary.107`):

```
--- step 1: abort cold transform mid-flight: curl -m 0.02 …&w=640&q=75 ---
    curl exit: 28 (28 = client aborted, expected)
--- step 2: re-request the same URL with a 15 s timeout ---
    000 in 15.006627s
    curl exit: 28 (28 = HANG reproduced)
--- step 3: control, same image at w=828 ---
    200 in 0.268416s
    curl exit: 0 (0 = fine)
--- server.log (note: no error, no warning, nothing) ---
    ▲ Next.js 16.3.0-canary.107
    ✓ Ready in 115ms
--- step 4: restart next start, probe the poisoned URL again ---
    after restart: 200 in 0.166564s

queries.body:

**Area:** Agents window, chat input status pills (`ChatInputPills`)

### Steps

1. Open the Agents window (`--agents`) and start a Copilot CLI session.
2. Send a prompt whose response streams markdown and code blocks for a few seconds.
3. Measure layout reads during the stream with a probe that wraps `clientWidth`/`scrollWidth`/`getBoundingClientRect` and attributes the calls to the caller stack. I used a mock CAPI endpoint, so the run is reproducible.

| 2 | 329 | 49 | 62.7 ms |

queries.title: Copilot CLI session: Undo on an agent edit fails with "The agent host doesn't support this"
queries.body:
### Description

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open a folder in VS Code 1.145.2 on Windows 11.
2. Start a Copilot chat session that runs through the Agent Host with the Copilot CLI provider (`copilotcli`).
3. Ask the agent to edit a Markdown file in a second workspace folder.
   In my case: a one-line wording change in `images/benchmark-ffmpeg/docs/usage.md`.
4. In the edit review UI, click **Undo** on the agent's change.

### Expected

The agent's change is reverted and any other uncommitted edits to the file stay in place, as with Undo in a local agent session.

### Actual

A notification shows:

> Could not undo the changes to 'usage.md': The agent host doesn't support this.

The file is unchanged.
It happens every time, including for a fresh single-line test edit.
**Keep** works on the same files in the same session.

### Notes from the logs

queries.title: Pass a conversation/session id to LanguageModelChatProvider.provideLanguageModelChatResponse
queries.body:
**Problem**

Extensions that contribute models via `LanguageModelChatProvider` (the `chatProvider` proposal) can't tell which chat a request belongs to. `ProvideLanguageModelChatResponseOptions` carries `requestInitiator`, `modelConfiguration`, `modelOptions`, `toolMode` and `includeEncryptedThinking`, and nothing that identifies the conversation.

Copilot's own Auto mode does get one. `IAutoModeRoutingRequest` in `extensions/copilot/src/platform/endpoint/node/automodeService.ts` takes `sessionId` / `sessionResource` and keeps a per-conversation routing cache. Its doc comment notes that the `vscode.lm` provider path has no `ChatRequest` to supply them.

**Why it matters**

A provider that routes between its own models (for example by cost tier or task difficulty) can't keep per-chat state. It can't remember that a chat needed a stronger model, can't apply the user's tier choice consistently within one chat, and can't avoid leaking state between chats. The only workaround is recomputing everything from the message history on each call, which loses signals and any prompt-cache affinity.

**Request**

Add a stable, opaque conversation/session identifier (and ideally a request id) to `ProvideLanguageModelChatResponseOptions`, scoped to the chat the request came from.

**Context**

Related to the demand for configurable routing in #345596, but this is about third-party providers, no

queries.body:
A save of a chat session that runs after the session's model has been disposed writes the session out with no requests. The index entry is flagged `isEmpty: true` and the session disappears from the list. I think this is the cause of #321290, which has the same symptoms, so I've put the code path below.

Environment: VS Code 1.142.0 (6d62b1d5), Copilot Chat 0.70.0, Remote-SSH from Windows to a Linux host. I lose a few sessions a day this way, usually ones with a long agent turn running in the background, and on 2 November three went in half an hour with no reconnect or reload.

The session file is replaced by a single line whose `requests` is `[]`. The index entry looks like this:

```json
{
  "title": "Deliver v1.3.0 issues - Pool",
  "lastMessageDate": 1793238296620,
  "timing": { "created": 1793238296620 },
  "isEmpty": true,

}

That's what `getSessionMetadataSync` produces for a live `ChatModel` whose `_requests` is empty, so the index was written from a model in memory rather than from the file. The Copilot transcript of the same session still has every turn.

queries.title: Source Control Graph: add an automatic current-branch-only mode
queries.body:
Type: Feature Request

With the Source Control Graph filter set to Auto, newer commits from the base branch can appear above the checked-out branch's latest commit. This makes it look as though the wrong branch is selected or the current branch's commits are missing.

In the case investigated, the checked-out branch's latest commit appeared 20th, below 19 commits included from origin/master. Git and VS Code both correctly recognized the checked-out branch.

Please provide a persistent "Follow current branch only" option that:
- Automatically follows the checked-out branch when switching branches.
- Shows commits reachable from that branch, including its ancestors.
- Excludes commits from the base branch that are not reachable from the checked-out branch.

Selecting a specific branch manually narrows the graph, but does not provide the same automatic following behavior. A clearer explanation that Auto includes the base branch would also help prevent confusion.

The requested behavior should retain shared ancestral history; the concern is the additional base-branch commits outside the checked-out branch's history.

queries.title: Let dictation reach chat inputs contributed by extensions (webviews), including over Remote Tunnels
queries.body:
## The Gap

Built-in dictation and the VS Code Speech extension write only into inputs the workbench owns. Those are the Chat view, editors and similar rich inputs, and the terminal. A chat panel an extension contributes as a webview gets nothing. Two widely used examples are the Claude Code extension (anthropic.claude-code) and the Codex extension (openai.chatgpt). With one of those panels focused, the microphone button, `Ctrl+I` and `Ctrl+Alt+V` do nothing for it.

This matters most over a Remote Tunnel or SSH. Dictation runs on the client, which is the one place a microphone exists. So it is the only route that could work there. The vendors cannot close the gap on their side. The Claude Code team has declined to integrate with VS Code's dictation (anthropics/claude-code#43375, closed as not planned). The speech provider API is a proposed API that only ms-vscode.vscode-speech can use, so no other extension can register or consume a session.

## What We Ask For

Either of these would close it:

1. Let the dictation commands target the focused webview input. Deliver the recognised text to the focused element the way terminal dictation does. The workbench would handle the live (partial) text as it does for the Chat view.

2. Finalise a consumer-side speech API. An extension could then request a dictation session on the client and receive `Recognizing` and `Recognized` events to

**Type**: Bug

### What happened

On Windows 11 with a Chinese (zh-CN) system locale, the **"Open with Code"** entry that VS Code registers in the modern File Explorer context menu renders as **garbled text** instead of a readable label.

The affected entry is the one registered by the MSIX sparse package `Microsoft.VisualStudioCode_*_neutral__8wekyb3d8bbwe`, CLSID `{1C6DF0C0-192A-4451-BE36-6A59A86A692E}`, implemented by `code_explorer_command_x64.dll`.

- `□2□2胯赊芾敕□2毒畾ξ`

### What did you expect

The entry should read `通过 Code 打开` (the value stored in the registry), or fall back to `Open with Code`.

1. Windows 11 (22621), system locale zh-CN, system ANSI code page 936

3. Right-click any file in File Explorer
4. Look at the VS Code entry in the Windows 11 modern context menu

queries.title: tasks.json: Add "group": "run" option for task, like the existing "build" and "test"
queries.body:
## Problem

The most common development loop `edit / build / run` is only partially modeled in `tasks.json`: build and test have a role, run does not.

Build and test can be declared as: `"group": { "kind": "build" | "test", "isDefault": true }`, and come with dedicated commands:

- `Tasks: Configure Default Build Task`
- `Tasks: Run Build Task`
- `Tasks: Configure Default Test Task`
- `Tasks: Run Test Task`

Running the program has no equivalent. A project can't cleanly declare "this is how you run it", so there is no default Run action - only picking a task by name from `Tasks: Run Task`, or a debug configuration. 

The `Run and Debug` view and the editor-title Run button belong to debug adapters, and `Debug: Start Without Debugging` still starts a debug session (with `noDebug`).

This is most painful for small projects where the run step is just a command after a build, and maintaining `launch.json` only to start a binary is overhead.

## Proposal

1. A new `run` group kind, behaving like `test` and `build`, including glob-valued `isDefault`:

```jsonc
   {
     "label": "run app",
     "type": "process",
     "command": "${workspaceFolder}/build/app",
     "dependsOn": "build",
     "group": { "kind": "run", "isDefault": true }
   }
```

2. Add commands mirroring the test and build groups:

- `Tasks: Configure Default Run Task`
- `Tasks: Run Default Run Task`

## Prior art

queries.title: Agent Host high CPU on macOS with repeated catalog reconciliation retries (sourceUnresolvable)
queries.body:
Type: Performance Issue

## Summary

My laptop becomes unusually hot while VS Code is running. Process sampling identified VS Code's built-in `agent-host` as the largest individual CPU consumer. Its log also contains a large number of repeated catalog reconciliation retries.

The retry activity and CPU load were observed during the same period, but I have not established that the retries cause the CPU usage.

## Environment

- VS Code: 1.141.0 (stable)
- Commit: 2a59476c9bfcb90b3ddc372c36762471b7dfad1c
- Build date: 2026-10-06
- macOS: Darwin arm64 27.0.0
- Hardware: Apple M4 Pro, 14 CPU cores, 24 GB RAM
- Bundled GitHub.copilot-chat: 0.69.0

## Observed CPU usage

On October 9, 2026, `code --status` identified PID 67571 as `agent-host`, with a `copilot-runtime --headless` child.

Repeated `top` samples showed:

| Process | CPU |
| --- | ---: |

queries.title: API Proposal: Support Custom Native Floating Modal Dialogs for Complex Data Workflows
queries.body:
### Problem Statement & Use Case
We are migrating complex developer tooling from Eclipse RCP to VS Code extensions. We have encountered a major layout and workflow blocker regarding advanced user input and data validation.

In Eclipse RCP, the `Dialog` architecture allows launching modal frames to handle heavy data orchestration (e.g., database schema mapping, multi-row environment setups, and complex multi-field forms) without breaking the user's active editor split layouts.

Currently, VS Code offers no viable alternative for dense, non-linear data collection:
* `showInformationMessage(..., { modal: true })`: Highly restrictive. It only displays static strings and buttons; it cannot collect complex user input.
* `showQuickPick` / Multi-step InputBox: Built for linear selection. It completely fails when workflows require structural matrices, multi-column tables, cross-field validation, or complex form controls.
* `WebviewPanel` (Editor Tabs): Opening a full-sized tab for a transient 10-second task disorients the user's layout, breaks active editor splits, and introduces a messy tab lifecycle management overhead.

queries.title: Explorer: add "Collapse All" and "Expand All" to the folder context menu
queries.body:
## Problem

In the Explorer, the only way to collapse folders is the "Collapse Folders in Explorer" button in the view title bar, which collapses the entire tree. There is no way to collapse or expand just one folder together with all of its subfolders. In large projects this means:

- Collapsing one deeply nested folder requires clicking each subfolder individually, or collapsing the whole tree and losing my place.
- Expanding a folder's full structure at once is not possible without expanding each level by hand.

## Proposal

Add two items to the Explorer context menu when right-clicking a folder:

- **Collapse All**: collapses the selected folder and all of its descendant folders.
- **Expand All**: expands the selected folder and all of its descendant folders.

Behavior details:

- The actions apply only to the selected folder's subtree. The rest of the tree is untouched.
- They appear only on folders, not on files.
- Expand All should be safe on very large trees (for example `node_modules`). I'd suggest it respects `files.exclude` and `explorer.excludeGitIgnore`, and I'm open to guidance on whether a depth or item limit is needed.
- Both would be registered as commands so they can be bound to keyboard shortcuts and used from the Command Palette.

## Alternatives considered

- The existing "Collapse Folders in Explorer" title-bar button only works on the whole tree.
- Keyboa

queries.title: Inconsistent behavior of `usePathname` with static rendering during build
queries.body:
https://github.com/amannn/nextjs-bug-repro-usepathnamessg/commit/c6b084df43e08a9b043548fb577be8db5f059bde 

Compare the output of `usePathname` in development vs during the static prerender when accessing the route `/test` which uses a rewrite in the middleware. 

`usePathname` seems to pick up a request-time pathname from a middleware rewrite. However, as this information is not available during a static build, `usePathname` will return a different value in this case. Then again, when running the app in production, `usePathname` will return the pathname that's displayed in the browser (i.e. after a rewrite), but only on the client side.

In the reproduction this leads to a text content mismatch, but more generally this breaks a dev/prod guarantee. I'd expect a static prerender to only be a performance optimization and not to change application logic.

I guess some unification would be necessary here.

Note that this only applies for static prerendering, if you use SSR in production then the behavior is the same as in dev.

A more real world use case where this behavior was encountered: https://github.com/amannn/next-intl/issues/1568
